title: Barclays is latest to redirect spending toward AI as it trims its workforce
summary: The cost of building out the infrastructure needed to satisfy booming demand for artificial intelligence is changing the way major companies allocate resources
story: The cost of building out the infrastructure needed to satisfy booming demand for artificial intelligence is changing the way major companies allocate resources

The cost of building out the infrastructure needed to satisfy booming demand for artificial intelligence is changing the way major companies allocate resources. That can mean an end to some jobs once done by humans. Yet in many cases it means repurposing money once spent on workers so that more capital can be devoted to boosting AI capabilities. Just how much money is being spent on AI is a hot topic as fears of a bubble in the sector grow, but the potential impact on workers in some sectors is clear.
Here's a look at some of the companies that have announced layoffs or hiring reductions this year that are tied in some way to massive spending on AI.
The U.K. bank and financial services company revealed in a quarterly financial report this week that it is looking to cut 5,000 jobs, or about 5% of its workforce.
The company said that it was seeking “organisational simplification and technology change efficiency driven by AI.” Approximately 60% of the cuts will be from support functions, including developers.

Financial institutions are among the most active in deploying AI, in many cases at the expense of workers. Norway's DNB and Commerzbank in Germany have also announced job cuts in parallel with a push into AI.
Kroger said last week that it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over the next three years as the national grocery chain ramps up its use of artificial intelligence.

“Technology is reshaping what’s possible,” CEO Greg Foran wrote in a memo to employees. “The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work and look closely at where work is best fit to be done.”
Kroger last month outlined its AI strategy, meant “to improve the customer experience, make work easier for associates and produce better business outcomes.”

The Cincinnati company is the largest standalone U.S. supermarket chain with 409,000 employees and more than 2,700 stores operating under various brands, including Ralphs, King Soopers, Smith’s and Fred Meyer.

The company that runs Facebook and Instagram said it would lay off about 8,000 workers, or about 10% of its workforce, as it continues to ramp up spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure and highly paid AI-expert hires.

The company said in April that it was making the cuts for the sake of efficiency and to allow new investments in parts of its business, as first reported by Bloomberg, which also said the company will leave about 6,000 jobs unfilled.

Meta had already warned investors that its 2026 expenses will grow significantly — to as much as $169 billion — driven by infrastructure costs and employee compensation, particularly for the artificial intelligence experts it’s been hiring.
Software giant Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to thousands of its U.S. employees.

The company planned to make the offers in early May to about 8,750 people, or 7% of its U.S. workforce, according to two people familiar with the plan who were not authorized to speak about it publicly.

Microsoft has spent billions of dollars operating an ever-expanding global network of data centers powering cloud computing services, AI systems and its own suite of productivity tools, including the AI assistant Copilot.
The U.K.-based bank is planning to cut more than 15% of its back office employees by 2030.

Standard Chartered said in May that it was “scaling practical uses of automation, advanced analytics and artificial intelligence to streamline processes, improve decision‑making and enhance both client service and internal efficiency.”
The cryptocurrency trading platform is cutting approximately 14% of its workforce partly due to AI.
In a blog post, CEO Brian Armstrong said that AI was changing the way that Coinbase worked.

“Over the past year, I’ve watched engineers use AI to ship in days what used to take a team weeks,” he wrote. “Non-technical teams are now shipping production code and many of our workflows are being automated. The pace of what’s possible with a small, focused team has changed dramatically, and it’s accelerating every day.”
Armstrong said that the company needed to take action.
“We are adjusting early and deliberately to rebuild Coinbase to be lean, fast, and AI-native,” he wrote.

Pinterest announced in January that it planned to lay off under 15% of its workforce as part of a broader restructuring as the image-sharing platform pivots more of its money to artificial intelligence.

In a securities filing, the company said that it was making the cuts to support “transformation initiatives” — which include reallocating resources to AI-focused roles and prioritizing AI-powered products. It said it was also working to reshape its “sales and go-to-market approach.”
The owner of social media platform Snapchat is eliminating about 16% of its global workforce, or about 1,000 jobs.

“The headcount reduction is designed to further streamline our operations and reallocate resources toward our highest-priority initiatives, leveraging increased operational efficiencies to accelerate our path toward net-income profitability,” the company said in a regulatory filing.
CEO Evan Spiegel said in a letter to staff in April that another 300 open roles would not be filled.
Financial technology company Block is laying off more than 4,000 of its 10,000 plus employees, reconfiguring to capitalize on its use of artificial intelligence.

“The core thesis is simple. Intelligence tools have changed what it means to build and run a company,” Jack Dorsey said in a letter to shareholders in Block, the parent company to online payment platforms such as Square and Cash App. “A significantly smaller team, using the tools we’re building, can do more and do it better,” he said.
Dorsey’s comments explicitly naming AI as a key driver behind the decision were also posted on X, or Twitter, a company he co-founded.
The announcement has sent shares of the company sharply higher this year, up 19%, reversing a 12% decline in the previous year.

title: Wall Street mostly loses ground under pressure from rising oil prices
summary: Stocks are mostly slipping on Wall Street under increasing pressure from rising oil prices
story: Stocks are mostly slipping on Wall Street under increasing pressure from rising oil prices
NEW YORK -- Stocks slipped on Wall Street Friday under increasing pressure from rising oil prices.

The S&P 500 fell 0.3%, adding to its decline from a day before. The index is on track for a second-straight week of losses. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 541 points, or 1%, as of 12:33 p.m. Eastern time.
The Nasdaq composite rose 0.1%, bolstered by gains for several big tech stocks that also helped ease losses elsewhere.

Rising oil prices weighed heavily on the market, where three out of every four stocks within the benchmark S&P 500 index fell. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 3.6% to $117.20. It has surged from less than $97 at the start of October and is now at its highest level since March.

Several AI-related companies made big moves. Micron Technology jumped 3.6% and Microsoft rose 0.8% and helped ease the impact on major indexes from a drop for most stocks. Advanced Micro Devices jumped 2.3%.

The tech sector's influence is also capable of quickly switching over to a heavy weight. Stocks that have benefited from the frenzy over AI have been swinging over rising worries about their path ahead. Investors are worried about whether their high prices are justified. Many of those companies have been borrowing to fund investments in AI technology and high interest rates are making those loans more expensive.

“Investors appear increasingly focused on the economics of AI, particularly the substantial upfront costs required to build AI infrastructure and the uncertainty around the timing of returns on those investments,” said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones, in a research note.

The latest round of corporate earnings are being closely watched to help get a better sense of whether those investments are paying off, or might pay off. Several influential AI-related companies report their latest financial results next week, including Google's parent, Alphabet, along with Microsoft and Amazon.
Industrial companies had some of the biggest losses. Caterpillar slumped 2.2%.

American Express slumped 3.6% and joined a drop for other financial companies, despite r eporting profits for its most recent quarter that beat analysts' forecasts. The company did announce its first major job cuts in roughly a decade.
Rising oil prices that weighed down much of the market helped boost energy companies. Chevron rose 2.9% and ConocoPhillips rose 4.6%.
European markets were lower. France’s main index fell 0.4%, though yields on French government bonds eased a bit.
Treasury yields in the U.S. edged higher following sharp drops on Thursday. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.99% from 4.96% late Thursday.

Yields have been rising globally, partly over worries about governments taking on too much debt. Inflation also remains a concern and is stubbornly well above 3% in the U.S. That prompted the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate at its last meeting in an effort to cool inflation.
Wall Street expects the central bank to hold rates steady at its meeting next week, but is leaning heavily toward another rate hike in December.

Wall Street will also get several big economic updates next week, including the Fed's preferred measure of inflation. The personal consumption expenditures index, or PCE, is expected to show that inflation rose at a 3.6% rate in September, sharply above the Fed's 2% target.
The U.S. war with Iran has severely cut the world's oil supply, driving energy prices higher and fueling a sharp jump in the cost of everything from gasoline to food and clothes.

title: Kathy Behrens, who developed NBA Cares, plans to leave the league office after a 26-year run
summary: Kathy Behrens, one of the highest-ranking female executives in the NBA, has decided to leave her position after 26 years
story: Kathy Behrens, one of the highest-ranking female executives in the NBA, has decided to leave her position after 26 years

Kathy Behrens started her high school basketball career at a time when her home state of New York had yet to even start a championship for girls. She played in college, long before the women’s game had the immense following it does now. And the WNBA had not even been dreamed of in those days.
Basketball became her life's work anyway.

Behrens — who became one of the highest-ranking women in the NBA office, holding her current title of President of Social Responsibility and Player Programs since 2015 — has decided to leave the league office after 26 years. Colleagues were informed on Tuesday, and she intends to depart at the end of the year.

“Last year I celebrated my 25th year at the NBA and my kids went off to college and I’ve spent the last year thinking about how it’s such a hard place to leave because it’s been just an incredible experience,” Behrens said in an interview with The Associated Press. “And the work is great and so meaningful. I love the people that I work with. But I had just started to think that it’s time to do some other things. It’s that time.”

Among her best-known accomplishments: She developed the wildly successful NBA Cares program, which has long been a top priority for the league in terms of community outreach, as well as oversaw the creations of the NBA Foundation and the National Basketball Social Justice Coalition during the pandemic.
Commissioner Adam Silver lauded Behrens on Tuesday for what he called “an extraordinary NBA career.”

“Kathy has supported generations of players in navigating the demands of their careers, developing interests beyond basketball and preparing for life after the game,” Silver said in a memo distributed to staff, a copy of which was obtained by the AP. “Throughout her career, Kathy has been a trusted colleague and friend and a passionate advocate for basketball’s ability to improve lives, and I am deeply grateful for everything Kathy has done for our leagues.”
In college, Behrens studied education but developed a fascination with politics and was president of Hartford’s student government. She figured that would be her career path.

After graduating, she worked for the United Way in New York as a fundraiser, then got asked to join Gov. Mario Cuomo’s administration. She worked for Cuomo for more than six years, and when he lost a bid for what would have been a fourth term in 1994 Behrens found herself looking for a new challenge.

She became executive director of a nonprofit program called New York Cares. In 1998, that organization worked with the NBA on events related to that year’s All-Star Game in New York. And a couple of years later, Behrens was asked to join the league office — which is when she started getting to know then-Commissioner David Stern.

“To me, David was sort of like the Mario Cuomo of the sports world,” Behrens said. “My final interview was with David, Adam and (then-deputy commissioner) Russ Granik. I thought I’d died and gone to heaven. I have always remained so grateful for the privilege to work around the game, to be connected to the game and contribute to the success and the growth that we’ve had.”

The name “NBA Cares” is a nod to New York Cares. Stern pushed for the name, and Behrens initially felt like it was too close to the name of her past employer. But in time, she, Stern and Silver realized it was the perfect moniker. The program officially launched in 2005, has seen NBA personnel give more than 6.5 million hours of their time to various causes and has generated hundreds of millions of dollars to groups that needed the support.
“It made sense and it clicked,” Behrens said. “We launched it and the enduring legacy of that is something I’m incredibly proud of.”

The decision to step away, she insists, was not easy. For a quarter-century or so now, Behrens has had a little tradition of standing with Dan Rube, one of the league’s executive vice presidents and general counsel, at an NBA Finals game. They always say the same thing, reminding each other to never take being part of the NBA for granted.
“It was a gift and it makes it hard to leave,” Behrens said. “But it’s time to give the gift to other people.”

title: LIV Golf's future and the ripple effect for PGA and European tours provide plenty of drama
summary: The suspense around LIV Golf is greater in court than it ever was on the golf course
story: The suspense around LIV Golf is greater in court than it ever was on the golf course

LIV Golf didn't generate this much suspense at tournaments when the music was blaring, the Saudi cash was flowing freely and players from the Cleeks and Majestics headed off in carts for the shotgun start.
Every day, there's more speculation. Who's leaving? Who's staying? Weren't these the same questions four years ago?

It was May 31, 2022, when a group of golf writers out to dinner in Ohio received emails announcing the field for the inaugural LIV Golf event — Dustin Johnson and 12 other PGA Tour members — and had to leave before the creme brulee arrived.
And now another waiting game, not for the launch but whether LIV survives.

LIV Golf is working through Chapter 11 bankruptcy with a pledge of $300 million from BC Partners Credit, a far cry from the $5 billion the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia dropped in four years before abruptly pulling the plug.

Key to the “LIV 2.0” version — at least 10 tournaments, player equity and prize money half of what it used to be — is getting a “critical mass” of players to buy into the plan. How many players comprise a critical mass is unclear. And while LIV officials don't plan to announce each decision piecemeal, players are doing that for them.

Jon Rahm and Sergio Garcia have court-approved separations from LIV and are free to go. Louis Oosthuizen, Ian Poulter, Tom McKibbin and Adrian Meronk have said they are leaving. Graeme McDowell added his name to the list Monday with a succinct message on social media.

Adding a wrinkle to the immediate future of LIV was a report by The Athletic that Johnson was among more than 10 players seeking severance deals from PIF worth more than $100 million in contract payments. Johnson's attorney suggested a deal was tied to players sticking with LIV 2.0.
“The decision to release potential claims against the PIF and join LIV 2.0 will be influenced largely by how the PIF manages the windup of LIV 1.0," David Cornwell told The Athletic.

An amended restructuring agreement approved by the New Jersey bankruptcy court indicates LIV no longer has a hard deadline for players to decide. The hope was to have a decision by the end of the month. LIV remains bullish about a 2027 season.
That won't be the end of the drama, however, and it would seem the golf landscape is still a long way off from being stitched back together, if it ever can be.

The PGA Tour has yet to say whether defectors — currently banned for one year from the date of their last LIV appearance — have a place. It's not a high priority as the tour seeks to fill out its lucrative “Championship Series” schedule in 2028 and find sponsors for the second tier.
The European tour, meanwhile, delivered a strong ultimatum when CEO Guy Kinnings said anyone staying with LIV need not apply for membership for the commercially known DP World Tour.

That made it an easy choice for Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton — particularly with Ryder Cup strings attached — and for youngsters Tom McKibbin and David Puig. They have status based on performance. That doesn't mean it sits well with those who stayed.

“Four years ago, they didn't give a (crap) about the DP World Tour,” Joost Luiten told Today's Golfer. “They made a decision to go after the money. And now all of a sudden, the money is gone and they want to come back and act like nothing happened. I don’t think that’s right.”
There's also the matter of sponsor exemptions for those who don't have status, or even those who never gave much thought to the European tour because they didn't need it. Now they do.
European tour officials are not in position to turn their back on a chance to strengthen fields.

“Given the high volume of inbound interest and enquiries we have received in recent weeks, we are exploring the terms on which we are willing to accommodate players provided they are free from third party contractual restrictions and are willing to abide by our membership regulations,” a European tour spokesman said.

It's possible such players are allowed only a set number of exemptions. And because the exemptions are for stock events — think Magical Kenya Open and the Soudal Open in Belgium — it might not be a case of squeezing out a more worthy player.
But then it's a matter of whether loyalty means more than name recognition.

Eddie Pepperell, among the most thoughtful players, missed the cut last week in South Korea and wound up one spot out of a full European tour card for 2027. He wrote in his “The Chipping Forecast” post that outside of players whom people pay to watch, send everyone else to Q-school.
But potentially losing a spot in the field to a player no longer interested in LIV because it no longer offers $20 million purses with no cuts?

“As someone who has gone through the wringer this game provides (mostly due to my own shortcomings of course) in recent years, and who has gone back to Q School and had two immensely divergent experiences, betrayal feels like the right word,” Pepperell wrote. “And unfortunately when one feels that way inevitably what follows is a loss of respect, and what tends to fill the void left behind is resentment and contempt.”
No matter what happens to LIV, one suspects it won't make the healing process any easier.

title: French soccer league moves games from Saturday amid public protests on streets
summary: The French soccer league is moving scheduled games from Saturday at the request of public authorities amid weekend protests across the country
story: The French soccer league is moving scheduled games from Saturday at the request of public authorities amid weekend protests across the country
PARIS -- The French soccer league is moving scheduled games from Saturday at the request of public authorities amid weekend protests across the country.

Lyon’s home game against Angers in Ligue 1 will now be played on Sunday afternoon instead of 8:45 p.m. local time on Saturday, the Professional Football League (LFP) said Tuesday in a statement citing a request from local government officials.
Ligue 1 games to be hosted Saturday by Nice and Lorient have also been changed to, respectively, Friday evening and Monday evening, the league said.
Hundreds of thousands of people took part in marches across France last Saturday to protest rising living costs and poor conditions in schools, adding to demands on police and security forces.
France’s worst civil unrest for years has seen city halls and public buildings attacked.

title: Naomi Osaka advances to 2nd round in front of home fans in Tokyo
summary: Naomi Osaka has defeated Italy’s Jasmine Paolini in front of her home fans at the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo
story: Naomi Osaka has defeated Italy’s Jasmine Paolini in front of her home fans at the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo

TOKYO -- Naomi Osaka defeated Italy’s Jasmine Paolini in front of her home fans at the Pan Pacific Open on Tuesday, winning 6-3, 7-6 (4) to advance to the second round of the WTA 500-level event in Tokyo.
The victory for Osaka — seeded No. 7 — avenges her loss to Paolini last year in the Miami Open, their only previous meeting.
The 29-year-old Osaka racked up seven aces to only one for Paolini in a match that lasted 1 hour and 37 minutes.
The four-time Grand Slam champion is playing some of her best tennis since returning after giving birth three years ago to her daughter, Shai.
But Osaka said this week that she would step away from the game if Shai asked her to.
Elena Rybakina is seeded No. 1 — she is also the WTA's top-ranked player — and had a bye in the first round.
Two top players have pulled out with injuries: No. 2 Maja Chawlinska and No. 4 Belinda Bencic.

title: Venus Williams 0-13 in singles this year after losing to rival 28 years younger at Guangzhou Open
summary: Tennis great Venus Williams has fallen to 0-13 in singles matches this year at age 46
story: Tennis great Venus Williams has fallen to 0-13 in singles matches this year at age 46
GUANGZHOU, China -- Tennis great Venus Williams fell to 0-13 in singles matches this year at age 46 after losing 6-2, 6-2 to teenager Lilli Tagger in the Guangzhou Open first round on Tuesday.
Their 28-year age gap was reportedly a record difference between opponents in a WTA Tour match.
The 18-year-old Austrian Tagger was born in 2008, the year Williams won the last of her seven Grand Slam singles titles at Wimbledon.
Now ranked No. 599, Williams was playing her first singles match for two months since the U.S. Open, where she lost in the first round to Sofia Kenin.
Williams now has lost 16 straight singles matches on tour going back to July last year.
She matched the 53rd-ranked Tagger with each landing 63% of their first serves, though Williams won just 60% of those points and her opponent won all of hers.
Williams created no break-point chances and Tagger took four of the 16 she had.
Kenin also lost her round of 32 match, beaten 6-4, 6-7 (5), 6-4 by Kaitlin Quevedo.

title: Ahead of Rome tipoff, basketball powerhouse Villanova embraces 'Pope Leo effect'
summary: Villanova University is deepening its ties to the Vatican, thanks to its famous alumnus, Pope Leo
story: Villanova University is deepening its ties to the Vatican, thanks to its famous alumnus, Pope Leo

VILLANOVA, Pa. -- At Villanova University, all roads — or at least many of them — seem to lead to Rome, thanks to famed alumnus Pope Leo XIV and the school's growing ties to the Vatican. Even its vaunted basketball program is getting in on the act.
“We certainly have a bigger footprint there now than we used to,” said the Rev. Peter Donohue, Villanova’s president. “People do know who we are, just because it’s the pope’s school.”

The pope graduated from Villanova with a degree in mathematics in 1977. He belongs to the Augustinians, the religious order that founded the university near Philadelphia in 1842. Now his alma mater is finding new and inventive connections to his papacy.

On Sunday, the men's and women's basketball teams from Villanova will open the season in Rome with a Catholic university matchup, playing Notre Dame 6 miles (9.6 kilometers) from the Vatican in what organizers are calling the Eternal City Tip-Off. The doubleheader comes only weeks after Villanova hosted a sustainability conference in Rome and awarded a cardinal with the inaugural Pope Leo XIV Sustainability Medal.
“It’s crazy,” Donohue said. “We’re taking over Rome.”
Villanova saw applications jump more than 10% during the first admissions cycle after the pope’s 2025 election.
“We claimed it was ‘the Pope Leo effect,’” Donohue said.
Villanova is the only American university that can claim a pope as a graduate — a distinction that has elevated its profile alongside a run of athletic success.
The school won the NCAA men's basketball championship in 1985, 2016 and 2018. Three alums dubbed the 'Nova Knicks were instrumental in the New York Knicks winning the NBA title this year.
Over Halloween weekend, the power of Catholic school basketball will be in full effect as 6,000 Villanova fans and 1,000 Notre Dame fans travel to watch their teams compete.
“The voice of the people of God will be very strong on the Villanova side,” Leo said in September.

The festivities were planned long before Leo’s recent cancer diagnosis and surgery. The sports-loving pope is scheduled — health permitting — to hold a private audience inside the Vatican on Saturday for the teams and their traveling fans. Philadelphia Archbishop Nelson Perez will also celebrate a private Mass for them in St. Peter’s Basilica.

Ed Hastings, who played on Villanova’s 1971 basketball team that lost the national championship to UCLA and now teaches at Villanova, will appear on a sold-out panel in Rome. He will be discussing sports and spirituality, bringing together “the passions of my life,” he said.
St. Augustine, who inspired the Augustinian religious order, wrote about self-knowledge. “And I learned a lot about myself through sports,” Hastings said.
The Rev. Bernie Scianna, Villanova's vice president for mission and ministry, is a friend of the pope, having met him almost three decades ago through their Augustinian order.

Scianna has seen an uptick in interest in Catholicism at the school, which has around 10,000 students and a large Catholic population. Last year, 24 people joined the Catholic Church on campus, most of them students, though fewer than 10 typically do each year. There are 56 people in the current class of potential new members.
“It’s really a great feeling for us to be in this moment,” he said.
Villanova has long sent students to Italy and the Vatican for internships and study abroad programs, but those opportunities are growing.

Senior Mike Whaley just returned from a fall break trip there with his humanities class. He had visited the Vatican on a previous student trip, where he was an altar server at a private Mass for Villanova students celebrated by then-Cardinal Robert Prevost.
“So, my fun fact at parties is that I served Mass for the now Pope Leo XIV,” Whaley said.
Megan Zuzarth, another senior, also was in Rome recently with her business school class.
The pope's connection to Villanova makes him even more relatable once you realize “he probably sat right here or he walked these halls,” Zuzarth said. “He’s one of us.”
Church bells rang at Villanova for hours after Leo’s election.
Cathleen Kershner, now a junior, was wrapping up her final exams. “I get a text from my grandma and she was like, ‘Your pope! He’s your pope!’”
Donohue was at a Chicago restaurant when he heard the Vatican conclave had chosen a new pope.
“It’s Bob!” he screamed. A manager brought out Champagne to celebrate the new pope, who was born and raised in Chicago.
Donohue, a fellow Augustinian, was two years ahead of Pope Leo at Villanova. Before assuming the presidency, he chaired the school’s theater department.
As a child, while “other people were playing basketball and football, I was taking tap dancing classes,” he said.

His background in musical theater has been surprisingly useful as he navigates fundraising and donor relations. “I tell everybody it’s the biggest acting job I’ve ever had,” he said, “and the longest run I’ve ever had.”

Villanova has not been immune to the financial pressures many universities face, but it’s faring better than most. The school has undertaken renovations and expansion projects and recently opened a new campus at a nearby shuttered Catholic college.
The Pope Leo effect certainly has not hurt.
“We’re very proud of him, and very proud that he’s an Augustinian, and very proud that he is leading the church,” Donohue said. “Whatever we can do to help him, we’re trying to do that.”

title: Tiny HB Køge faces mighty Barcelona, City hosts PSG in Women's Champions League
summary: Tiny Danish club HB Køge must find a way to stop Barcelona’s scoring machine when it hosts the defending champion in the Women’s Champions League on Thursday
story: Tiny Danish club HB Køge must find a way to stop Barcelona’s scoring machine when it hosts the defending champion in the Women’s Champions League on Thursday
PARIS -- Tiny Danish club HB Køge must find a way to stop Barcelona's attacking power when it hosts the defending champion in the Women’s Champions League on Thursday.

Køge plays its home games on artificial turf, and its players took confidence from a 5-1 win over Swiss champion Servette. But last-place Servette has already conceded 13 goals in two games in the competition, so facing four-time champion Barcelona is a different level again for Køge in terms of difficulty.

Barca routed eight-time champion OL Lyonnes 4-0 in last year's final for a third European crown in four seasons and is vying for a seventh straight final appearance. Barca has netted 11 goals in two games with free-scoring winger Caroline Graham Hansen leading the competition with three goals. The Norway international also has three assists. Furthermore, the past six women's ballon d'Or  awards have been evenly split by Barca players Aitana Bonmati and Alexia Putellas, who won it for the third time on Monday.
“Believe in yourself, that's the most important thing,” said Putellas, who played for Barca last season before joining London Lionesses. “If you have a dream, go for it.”
Père Romeu won coach of the year after guiding Barca to a domestic treble as well as the European title.
The coastal town sits on the Bay of Køge some 40 kilometers (25 miles) from Copenhagen, and has a population of around 40,000.

A sea battle took place there against a Swedish fleet in 1710 and in 1807 Danish militia fought British troops led by Arthur Wellesley — later known as the Duke of Wellington. The Battle of Køge went down in folklore as Træskoslaget (the Clogs Battle).
After drawing with Real Madrid in the previous round, Manchester City is hosting Paris Saint-Germain.

City won a domestic league and cup double last season and is chasing a first women's Champions League title. So is PSG, which routed Belgian club OH Leuven 5-0 in the last round, with France forward Naomie Feller scoring twice.

Earlier this month, PSG won 4-2 away to City in a men’s Champions League contest featuring current and former champions. City is fighting a damning verdict into inflated revenue of more than 900 million pounds ($1.19 billion), but the women’s team is not implicated.
A rarity in the competition saw OL Lyonnes held to a scoreless draw by Chelsea three weeks ago.

Coach Jonatan Giráldez's Lyon side hosts Inter Milan on Wednesday. Inter has only scored twice so far and needed a goal from captain Ivana Andres Sanz with seconds left to salvage a draw at Austria Vienna.
Benfica defender Marit Bratberg Lund is aiming for her third goal of the competition when the Portuguese club travels to 2025 champion Arsena l on Wednesday.
Real Madrid has made a sluggish start with two draws and has a challenging match at Bayern Munich, touted as one of the pre-tournament favorites.
After blanking Lyon, 2021 runner-up Chelsea takes on Italian club Roma on Wednesday. Roma's confidence will be low after being crushed 6-0 by Barca and held goalless by Belgian side OH Leuven.
Servette needs a morale-boosting win on Wednesday when it hosts Leuven.
In Thursday's other matches, Paris FC hosts Häcken at Stade Charlety and Juventus goes to Vienna.
The competition has six match days, with the top four teams advancing to the quarterfinals and those finishing between fifth and 12th entering knockout-phase playoffs.

title: Small colleges are starting football programs, hoping to boost enrollment as student shortage looms
summary: Ten small four-year colleges and universities started or re-started football programs this season
story: Ten small four-year colleges and universities started or re-started football programs this season

A bagpiper in a kilt led hundreds of Azusa Pacific University students and the school president into the Cougars' stadium before kickoff against Whittier College earlier this season, a sun-splashed celebration of what once were two of the biggest brands in California small-college football.
Azusa Pacific had dropped the sport in 2020 after 55 years and Whittier in 2022 after 115 years, mainly for financial reasons.

The two are back on the field, not in a full re-embrace of the sport's tradition and what it can do to enhance campus culture, but for another reason: Administrators saw an opportunity to bump shrinking enrollment numbers, a problem shadowing hundreds of colleges and universities across the country. Football rosters, after all, can number about 100 players and the sport is seen as a popular marketing anchor.

The two schools are among 10 four-year colleges and universities that started or re-started programs this season, the most in a single year since 2013, according to the National Football Foundation. Seven schools have announced plans to start programs in 2027 or later.

Azusa Pacific won the 1998 NAIA Division I championship and became a full NCAA Division II member in 2013. The Cougars made playoff appearances in 2016 and ’18, but a decline in the number of West Coast Division II football schools made travel too costly.

School president Adam Morris said he first approached athletic director Gary Pine about re-starting football five years ago. A $1 million private gift funded start-up costs, and the school moved from Division II to Division III and joined a Southern California-based conference. APU also will begin competition in women’s flag football in the spring.

“Yes, it’s an opportunity to grow enrollment and there is some financial upside to the decision,” Morris said. “Really, it’s a great opportunity to touch the lives of 110 young men who will leave this place to go out into this community and have an impact in a significant way.”

APU’s on-campus fall enrollment is 1,900, down 46% from 3,359 in fall 2020. APU brought in 652 freshmen (49 were on the football roster) and transfer students to campus this fall, up 19% from a year ago. The school’s online learning program raises total enrollment to about 6,000.

On the same day Azusa Pacific and Whittier returned to the field, Mount Mercy University in Iowa played its first-ever home game. More than a thousand fans showed up, many tailgating in the parking lots before and after and, in a nod to the Mustangs' NAIA champion men's bowling team, some wore T-shirts reading, "Mount Mercy. A bowling school with football.”
As much as any small college, Mount Mercy has used athletics to drive enrollment, which numbers 1,450 this fall. Some 60-70% of the student body participates in one of 22 sports Mount Mercy offers.

The football team brought about 100 new male students to campus. A local family foundation provided start-up costs, including $2.1 million for a 9,000-square-foot football building that includes a weight room, athletic training space, coaches' offices and meeting rooms. The facility rates among the best in the NAIA.

While administrators describe how a football team can bring a sense of community to a campus and enhance student life, athletic director Paul Gavin acknowledged the underlying motivation was to generate revenue, whether from students who want to play for the Mustangs or from those who want to attend a college that has a team.

“There’s no doubt if football is done right, if you stay within budgets and financial constraints and scholarship limitations, it’s a cash cow from a tuition revenue and then from auxiliary income from housing and meal plans, not to mention philanthropy,” Gavin said. “If you do it right, people will come. If you don’t, you can have the adverse aspect. I don’t want to think about that or have to deal with that.”

U.S. high school graduation peaked at an estimated 3.9 million in 2025, according to the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education. It's projected to decrease by 2041 to an estimated 3.4 million, a drop of nearly 13%, because of a falling birth rate. College enrollment is projected to follow suit. Many small private colleges already have been been hit by severe enrollment drops coming out of the pandemic.

A number of schools have added sports in hopes of boosting enrollment — Adrian College launched more than two dozen a generation ago and is now up to more than 50 — but football is often considered an anchor sport. It is also expensive.
Research has shown that adding football may not be the solution colleges hope it will be.

A 2024 University of Georgia study looked at 36 small colleges that added football between 2004-16. Researchers examined how starting a program affected enrollment, demographics and net tuition and fee revenue compared with schools that did not start a program.

Aside from a one-year jump in male enrollment tied to bringing in football players, overall enrollment patterns were similar to those at non-football schools. Factoring in costs of operating the program, tuition revenue per student did not increase even the first year at the new football schools. The study did find positive impacts on student life.
Welch Suggs, one of the study’s authors and an associate professor of journalism and mass communication at Georgia, noted the study was done over a period of growth in higher education.

“What it says to me is if a school is adding football right now, it’s one of several last-ditch efforts to try to maintain enough enrollment to keep the doors open, because this year’s graduating high school class is going to be the smallest in a generation in terms of sending students to college,” Suggs said.
In all, 62 four-year college football programs have been added or re-started in the last decade. The net gain is 56 because three of those programs shut down and three of the schools closed.
In the 10 years before that, from 2006-16, a total of 10 four-year schools with football closed and three dropped their programs, according to the NFF.
The return of football at Azusa Pacific and Whittier has been greeted with much fanfare by alumni who remember the schools' heydays.

Christian Okoye, the 250-pound “Nigerian Nightmare,” played for APU in the 1980s before he became a beloved Kansas City Chiefs running back and the 1989 NFL rushing leader. Pro Football Hall of Fame coaches George Allen and Don Coryell started their careers at Whittier, and President Richard Nixon was a lineman for the Poets.
Whittier's original football program dated to 1907, and the move to drop football along with lacrosse and golf in 2020 saved money but cost the school many of the 120 athletes who were affected.

When school President Kristine Dillon arrived in 2023, alumni immediately asked for football's return and raised more than $800,000 in initial funding. The reintroduction of football has helped increase enrollment from 764 in 2024 to 905 this fall, with 41% of students playing a sport.
Dillon noticed a change in the campus vibe once the fall semester started. Her house is on campus, and she started noticing cheerleaders outside her window practicing almost every night.

“We've got more students as a percentage living on campus, so the level of activity in clubs and our version of fraternities and sororities is growing,” Dillon said. “I'll give at least some credit to the growth football has had, not just for enrollment but for the sense of a lively campus.”

title: A flag-filled afternoon: Packers-Lions showdown overshadowed by rash of debatable penalties
summary: Tom Brady criticized the officiating in the Green Bay Packers' game against the Detroit Lions
story: Tom Brady criticized the officiating in the Green Bay Packers' game against the Detroit Lions

The officials really got under the Green Bay Packers' skins in Week 7, and Tom Brady was squarely in their corner, disputing call after call during a flag-filled showdown the Detroit Lions won 20-17 on Sunday.
The superstar QB-turned-TV commentator took issue with multiple debatable calls by referee Alex Moore's crew Sunday at Ford Field that had the Packers flummoxed.

“You can't keep tacking on 15 yards,” an exasperated Brady said on Fox's broadcast after Green Bay defensive tackle Karl Brooks was flagged for roughing the passer late in the fourth quarter, one of several questionable rulings in the marquee matchup, most of which went against the Packers.

Fox brought in rules analyst Dean Blandino, and the former NFL vice president of officiating, as he had all afternoon, concurred with Brady: “This is teach-tape tackle. That's not roughing the passer.”
Brady and Blandino also disputed the other roughing-the-passer penalty on the Packers — although not as forcefully — when defensive end Brenton Cox Jr. was flagged in the third quarter.
A delayed intentional grounding call on Packers quarterback Jordan Love had Brady and play-by-play man Kevin Burkhardt confused.
“Tucker Kraft was right there” Brady said, adding it was “certainly in the direction” of the tight end and “definitely not grounding.”
“They really missed that call,” Brady added. Burkhardt called the flag “crazy” and Blandino agreed with their analysis.

“So we ruled that although the quarterback was outside of the tackle box, the pass did not make it to the line of scrimmage," Moore told a pool reporter after the game. "So, that’s where the intentional grounding came in.”
Moore said the ball couldn’t merely be in the direction of Kraft and that “it has to actually reach where he is if it doesn’t get to the line of scrimmage” to avoid an intentional grounding penalty.
“That is not grounding,” Blandino said on the telecast.

Brady also took issue with a call against Detroit, suggesting Lions linebacker Derrick Barnes didn't deserve an unnecessary roughness flag for bumping running back MarShawn Lloyd after a pass sailed over Lloyd's head.

“He's just turning his right shoulder away from it,” Brady said. “That's allowed 99 out of 100 times. It’s a bang-bang play. When you’re on the field, you’ve got to pursue that ball. If he catches it, he needs the force to knock him on the ground as a pass defense.”

In the third quarter, Detroit’s Amon-Ra St. Brown got tackled after catching a pass, then started running again before defensive tackle Devonte Wyatt chased him and brought him down. Wyatt was called for unnecessary roughness, and Jared Goff threw a 10-yard touchdown pass to Jameson Williams two plays later.
Packers coach Matt LaFleur and Wyatt said after the game that they didn’t hear a whistle before St. Brown got up.

“We ruled the play was over,” Moore told a pool reporter. “I can’t honestly hear if there was a whistle or not, but the tackler made the tackle, the play was over. Then, there was an additional action, and he basically tackled him again with force after the play was over.”

“Yeah, well, there was no whistle blown," LaFleur said. “And the guy continued to run. And our guy didn't hear a whistle. He continued to play, too. And then we get called for penalties. So, I don't know. They were trying to tell me that the play was obviously dead. I'm like, 'How do you know if you don't hear a whistle?'”

All the yellow flags that had so many seeing red overshadowed a big gamble by Lions coach Dan Campbell. Known for taking risks, he seemed to make a reckless decision to go for it on fourth-and-1 from his 24 with just under 5 minutes to play in a tie game and Jahmyr Gibbs lost 2 yards on the play.
“I thought we would get it, No. 1,” Campbell explained. “No. 2, I knew we would get the ball back if it didn’t work out.”
He was right on that latter point.
Detroit got the ball back after Packers rookie Trey Smack missed a 35-yard field goal when D.J. Wonnum got a finger on the football.
Jake Bates made a 22-yard field goal as time expired to give Detroit the win, capping a drive that featured the debatable roughing call on Brooks.
Then, facing third-and-5 at the 2-minute warning, the Lions successfully drew a neutral zone infraction on Brooks, which helped them run down the clock before Bates kicked the winner as time expired.
When Brooks was flagged for the infraction, the Lions offense broke into a synchronized chaotic celebration, an homage to the classic animated dance from “A Charlie Brown Christmas.”

A week earlier, Packers receiver Matthew Golden had drawn a taunting flag for flexing his biceps after a crucial catch against the Cowboys even as the broadcast had one player posing in that very position for introductions.

There were no flags thrown at Detroit as several Lions players performed independent wildly animated dances after Brooks jumped and guard Christian Mahogany got into Brooks' face, pointing at the culprit and appearing to even tap Brooks' helmet as his teammates gyrated around him.
His team ultimately bailed out Campbell for his dicey decision on fourth down — with some help from the officiating crew.
With contributions from AP Sports Writer Larry Lage in Detroit.

summary:

story: LONDON -- Harry Kane became the first Englishman in 25 years to win the Ballon d’Or on Monday thanks to his prolific scoring last season.

Kane scored 73 goals for club and country last campaign — he was Europe's top scorer — and smashed scoring records in Germany for Bayern Munich and at the World Cup, where he captained England to a third-place finish.
The 33-year-old Kane says winning the prestigious individual award was built on so much more.

“Anything is possible with hard work, when no one else is watching, to go through the ups and downs, to learn through resilience, determination and self-belief,” an emotional Kane said in a message to young players, after reflecting on his early career struggles.

“My journey wasn’t straightforward. I wasn’t the kid who went straight to the top. I had to experience the downs,” he added. “I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration as well.”
Kane was followed in the voting by Kylian Mbappé, Lamine Yamal — voted best young talent for a third straight year — 2024 winner Rodri and record eight-time winner Lionel Messi.

Kane thanked his teammates, coaches, parents, children — “It's past your bedtime” — and wife Kate, “ my best friend. We’ve been through ups and downs for sure. You’re my biggest supporter. You always want the best for me.”
Kane led Bayern to the Bundesliga and German Cup double, scoring a hat trick against Stuttgart in the cup final. Bayern also reached the Champions League semifinals.

At the World Cup, he scored six times to pass Gary Lineker as England’s all-time leading World Cup scorer and placed himself among the all-time top five in tournament history. His lineup lost to Argentina in the semifinals but beat Mbappé's France for third place, England's best World Cup placing in 60 years.
An Englishman hadn’t won the Ballon d’Or since Michael Owen in 2001.

“It's massive for England, for our country. (The ceremony) being here in London was a good omen for me,” Kane said. “It's been too long. Certainly (there have been) incredible English players... To put us back on the map, to put us here with this trophy I'm extremely proud. Playing for England is my biggest honor, the thing I love to do the most.”
England coach Thomas Tuchel told Kane the Three Lions are “lucky to have you as our leader.”
“I ran out of superlatives to describe your performances a long time ago, but I’m delighted to see that you have now been formally recognized by the football world,” Tuchel said.
Fans packed the streets and climbed light poles near the London Palladium, where the event was held, for a glimpse of the arriving athletes. Kane stopped to sign autographs on his way in.
They stayed through the ceremony and chanted Kane's name as he left the theater near Oxford Circus after midnight.
Kane planned to celebrate with family and friends, but just a little.
“We have a cup game on Wednesday so it can't get too messy,” Kane said, noting he has an early Tuesday flight back to Munich in time for team training.
Monday’s ceremony was held in London for the first time in recognition of the inaugural winner 70 years ago, England’s Stanley Matthews in 1956.
Earlier, Spain star Alexia Putellas won her record-equaling third women’s Ballon d’Or after leading her former club Barcelona to multiple trophies last season including the Women’s Champions League.
Putellas, who joined London City Lionesses in the offseason, also helped Spain win the Women’s Nations League last December.
The 32-year-old midfielder ended Spain teammate Aitana Bonmati’s three-year reign.

Putellas won the prestigious award in 2021 and 2022, tore her ACL and saw Bonmati rise to stardom. Bonmati, who completed her women’s Ballon d’Or three-peat in 2025, was not on this year’s shortlist after breaking her leg in December.
There wasn’t a women’s Ballon d’Or until 2018, when Ada Hegerberg won it.
Putellas urged young players to approach the sport with “love and passion.”
“Believe in yourself, that’s the most important thing,” she said. “If you have a dream, go for it, even if at some point you have to start from zero.”
Putellas had joined Barcelona in 2012 and called her time at the Catalan club “something special.”
“I'm really grateful for having 14 seasons as a player (at Barcelona),” she said. “What I experienced last year was like a perfect story.”

title: Chase leader Kyle Larson has easier path to 3rd NASCAR championship after surviving Talladega chaos
summary: Kyle Larson could become the first driver in Chase history to clinch the title before the season finale
story: Kyle Larson could become the first driver in Chase history to clinch the title before the season finale
Kyle Larson’s team needed directions at Talladega Superspeedway to find the NASCAR driver after his first victory at the mammoth 2.66-mile oval.

“It’s hard to believe,” crew chief Cliff Daniels said after Larson gained 10 spots on Sunday's final lap for his first victory in 24 starts at the treacherous track in Alabama. “I had to ask where victory lane was. I’ve never seen the place; didn’t even know where it was.”
The Chase points leader won’t need help finding his way if Larson celebrates a third Cup Series championship during the next two weeks.
Larson and Hendrick Motorsports know their way around the season’s final two tracks as well as anywhere on the NASCAR schedule.
With a 73-point lead over Denny Hamlin, a strong performance Sunday at Martinsville Speedway could make Larson the first driver in Chase history to clinch the title before the season finale.

Hendrick is NASCAR’s winningest team at Martinsville with 31 victories (including wins in seven of the past 12 races). Larson has eight consecutive top 10s (including a 2023 win) at the 0.526-mile oval.
He is even better at Homestead-Miami Speedway, where the Cup season ends Nov. 8. Larson has two wins at the 1.5-mile track, is tied for second in top fives (six) and ranks fourth in average finish.
Martinsville and Homestead are stronger fits for Larson’s aggressive style than the unpredictable draft of Talladega, which ranked among his worst tracks in Cup and seemed a major title roadblock.
A disastrous 34th-place finish at Phoenix Raceway left Larson clinging to a five-point lead, and five former Talladega winners were within striking distance.
It’s no wonder he was much looser after surviving the caution-plagued stress of 500 miles at Talladega, where the nine drivers behind him in the Chase standings were involved in incidents Sunday.
“I feel good,” Larson said. “Never in a million years would I have imagined leaving here plus-73. That makes the win feel even way cooler.”
After finishing eighth at Talladega, Hamlin conceded that Larson is destined for the title if he avoids misfortune in the next two races.

Hamlin still should be able to keep the pressure on at Martinsville. The Joe Gibbs Racing star ranks first among active drivers at the Virginia short track in wins, laps led and points per race, and he led a race-high 292 laps for a runner-up finish there on March 29.
Teammate Christopher Bell, ranked third in the Chase 74 points behind Larson, won at Martinsville four years ago and has four top 10s in the past six races there.
The competition is concerning to Daniels, who plans to keep the No. 5 Chevrolet on offense at Martinsville instead of protecting the Chase lead.

“The points can swing a lot,” said Daniels, who led Larson to championships in 2021 and 2025. “There’s always been this question of what is a comfortable points gap. The Chase so far has shown some volatility. You just never know what’s going to lie ahead.”

Though Larson can wrap up the title by scoring 59 points at Martinsville (he amassed 71 of a maximum 76 at Talladega), he and his team are downplaying their chances by noting that alternate tire strategies and the timing of cautions can negate a fast car.

“It’s certainly not over by any means,” said Hendrick Motorsports vice chairman and NASCAR Hall of Famer Jeff Gordon, whose nine wins at Martinsville tie him for the team lead with seven-time champion Jimmie Johnson. “You’ve got to execute, and there’s so much on the line. So many different strategies can play out now. I know Hendrick runs good at Martinsville, but that’s just not a guarantee.”
Since joining Hendrick in 2021, Larson has finished outside the top 10 only twice at Martinsville. He is mindful it’s still easy for things to go wrong at the smallest track on the Cup circuit.
“If there’s a stackup on the first lap, I could cave in the radiator and be done,” Larson said. “There’s still a lot of racing left in the Chase. I’m not getting ahead of myself at all.”

title: Sports equinox underway with MLB, NFL, NBA, WNBA and NHL all in play at the same time
summary: If you love sports, it's tough to beat Monday night
story: If you love sports, it's tough to beat Monday night
If you love sports, Oct. 26, 2026, is tough to beat.
Five professional leagues in North America were in action at the same time on Monday night, a phenomenon known as a sports equinox.
Major League Baseball and the NFL were competing for the most viewers while the NBA, WNBA and NHL gave their diehard fans games to watch.
Monday marks the 33rd sports equinox, the first since Oct. 27, 2025, and the fourth instance with women's professional basketball included, according to Sportradar.
Here's a guide on how to sample a little bit of this and that in the sports smorgasbord:
The Tampa Bay Rays hosted the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of the World Series, with the game starting shortly after 8 p.m. EDT on Fox.
The Brewers won the first two games by one run, taking a 2-0 lead in the best-of-seven series.
Even though the Philadelphia Eagles and Dallas Cowboys are each 2-4, the NFL always draws a lot of interest and millions care about the NFC East matchup that kicked off at 8:15 p.m. on ESPN.
The Eagles went in having lost four in a row, reeling with quarterback Jalen Hurts on injured reserve because of blood clots. The Cowboys won only one of their previous four games.

Reigning NBA Rookie of the Year Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving returned to the Dallas Mavericks' lineup for their game at the Miami Heat. That game tipped off at 7:30 p.m. on NBA TV, well before baseball and football got underway.

In the middle of the World Series and “Monday Night Football,” the NBA had an intriguing matchup to compete for attention. Stephen Curry and the Golden State Warriors faced Nikola Jokic and the host Denver Nuggets at 10 p.m. on NBCSN and Peacock.
The WNBA was vying for eyeballs against MLB, the NFL, NBA and NHL for the first time since 2000, when the league did it three times in September of that year.
The Golden State Valkyries hosted Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream in Game 5 of the Finals at 8 p.m. on USA Network, CNBC and Peacock. The best-of-seven series was tied at two games apiece.
The NHL had some of its top scorers skating in three games.

The New York Rangers and Los Angeles Kings were on the ice at Madison Square Garden in a game that started at 7 p.m. on NHL Network. The Kings scored three times and chased Rangers goaltender James Reimer before either baseball or football started.

Edmonton star Leon Draisaitl of Germany had a shot to become the first NHL player born outside of North America to score at least two goals in four straight games when Connor McDavid and the Oilers hosted the Detroit Red Wings at 9:30 p.m. on ESPN+ and Sportsnet.

title: Rafael Nadal to play in Las Vegas exhibition in February for 1st US action since retirement
summary: Rafael Nadal will take part in a tennis exhibition in Las Vegas early next year to mark the first time he plays in the U.S. since his retirement two years ago
story: Rafael Nadal will take part in a tennis exhibition in Las Vegas early next year to mark the first time he plays in the U.S. since his retirement two years ago
LAS VEGAS -- LAS VEGAS (AP) — Rafael Nadal will take part in a tennis exhibition in Las Vegas early next year to mark his first time playing in the U.S. since retiring two years ago.
The 22-time Grand Slam champion will headline “The MGM Slam presented by Capital One” at T-Mobile Arena on Feb. 28, organizers announced Monday.
Nadal faced Carlos Alcaraz in the Vegas exhibition in 2024 during his final year on tour.

“I remember how impressive it was to feel the energy of a full arena in a city like Las Vegas,” the 40-year-old Nadal said. “Now I return in a different stage of my life, without the pressure of the tour but with the same passion for this sport. I have always loved competing, and even if my professional career is finished, that feeling never really goes away.”
Additional players and the format for the event will be announced in the coming weeks. It’s slated for just before the ATP 1000 event in Indian Wells, California.
Last year, eight players competed in a tiebreaker format.

title: NBA strikes deals with prediction markets, with eye on integrity and regulations
summary: The NBA has struck deals with Kalshi and Polymarket, making them the league’s preferred prediction markets
story: The NBA has struck deals with Kalshi and Polymarket, making them the league’s preferred prediction markets
MIAMI -- The NBA has struck deals that will make Kalshi and Polymarket the league’s preferred prediction markets, along with an agreement with a federal agency tasked with regulating those exchanges.

Those agreements, announced Monday, are intended to provide “significant integrity protections for NBA-related markets,” including limitations on what can be offered on those exchanges, transparency when it comes to suspicious patterns by site users, and banning league and team personnel from making trades related to league events.

The prediction markets will have “information-sharing obligations relating to investigations and suspicious trading,” the NBA said. The NBA has had similar guardrails in place with its sportsbook partners for some time and has cited instances where that system has flagged irregularities in betting patterns.

“If you’re going to be betting on our games or trading on our games or playing fantasy around our games, it’s better for it to be regulated than unregulated,” said Scott Kaufman-Ross, the NBA’s head of media distribution and partnerships. “And clearly, our fans have interest in this activity. So, we’re in a better position to protect the integrity of our games in a regulated market where there’s transparency, where things can be monitored and we have insight into what’s happening.”

The NBA is also expanding its agreements with current official sports betting partners, such as DraftKings, to include their prediction-market offerings. Not all states offer legalized sports betting but predictions markets — at least on some level — are essentially available in all 50 states.

More than a dozen states are involved in litigation over prediction markets and earlier this month the NFL asked the Supreme Court to rule on the regulation of such markets. The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission contends that it has exclusive jurisdiction on oversight, though some states believe it should fall under their purview.

Earlier this month, the NBA told sportsbooks they will not be permitted to offer certain types of wagering this season, including but not limited to which players record the first stat of a game, the outcome of the opening tip and taking the “under” involving players not expected to play more than a few minutes. The deals announced on Monday are expected to have similar restraints.

“A big part of this is a limitation on the types of markets that can be offered,” Kaufman-Ross said. “We will have the right to approve the types of markets that are available on our games, which is a very important component for us. And we’ve had very constructive dialogues with the companies as part of that.”

The NBA’s memorandum of understanding with the CFTC “reflects a shared commitment to ensuring that NBA-related prediction markets are subject to appropriate regulatory oversight and integrity protections,” the league said.

Kalshi and Polymarket, as part of their partnerships with the NBA, will now be able to describe themselves as the “Preferred Prediction Market Exchange of the NBA,” plus have access to league intellectual property such as logos, be able to get NBA statistical data from league partner Sportradar “to operate and settle authorized NBA-related markets,” and other marketing activations.

The terms of the NBA’s agreements with Kalshi and Polymarket were not disclosed, other than the league confirming that they are for multiple years. There are NBA stars with business relationships with those markets; Miami’s Giannis Antetokounmpo has promoted Kalshi and Philadelphia’s LeBron James recently signed a deal with Polymarket. At least one other NBA star, San Antonio’s Victor Wembanyama, recently said he will never endorse such sites.

title: Smotherman makes it two wins in a row on PGA Tour with playoff victory over Seamus Power
summary: It took Austin Smotherman 100 starts on the PGA Tour to finally get a win
story: It took Austin Smotherman 100 starts on the PGA Tour to finally get a win

SOUTHAMPTON, Bermuda -- Austin Smotherman captured his second straight FedEx Cup Fall event Monday morning when he outlasted Seamus Power of Ireland with a par on the third playoff hole to win the rain-shortened Butterfield Bermuda Championship.
Smotherman also won the Bank of Utah Championship three weeks ago. The two victories in tournaments offering full FedEx Cup points gets him in the U.S. Open next year at Pebble Beach.

Smotherman and Power were tied at 16-under 197. The final round was canceled because of wind so strong at Port Royal that conditions were deemed unplayable. They returned for a playoff held on the par-3 16th hole with a strong wind gusting off the ocean left of the green.

Both made par when the pin was all the way back at 178 yards — Power missed a 20-foot birdie putt for the win on the first extra hole and made an 8-foot par putt for a bunker save the next time. The hole was moved to the front of the green for the third extra hole.

Smotherman, who twice hit 8-iron to the front section when the pin was in the back, stayed with an 8-iron and left himself a birdie chance just inside 15 feet. Power again didn't get enough help from the wind and his shot buried in deep rough left of the green. He chopped it out to just outside 15 feet and missed the par putt.

Smotherman won the Bank of Utah Championship three weeks ago for his first PGA Tour title in his 100th career start. Now he has two in a row and moves to No. 51 in the FedEx Cup, assuring him a spot at the $20 million signature events at Pebble Beach and Riviera next year.

The consolation for Power, who was trying to become the first multiple winner of the Bermuda Championship, was locking up his card for 2027. He was at No. 103 — the top 100 at the end of the fall keep full status — and the runner-up finish moves him to No. 68.
It was the second time this year a playoff began on a Monday morning because of weather. Viktor Hovland defeated Scottie Scheffler on the par-4 18th to win the Travelers Championship in June.
Smotherman becomes the first 54-hole winner on the PGA Tour because of weather since Wyndham Clark won the AT&T Pebble Beach Pro-Am in 2024.

title: Kimi Antonelli's Austin win points to potential dominance in 2027, not just this year
summary: Victory in Texas didn’t just put Kimi Antonelli on the verge of winning the Formula 1 title
story: Victory in Texas didn’t just put Kimi Antonelli on the verge of winning the Formula 1 title
Victory in Texas didn't just put Kimi Antonelli on the verge of winning the Formula 1 title. It gave an important signal he could repeat the feat next year.

In recent weeks, Antonelli and Mercedes had been struggling with a package of car upgrades that often seemed more like downgrades as Max Verstappen and Red Bull took advantage to win back-to-back races.

But Antonelli’s dominant win from pole position at the Circuit of the Americas on Sunday showed he’s now confident of getting the best out of the car over a full race distance at a pace Red Bull and Ferrari largely couldn’t match.
“All this time putting so much work into bringing this new package and finally seeing the result is very pleasant,” he said.
In Singapore earlier this month, Antonelli said there was only a “very, very small” window of performance to unlock the new design's benefits before it became skittish and unpredictable.
Now the car is working as intended, he says there's more to come.

“In some places, I would say, still not as much as we expected, but in other places it is delivering very well,” Antonelli said. “We’re still struggling a little bit in low-speed with front locking, but overall, I feel like the package is finally starting to deliver.”
With much smaller regulation tweaks coming for 2027 compared with the sweeping changes implemented this year, what teams learn from late-season developments can have a direct benefit next year.

Only one of Mercedes' drivers is seeing the benefit. George Russell was at a loss for his “rubbish” pace as he finished eighth in Texas. A five-second penalty didn't help, but Russell told Sky Sports he was clueless about the rest of the yawning gap to Antonelli.
“Hopefully there are some answers somewhere but at the moment I don’t have them,” he said.
Russell has less experience with the upgrades after the team put him back on the old package in Singapore to make a side-by-side comparison.

Verstappen's still a threat after Red Bull developments made his set up more predictable, but the car is slow off the line at the start of the race and it's costing him. Verstappen started second alongside Antonelli but spent his first lap under attack from Charles Leclerc as Antonelli zoomed off into a lead that was never seriously under threat.
“The start definitely is something we’ve improved massively,” Antonelli said. “We were nowhere at the beginning of the season, and now we’re good, so that’s definitely one less thing to worry about.”

summary: The St. Louis Blues and the Montreal Canadiens meet in a non-conference matchup
story: The St. Louis Blues and the Montreal Canadiens meet in a non-conference matchup

title: Quirky Tropicana Field isn't a pretty ballpark but the Rays love their home
summary: With its unappealing concrete exterior, massive, sloping dome and cavernous indoor atmosphere, Tropicana Field possesses little of the aesthetic beauty and charm associated with baseball’s most celebrated stadiums
story: With its unappealing concrete exterior, massive, sloping dome and cavernous indoor atmosphere, Tropicana Field possesses little of the aesthetic beauty and charm associated with baseball’s most celebrated stadiums

With its unappealing concrete exterior, massive, sloping dome and cavernous indoor atmosphere, Tropicana Field possesses little of the aesthetic beauty and charm associated with baseball’s most celebrated stadiums.
But the Tampa Bay Rays love their quirky ballpark, especially after being forced out for a season because of destruction from Hurricane Milton.

A sellout crowd of more than 40,000 towel-waving, cowbell-ringing fans will welcome the Rays back for Game 3 of the World Series on Monday night after a pair of gut-wrenching, one-run losses in Milwaukee.
The Brewers lead 2-0 and are two wins away from the franchise’s first World Series title. The Rays need to win four of five to secure their first championship in their 29th season.

When a powerful storm swept through downtown St. Petersburg on Oct. 9, 2024, shredding the roof and causing extensive damage to the Trop, there were concerns that the Rays would never play again at the only place they had called home since the franchise’s debut in 1998.

Nearly $60 million was spent to replace the roof and rebuild the stadium before the Rays returned 18 1/2 months later to start this season. They played their 2025 home games across the bay in Tampa at Steinbrenner Field — the spring training home of the New York Yankees.

During the renovation, the Rays were sold to a group led by real-estate developer Patrick Zalupski. The new ownership team spearheaded an agreement to build a 31,000-seat ballpark in Tampa near the home of the NFL’s Buccaneers.
In August, the Rays received county approval on a financing plan for the $2.3 billion project that features what they’re calling their “forever home” within a mixed-use entertainment district.
The new stadium is scheduled to open in 2029. The Rays and their fans are hoping a World Series banner will hang in the stadium.

“We love playing at The Trop. We played so well at The Trop all year,” second baseman Richie Palacios said Sunday. “It’s going to be exciting to go out there and put on a show for our fans and hopefully bring them a couple more wins.”

The Rays and Brewers tied for the best home record in the regular season, going 55-26. Though Rays fans have often been criticized for not showing up — the team finished 28th in attendance at 1.4 million — they’ve rocked the Trop throughout the postseason and made sure to give the rival Yankees an earful in the AL Division Series when the crowd included plenty of New Yorkers.
Large crowds also gathered at the Trop for watch parties during Games 1 and 2 while the Rays and Brewers played at American Family Field in Milwaukee.
“These Milwaukee fans have been really loud. I know our fans are going to be really loud and excited to see us come back and kind of reset ourselves a little bit,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said.

Tropicana Field has only hosted two World Series games in 2008 when the Rays split at home and then lost three in a row in Philadelphia. The 2020 World Series was played on a neutral field in San Diego due to the coronavirus pandemic. The Rays lost that series to the Dodgers in six games.

One of the Trop’s most distinctive features is its catwalk system, consisting of four circular steel rings suspended beneath the stadium’s non-retractable, cable-supported roof that stabilize the structure.

Sometimes the catwalks interfere with baseballs. It happened in Game 2 of the AL Division Series when Yankees rookie Spencer Jones hit a towering flyball off a catwalk that was caught by Mesa, who ran over to center field from right field to make the play.
A batted ball that strikes either of the lower two catwalks is a home rune, per stadium ground rules. A batted ball that hits either of the two upper catwalks is in play.

“It’s very much a different place,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said. “It seems like a great place, and you have to make adjustments to it. That’s part of being a big leaguer. You have to make adjustments to it.”

The Trop is also the only ballpark in the majors where fans can touch stingrays. Seven cownose stingrays who weathered Hurricane Milton returned to the stadium for opening day inside the “Cownose Clubhouse,” a 10,000-gallon touch tank experience located just beyond the right-center-field fence.
“They have stingrays in the outfield here? I didn’t know that,” Brewers reliever Aaron Ashby said.
Second baseman Brice Turang asked if the stingrays can be touched. They can.
“That’s really cool,” he said.
If Milwaukee wins two of the next three, Turang and Ashby could pose for photos with the stingrays and the World Series trophy.

title: Thunder lose Jalen Williams to serious lower leg injury late in win over Clippers
summary: Jalen Williams of the Oklahoma City Thunder was taken off the court on a stretcher Sunday night, after suffering a serious injury to his lower left leg while getting fouled in a scene that moved some of his teammates to the brink of tears
story: Jalen Williams of the Oklahoma City Thunder was taken off the court on a stretcher Sunday night, after suffering a serious injury to his lower left leg while getting fouled in a scene that moved some of his teammates to the brink of tears

Jalen Williams of the Oklahoma City Thunder was taken off the court on a stretcher Sunday night, after suffering a serious injury to his lower left leg while getting fouled in a scene that moved some of his teammates to the brink of tears.

He was injured on a drive with 1:14 remaining of Oklahoma City's game against the Los Angeles Clippers, getting tended to almost immediately by medical personnel after going down underneath the basket on the Thunder's offensive end.

Williams' ankle was draped by towels and players from both teams acted in immediate dismay and disbelief as the stretcher was brought out. The game was stopped for about five minutes, and the Thunder went on to finish a 108-101 victory.
“Just feel bad for him,” Thunder guard Shai Gilgeous-Alexander said in a postgame televised interview, fighting back tears as he spoke. “Nothing more than that.”

There was no immediate diagnosis from the Thunder, though it was obvious that the injury was severe — and the stretcher was called for within just a few seconds of the play ending. Oklahoma City coach Mark Daigneault said the team would be briefed Monday morning with the latest updates on Williams' condition.
“We're not doing great,” Daigneault said.
Williams, seated up on the stretcher, saluted the cheering fans with two thumbs-up signals as he was wheeled off the court.

“Our whole city will have JDub in our thoughts and prayers as he deals with this adversity and as he makes his way through his recovery,” Oklahoma City Mayor David Holt posted on social media after the game.

Williams — a shooting guard who entered Sunday having averaged 18 points per game in his first 250 NBA contests — has been an All-Star and an All-NBA player already in his career, plus was a huge part of the Thunder team that won the 2025 NBA title. He missed 49 games last season with an array of issues, mostly hamstring problems and recovery from a significant surgery on his right wrist.
“He just loves playing, loves the competition,” Gilgeous-Alexander said. “That's who he is. ... It's unfortunate, his luck so far. But he's equipped for it.”
The Thunder play again Monday night at home against Phoenix. The schedule gives Oklahoma City little choice but to try and move on somewhat quickly, Daigneault said.

“We don’t have a choice,” Gilgeous-Alexander said. “It’s what we signed up for. It’s obviously going to be tough without a player like that. He’s not gone forever. He’ll be back better than ever. We know it. We’ve just got to hold the fort down until he comes back.”
