title: DOJ asks Washington to set aside ballots from 400 alleged noncitizens
summary: Federal prosecutors said they sent a letter to the Washington secretary of state with a list of 400 people they claimed are not U.S. citizens.
story: Washington — Federal prosecutors in Washington state asked its top election official Monday to set aside ballots from more than 400 people who they believe are not U.S. citizens, expanding the Justice Department's efforts to call into question the accuracy of states' voter rolls just days before the midterm elections.

Neil Floyd, the acting U.S. attorney in Seattle, and Pete Serrano, the top federal prosecutor in eastern Washington, said they believe that many of the more than 400 registered voters are green-card holders, who have legal immigration status but are not U.S. citizens and cannot vote in federal elections.
Still, the prosecutors said that the suspected noncitizens have voted in multiple elections, and Floyd estimated that more than 1,500 ballots have been illegally cast.
"This is not the full number of noncitizens who have been voting in Washington," Floyd said. "This is only the tip of the iceberg."

Floyd and Serrano said they provided Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs with a list of the 405 people who the Justice Department claims are illegally registered to vote and asked for ballots they may cast to be segregated until their citizenship status is confirmed.

In a letter to Hobbs dated Monday, they said some of the people identified by the Department of Homeland Security as noncitizens voted in elections as recently as the August primaries. Some of the people have voted in Washington for more than a decade and have voted more than two dozen times, Floyd and Serrano said.
DHS is expected to send a second list of people who it believes are not U.S. citizens "imminently," which will then be shared with Washington elections officials, the prosecutors said.

Floyd and Serrano gave the secretary of state 48 hours, until Wednesday, to review the list of 400 registered voters to determine whether they are U.S. citizens and direct election officials to not tabulate any ballots received from them until citizenship can be determined.
"If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," they wrote.

Hobbs confirmed his office received the letter from the Justice Department but raised concerns with the accuracy of its list, which shows the last time each person voted. The department included multiple records for people who appear to have last voted in the 1990s, including a record for one individual who last voted in 1994, according to the secretary of state's office. More than 113 million primary and general election ballots have been cast since then.

"We take our responsibility to protect voter information seriously and will only respond to requests that follow due process. We saw what happened in California and don't want Washingtonians to be harassed," Hobbs said in a statement.
He said the timing of the Justice Department's request, made one week before the Nov. 3 election, "is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results."

The Justice Department sought Washington state's unredacted voter registration list last year. After Hobbs refused to turn over the information, the Trump administration sued the state in an effort to obtain the material, which includes voters' names, addresses, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers.

A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuit last month. The Trump administration has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to get their complete voter rolls, and 27 of those lawsuits have been tossed out by federal judges. Three cases remain pending. One, against Oklahoma, was voluntarily dismissed.

Floyd said during a press conference that because Washington refused to provide its unredacted voter rolls, the Department of Homeland Security used a publicly available list of registered voters in the state and compared it with government information to identify those who are allegedly not U.S. citizens. The Trump administration then conducted further investigation to see if those people cast ballots in Washington, he said.
But the secretary of state's office warned that the system used by the Justice Department mistakenly flags legitimate U.S. citizens as noncitizens, which puts their right to vote at risk.
Under federal law, it is a crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and instances of noncitizen voting are rare.

"At a time when thousands of Washington voters already face ballot rejections due to delayed postmarks, our focus should be on ensuring every eligible voter can exercise their right to vote, not creating additional uncertainty about their eligibility," Hobbs said.

The effort to set aside hundreds of ballots in Washington comes after the Justice Department sent letters to election officials in California earlier this month asking them to separate mail ballots cast by registered voters who the government claims are noncitizens.
Trump administration lawyers gave California election officials 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizens and verify their citizenship status.

The Justice Department went on to file a lawsuit against California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan. It asked a federal court to block the state from tabulating mail ballots received from 20,000 people who it believes are likely noncitizens until their citizenship status can be verified.

A hearing is set for Tuesday on the Justice Department's bid to force California to set aside the mail ballots from registered voters on its list. A longshot effort by the Trump administration to obtain an order from a federal appeals court was dismissed Monday night.

So far, the Justice Department has only sent a letter to Washington and has not yet filed a lawsuit seeking to force its election officials to separate mail ballots returned from the 400 alleged noncitizens.

title: Trump says Obama "wouldn't understand" White House renovations
summary: "I would try and explain that to a guy like Obama, but he wouldn't understand," President Trump said at a rally in Mississippi.
story: Washington — President Trump said Monday that former President Barack Obama "wouldn't understand" the renovations he's undertaken at the White House after the former president said Mr. Trump "has got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."
At a campaign stop in Mississippi, Mr. Trump addressed Obama's comments, which have gone viral, saying "the White House represents our country, and has to be pristine."

"I would try and explain that to a guy like Obama, but he wouldn't understand," Mr. Trump continued. "He doesn't understand the White House has to be clean, pristine, beautiful. It can't have cracks in the column."

At a rally in Michigan for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Saturday, Obama listed some of Mr. Trump's changes at the White House, including the construction of a massive ballroom, the new helipad on the South Lawn and more decorating changes.

"I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovations," Obama said. "He should be on HGTV. Guy's building a ballroom that's bigger than the White House. He's paved over the Rose Garden. He's put a helicopter pad on the South Lawn. And there's gold everywhere — what's up with the gold? Everything, more gold. He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."
Many Democrats applauded the comments while conservatives criticized them as out of touch.
Mr. Trump mentioned Obama's remarks several times at Monday's rally, saying the money being spent on renovations is "peanuts" and "the White House is now in better shape than it was in 1792."

"He said, this isn't a Cheesecake Factory," Mr. Trump said. "Can you believe it? Which is a very successful company. He doesn't like successful companies. But, you know, he was very critical about me because I spent time. And if you would have seen the White House, I took over the White House and it was in horrible condition."

Both Mr. Trump and Obama are campaigning in battleground states in the final days before Election Day, and Mr. Trump has also raised eyebrows with trips to some deep-red areas, such as Monday's trip to Mississippi.

title: John Thune's balancing act: Inside his push to save the GOP majority
summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune has tried to balance passing the president's agenda and preserving the independence of the Senate. The midterms are his biggest test yet.
story: Sioux City, Iowa — Less than 24 hours after President Trump held a raucous rally inside an airplane hangar in this western Iowa town, Senate Majority Leader John Thune stood alongside Rep. Ashley Hinson in a strip-mall bar and grill a few miles away.

Looking out over a giant water tank that punctuated the flat plains stretching out to the horizon, Thune and Hinson were hosting a roundtable with six local business owners last Friday, a decidedly less boisterous crowd than the one that had greeted the president. The event last Friday was part of Thune's final campaign sprint before the midterms, one of several stops he's made to support his GOP candidates for Senate.

Hinson fielded a reporter's question that has trailed Republican candidates all fall: How is she threading the needle between the president's demands for loyalty and his increasingly unpopular policies? She offered a version of what has become her standard answer: that she would back the president when she agreed with him, and be a "thorn in his side" when she did not.

Thune barely flinched. The exchange was representative of the balancing act he is all too familiar with — a line he's been walking for nearly two years. The South Dakota Republican has led his colleagues through unforgiving terrain, trying to do two things at once: advance the president's agenda and preserve the Senate's independence.

Now, with one week to go before the midterms, the election stands as the clearest test yet of whether that balancing act has paid off. A map that once favored Senate Republicans has turned perilous amid an unpopular war with Iran and stubbornly high gas prices, and their low-key leader faces questions voters are about to answer: Has Thune's approach worked — for Republicans, and for him? And has it been enough to keep the majority?
"Nothing's a guarantee"

One day in early fall, as the Senate prepared to leave Washington for the campaign trail, Thune was in his leadership office near the Senate chamber, where staffers were celebrating the first fireplace lighting of the season.
"Nothing's a guarantee. There are no layups," he told CBS News.

It had been almost two years since his conference chose him as leader, kickstarting a tenure that has largely been spent guiding Republicans through Democratic opposition and navigating the whims of the White House. With the midterms approaching and gas prices glowing on street corners like daily reminders, Thune made the case for staying the course.

"Right now, short-term, you have the gas price issue," Thune said. "But I think we have done the kinds of things that have set the economy up, and job creators up, for success … I think the conditions for growth are there."

Just steps away, behind the closed doors of the Old Senate Chamber, Senate Republicans had elected Thune leader on the heels of the 2024 election. There, beside Ionic columns and crimson drapes, the conference chose a man who was a far cry from the thundering, partisan politics of the moment — one whom colleagues describe with phrases like "team player" and adjectives like "kind."
It was an unorthodox match for the incoming Trump White House, and for a House speaker across the Capitol who had tied himself closely to the president, raising questions about the dynamic to come.

Thune, 65, is a conservative. He's moved much of Mr. Trump's agenda through the Senate. And in more than two decades in Congress, he's built a reputation for working behind the scenes to get results. But he is decidedly not, to the great frustration of online rabble-rousers, the frontman of the MAGA faithful. And his conference might just prefer it that way.

"He's steady, conservative, doesn't lose his temper very easily at all," said Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota. Bernie Moreno of Ohio called him a "super nice guy, incredibly well respected" and "just a very kind human being." Lisa Murkowski of Alaska said he is "a really decent man."

Even among Democrats, it is hard to locate someone who will find fault with him personally. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has called his counterpart a "good and decent American" and "someone who loves his country — as we all do."

With Thune at the helm, the Senate has approved the president's massive tax, border security and defense agenda, grinding through half a dozen marathon overnight vote sessions. There were bipartisan wins, too: a landmark housing measure, stablecoin legislation, a bill to combat revenge porn and one aimed at stopping the flow of fentanyl.
But heading into the midterms, that track record is at risk of being overshadowed by the war's toll on the economy — and by questions about what the Republican majority did, or didn't do, about it.

Though Republicans have increasingly expressed concern over the war and its impact on energy prices, only a handful have been willing to break with the president since the conflict began in February. Across more than a dozen votes forced by Democrats to rein in the president's war powers, the vast majority of the GOP conference has remained united in opposition, granting the president wide deference in steering the conflict. Now, that record is following them on the campaign trail.

Looking out on the Washington Monument from his office, Thune said voters are choosing a path for the future. If Republicans can sell the long-term dividends of their agenda and draw a contrast with Democrats, he argued, "we have a really good chance at keeping the majority."
It would come down to the "home stretch," Thune said, his foot swiveling back and forth on its heel: the messaging, the ground game, the "blocking and tackling of elections."
It's not the picture some had anticipated, Thune conceded. He framed the moment as a test of endurance, echoing a mindset he traces to his Scandinavian ancestors.
"Life is supposed to be hard," Thune said. "I'm willing to do things the hard way."
From South Dakota to the Senate

Thune's grandfather left Norway for the northern plains, laying railroads that would stretch west across South Dakota. Born in 1961, John Thune grew up in Murdo, a town with no stoplights and a population today of around 500.

His father — a World War II veteran, teacher, coach, athletic director and school bus driver — is at the center of almost every origin story Thune tells. His name, Harold Thune, now adorns the high school auditorium.
"He was our hero," Thune said of how he and his four siblings saw him.

Basketball features prominently in the stories Thune and those around him tell about his upbringing. At 6 feet 4 inches tall, Thune was a standout in high school, making first-team all-state his senior year.

After one game in which Thune scored 36 points, he remembers his father pointing out that a teammate had been wide open on a play. "He hated ball hogs," Thune said in his first floor speech of the new Congress in 2025, calling it an attitude he has carried throughout his life.

Another game became the basis for what he calls his "political heritage." After Thune sank five out of six free throws, Jim Abdnor, then a congressman, approached him and joked, "I noticed you missed one." It was the start of a decadeslong mentorship. Thune went on to play basketball at Biola University in California and later worked in Abdnor's Senate office in the 1980s. He served in the Small Business Administration under Ronald Reagan, then returned home to be executive director of the state Republican Party, serve as railroad director and head the state's municipal league. In 1996, he was elected to the first of three terms as South Dakota's at-large representative in the House.

His first Senate bid, in 2002, fell short by fewer than 600 votes. Two years later, he took on Senate Democratic leader Tom Daschle for the seat that Abdnor once occupied, orchestrating a shakeup that would be felt at the Senate's highest levels.

"That was a war," Thune said. He recalled the campaign's first debate at Dakotafest, an agriculture trade show outside Mitchell, where Daschle's wife, mother and daughters were seated directly in front of him. His campaign manager, Dick Wadhams, said the debate was when Washington began to take the race — and Thune — seriously.
"You had several hundred people at this debate in this open field outside of Mitchell, South Dakota," Wadhams said. "I mean, without sounding too much like a homer on this thing, Thune won."

Thune would pull off the upset that November, winning by more than 4,000 votes. Recruited by President George W. Bush, he became the first challenger in half a century to oust a Senate party leader. His stock skyrocketed, and he became a celebrity — at least by Washington standards — overnight. When he arrived in the Senate that winter, days before his 44th birthday, his reputation preceded him.
"He was like the dragon-slayer," said Alaska's Murkowski, who has served alongside him since 2005.

He won in part by casting Daschle as the "chief obstructionist," faulting him for blocking the president's nominees and stalling his agenda. More than two decades later, echoes of that fight remain. Thune rails, in his own Midwestern way, against what he has dubbed the "party of no," after two record-breaking government shutdowns and a Democratic blockade of the president's nominees.
But he has also faced accusations of obstruction himself — from the leader of his own party.
Thune and Trump
Thune's traditional style clashed early with the man who became the GOP's presidential nominee in 2016, nearly a decade before the two were joined in an unlikely partnership.

After the Access Hollywood tape surfaced in October 2016, Thune became the highest-ranking Senate Republican to call for Mr. Trump to withdraw from the race, and he broke with the president on a handful of policies during his first term. When Mr. Trump sought to overturn the 2020 election, Thune said the effort would "go down like a shot dog" in the Senate. After the Jan. 6 attack, he called the president's actions "inexcusable," though he voted to acquit him in the impeachment trial that followed. In the 2024 presidential race, Thune initially backed Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina. But when the party coalesced behind Mr. Trump, so did Thune.

The two worked to mend their differences before taking power in 2025. When Senate Republicans chose Thune as leader to replace Sen. Mitch McConnell, the president-elect said he would "do an outstanding job." Thune, in his first remarks after his election, vowed to work with Mr. Trump on his agenda while preserving the Senate's role as an independent body.

It wouldn't be easy. There were messy confirmation fights over controversial Cabinet picks, the era of DOGE and back-and-forths over trade policy. There was talk of a military invasion of Greenland, the uproar over Jeffrey Epstein, strikes on alleged drug boats, the surprise capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and, finally, the war with Iran.

Every day the Senate is in session, reporters in the halls outside his office pepper Thune with questions about the latest from the White House. But he seldom draws sharp lines between himself and the president, instead signaling disagreement through facial expressions and carefully hedged phrasing. Even as a series of poorly timed administration announcements derailed Senate GOP plans this summer, he spoke out only sparingly.

One day in late June, the tension spilled into public view. The president was set to attend the Senate GOP lunch — not at Thune's invitation — as he pushed a controversial elections bill known as the SAVE America Act, which Thune had repeatedly said lacked the votes. But first, Mr. Trump was due to attend a bill signing in the Capitol Rotunda, where lawmakers from both parties planned to celebrate the landmark housing legislation they had ushered through both chambers. At the 11th hour, the president canceled the signing, demanding that the elections bill pass first.

Thune was on the Senate floor when the president made the announcement. He walked out moments later to a growing crowd of reporters, saying he had just heard the news. Heading back to the floor later that morning, he said the cancellation was the president's call, but he hoped Mr. Trump would find a way to sign the bill. The president was still coming to lunch, and the day was just beginning.

Leaning against a desk, Thune fidgeted constantly as the chamber voted and the president's arrival neared. A stream of senators approached with back slaps and pitying looks. One GOP senator joked about being dressed for a "serious meeting." "Saddle up," said another, to laughter.

It had become a pattern: a White House move that upended Senate GOP plans with no warning to the leader, followed by Thune working the floor, polling his members on what came next, picking up the pieces.

The lunch meeting was explosive and in many ways emblematic of the president's approach to the Senate. Mr. Trump railed against the handful of GOP members who had supported a measure to rein him in on Iran the day before, and got into a shouting match with Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana. Thune said afterward that there hadn't been "much of a back-and-forth."

The pressure around the SAVE Act has been the most unrelenting, underscoring a broader tension between the filibuster's fiercest defender and a president who wants to kill it. Thune forecast the fight in his first floor speech as leader, arguing that the filibuster, and the voice it gives the minority, is essential to keeping the Senate a distinct body.

"Unfortunately, today there are a lot of people out there who would like to see the Senate turn into a copy of the House of Representatives," Thune said. "One of my priorities as leader will be to ensure that the Senate stays the Senate. That means preserving the legislative filibuster, the Senate rule that today has perhaps the greatest impact on preserving the founders' vision of the United States Senate."

The stance has earned him plenty of scorn from the right, amplified on social media, and simmering impatience from the president, who has repeatedly warned that Democrats will scrap the filibuster as soon as they get the chance. But Thune hasn't budged. Democrats may at some point "try and steal the car," he said, "but we're not going to hand them the keys."

Days after the president's lunch visit, the backlash hit home. The South Dakota Republican Party took up a resolution to censure Thune for his "failure" on the elections bill, claiming he had "wantonly and repeatedly acted as a roadblock" to the president's agenda. Delegates swiftly rejected it, but the effort showed the fury Thune faced on the right.

Others back home fault him for the opposite. Mike Levsen, a Democrat and former nonpartisan mayor of Aberdeen, South Dakota, has long viewed Thune as a patriot trying to do the right thing. But he now criticizes him in local news columns for not standing up to the president enough.

"I would say, 'John, what do you think when you get up in the morning, or when you go to bed at night, about what you're doing?'" Levsen said. He called Thune's posture "revolutionary" compared with House Speaker Mike Johnson's. "But boy, we needed some people with some guts. And we just haven't had them."

Since becoming leader, Thune has never publicly sparred with the president. The furthest he has gone came in July, when then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the president's patience with him was "running out" over the SAVE Act.
"Well, maybe she or somebody else ought to get on the phone and get the votes, right?" Thune said. "It's 50 around here."
At the campaign stop in Iowa last week, Thune stuck to his guns and defended how he has led.

"We do things differently, which frustrates people, the president, for example, who wants to get his agenda done quickly. That's not the nature of the beast in the Senate," he told CBS News. "So what we try to do is figure out ways to be able to work constructively with [the president] and his team to get things done."
Would he do things differently, with the benefit of hindsight?
"Not really," he said. "Not stuff that we can control."

Thune has also acknowledged the cost of his pushback. In August, when Mr. Trump declined to endorse him for another term as leader, Thune told reporters, "That's probably expected." But the next month, when Thune's name drew boos from a MAGA-aligned crowd at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, the president came to his defense. Mr. Trump's chief of staff met with Thune before the Senate left for the campaign trail, and Thune visited the White House with his family early this month. The relationship appears to have improved — for now.
With the majority on the line, that goodwill could evaporate quickly.
The fight for the Senate

One week from Election Day, Senate Republicans are looking anxiously at a map that is nearly unrecognizable from the one they saw after the 2024 elections. Then, Democrats, battered by their losses and contending with retirements of their own, appeared boxed out in all but a few states. Now, facing headwinds that the Senate GOP sees as largely beyond its control, Republicans are locked in a fight for their majority's survival.

Long before the war became a driving force in races from Ohio to Texas, Thune was working behind the scenes. He built a slate of candidates with an early focus on heading off primary clashes, along with a formidable fundraising operation that would allow Republicans to flood the airwaves down the stretch.

In Michigan and Iowa, where retirements opened up key seats, Thune moved quickly to back Mike Rogers and Ashley Hinson. He secured the president's endorsement for both despite some reluctance, according to a source familiar with the recruitment effort. (Rogers had been a CNN commentator, and Hinson didn't endorse Mr. Trump's 2024 bid until after the Iowa caucuses.) In New Hampshire, while Republicans courted Gov. Chris Sununu, Thune was quietly talking to his brother, former Sen. John Sununu, with whom he had served.

Elsewhere, it wasn't as straightforward. The push to recruit Gov. Brian Kemp in Georgia fell short, leaving a messy primary to play out. In Texas, where Senate Republicans had backed Sen. John Cornyn for reelection, the president endorsed his opponent, Ken Paxton, a dramatic and costly blow. And in North Carolina, the main super PAC supporting Senate Republicans — the Senate Leadership Fund — scaled back its spending for Michael Whatley earlier this month, a sign of the dimming prospects for holding the seat.

Alex Latcham, the executive director of the Senate Leadership Fund, said Republicans entered the final stretch with an "unprecedented financial advantage and tremendous candidates," crediting Thune's "tireless work."
Whether it's enough to keep the majority remains to be seen.

Kyle Kondik, the managing editor of the nonpartisan Sabato's Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia's Center for Politics, said if Republicans lose the Senate, it won't be because they didn't have enough money, citing SLF's financial advantage. And he said if Thune had had his way on candidates across the board, Republicans could be in better shape, pointing to Cornyn's viability against Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.

"I think Republicans are 50-50 at best to hold the Senate," Kondik said. "The Democrats might actually be a little bit ahead here in the final week. I think it's really close, but they're running a serious risk of losing the majority."
If that happens, Kondik said, he would place the blame for the loss "more at the feet of the president."

"The decision to attack Iran and the consequences of that really opened the door for the Democrats in the Senate in a way that might not be the case had that not happened, because Trump's approval is significantly worse now than it was before the attack, and it's also led to this gas price problem that I think is politically pretty damaging," he added.
Thune has campaigned with GOP Senate candidates in Kentucky, Mississippi, Georgia, Minnesota, South Carolina, Florida, Nebraska and Iowa, along with several fundraising swings.
"I said, 'I'll do whatever I can to help the team,'" Thune told CBS News. "And if that's just staying out of the way, I'm fine with that."
As the war and gas prices have darkened the picture, Thune has urged candidates to "run their own campaigns."
"The president's going to be a factor in every election," he told reporters before the recess. "But I think they need to be their own person, and I think that's the best way to win."

That is where Thune's approach meets the ballot. After two years of approving much of the president's agenda and rarely speaking out against the White House, Senate Republicans may find that distinction hard to draw. It's the same bet Thune has made as leader: that Republicans can stand with the president on policy while keeping some distance from his most unpopular pursuits. Next week, voters will weigh in.
"The job sucks"

Outside Thune's office, where a massive wall-mounted bison head named Murdo for his hometown stands guard, Thune projected tepid optimism as the Senate prepared to leave Washington. Asked whether Republicans had done enough in two years to keep the majority, he said emphatically, "Of course we have."

"We've just got to start talking about it," he said. "If we can stay focused, talk about the future and the two paths over the course of the next several weeks, based on our record of accomplishment, things we got done, things we still need to do, we've got a great argument."
Some of his own members saw it differently, and the frustration was palpable.

"We're going home, preparing for the midterms, and we've not addressed what all of you care about so deeply. That's affordability," GOP Sen. John Curtis of Utah said in a video to his constituents, pointing to high gas and diesel prices. "We just have not done a good job, and I think the voters are going to be loud and clear about how they feel about that."

GOP Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana, who has criticized Thune in recent months as "too cautious" with the Senate agenda, told reporters that Republicans should have turned to affordability immediately after passing Mr. Trump's signature tax bill in summer 2025. Another party-line bill could still come after the midterms, he said, but "you don't know what people's mood is going to be."
If Republicans fail to hold the Senate, the blame game and finger-pointing will be intense. But Thune objected to the idea that he hasn't been aggressive enough with the agenda.
"I don't know how you could be more aggressive," he said in Iowa. "I look back at the last couple of years, and I think we had wins pretty much at every turn."

Some frustration is par for the course in a 53-seat majority, where Thune can lose only three Republicans. He has often described the majority as closer to 46 in practice, with several members emboldened to chart their own path after losing primaries or deciding not to seek reelection. Corralling them, his GOP colleagues understand, isn't for the faint of heart.
"The job sucks," said Ohio's Moreno. "He's got an extraordinarily unwieldy conference, where you have 53 Republicans with 175 ideas, and everybody demands that their idea be the most important one."

There's been no sign that Thune would lose his conference's support in the leadership elections after the midterms. The bigger questions are what Thune himself wants, and whether the president might intervene, especially if Republicans see brutal losses across the board.

In September, reporters had been pressing Thune on whether he planned to run again as leader, and he suggested the midterm results would factor into his decision. In his office, he said he doesn't "like to get the cart ahead of the horse." But asked directly, he told CBS News, "Obviously I'm very interested in seeing how things turn out in the election, but my expectation is, yes."

Murkowski said it's easy to say "woulda, shoulda, coulda" about how aggressively he has steered the conference. But she said she can "only pretend to imagine the different pressures that he is under, the different levers that others are trying to pull."
"More often than not, it's just kind of like, 'Just hang in there, John,'" she said.

Former Sen. Joe Manchin, the Democrat-turned-independent who once offered to caucus with Republicans to help Thune win the top job, lamented his position under a president "who's demanding total loyalty above everything else." Manchin said his hope for Thune going forward is that he "gets his support."
"Who do you think would be able to do a better job than John, trying to hold it all together?" Manchin said.
Thune said the decision on his leadership is "going to be up to our colleagues."
Does he expect support from the president, who could push to replace him if the midterms go badly for Republicans? Thune laughed.
"Hard to say. I don't know. I mean, I don't bank on it," he said. "But yeah, if he found his way to do that, that'd be great."
In:
John Thune
John Thune

title: DOJ takes steps to charge James Comey again
summary: The DOJ took steps to charge James Comey with leaking information earlier this month, in its third attempt to bring criminal charges against the former FBI director and Trump foe.
story: The Justice Department took steps to charge James Comey with leaking classified information earlier this month, court records show, in its third attempt to bring criminal charges against the former FBI director and Trump foe.

Prosecutors are seeking to charge Comey with two counts of violating the Espionage Act by transmitting national defense information to a person not entitled to receive it. He has not been indicted by a grand jury or charged by criminal complaint, and was instead targeted through a criminal information filing.

In this case, the information was filed in order to preserve the statute of limitations before it expires, according to a Justice Department spokesperson. The official added that "this is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further."
A criminal information does not require approval by a grand jury, or a finding by a magistrate judge of probable cause that there is evidence to establish that a crime was committed.
Comey's attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said Comey "steadfastly maintains his innocence."
The latest effort by the Justice Department stems from allegations that Comey gave national defense information to an unnamed individual for disclosure in a newspaper in October 2016.

According to court filings in the case, The New York Times published an article on Oct. 5, 2016, titled, "Yahoo Said to Have Aided U.S. Email Surveillance By Adapting Spam Filter." The article cited two unnamed government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The Justice Department alleges that it has uncovered evidence that Comey sought to "correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before" and that Comey "directed staff" to speak with the Times reporter about the accuracy of the Reuters article.

Fitzgerald said the information "purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit," adding that investigators looked into the matter twice during the first Trump administration and "determined that no charges should be brought against anyone."

In a separate video statement, Comey said, "well, they're back again" — a reference to the two prior attempts to charge Comey, including a dismissed indictment accusing him of lying to Congress and a still-pending indictment accusing him of threatening President Trump via a social media post of a photo of seashells arranged to say "86 47."

"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to," Comey said. "Nothing's changed with me. I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."
Asked about the case late Monday, Mr. Trump told reporters he'd "just heard about it."
"I think he's a dirty cop, James Comey, but I know nothing about it," the president said.

In a statement posted to social media, the Justice Department said: "Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals."

Former prosecutors and defense attorneys told CBS News they had not seen a criminal information filed in a felony case in this manner before, and called the maneuver highly unusual. The practice had been approved in other federal appellate court districts in some cases, but is less common in Washington, D.C.

Greg Rosen, a former federal prosecutor who helped lead Jan. 6 cases, told CBS News: "In years of practicing in D.C., I never saw one used this way, let alone in the third attempt by the same Department to charge the same man."

Michael Bromwich, a former Justice Department inspector general who is now a defense attorney, told CBS News that he has never encountered a situation where a criminal information was filed to pause the statute of limitations. Normally, such charging documents are filed when a defendant plans to waive their right to have a grand jury weigh charges and opts to plead guilty.

"I have never heard of proceeding by information to toll the statute of limitations. Most prosecutors you have ever dealt with have never heard of that. This seems to be a way to do an end-run around the statute of limitations and keep a case alive that deserved to die 9 years ago," Bromwich said. "This is just absolutely bizarro world stuff."
DOJ and Comey fought in secret over charging efforts
The criminal information were filed under seal in early October, and were unsealed by U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden on Monday at Comey's request.
For much of this month, Comey's attorneys and federal prosecutors waged a behind-the-scenes fight over whether the Justice Department's effort to charge him should be dismissed.

In an Oct. 9 court filing, Comey's legal team argued the government "filed a faulty information under seal … in an effort to toll the applicable statute of limitations." The crime that the government is seeking to charge Comey under has a 10-year statute of limitations, which would run out in October of this year — but the ex-FBI director's lawyers say the statute of limitations applies to indictments and can't be extended if the government files a criminal information.

They also said Comey had "reason to believe that the government plans to use that information to seek an arrest warrant as soon as today, which could result in an after-hours arrest that would ensure Mr. Comey sits in jail over a holiday weekend."

"Mr. Comey has reason to believe multiple federal law enforcement officers have surveilled his whereabouts while traveling to a family members' residence and around his own neighborhood throughout the week," Comey's lawyers wrote on Oct. 9, just before Columbus Day weekend.
In an emergency court hearing, the government agreed to hold off on seeking an indictment for 30 days, attorneys for Comey later wrote.
The Justice Department argued that Comey's efforts to dismiss the criminal information was premature because no indictment has been returned.
"This is not the proper time for him to file pretrial motions or attempt to chip away at charging documents before he subjects himself to the Court's jurisdiction," the government said.
Further, the department said the law allows the government to proceed because it permits prosecutors to meet the deadline if the "indictment is found or the information is instituted."

In an unusual move, the criminal information filed by the department were signed by two senior officials — acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter and Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General Aakash Singh — as well as several special assistant U.S. attorneys who are not originally from the U.S. Attorney's office in Washington, D.C.

McFadden, the Trump-nominated judge overseeing the case, ordered the court docket to be unsealed Monday, writing: "Criminal charges against a former FBI director for his conduct while in office are of significant public interest."
He also said Comey "is aware of the criminal information and has offered to 'self-surrender,'" so there is no need to keep the case secret in order to help the government apprehend him.
The judge did not rule on the merits of the case.
Two prior investigations into FBI leaks
This is not the first time that the Justice Department has sought to investigate the disclosure of classified information in connection with a 2016 Times article.

Former U.S. Attorney John Durham of Connecticut, who was later appointed special counsel by Attorney General William Barr, investigated the matter in 2017, according to court filings in the case from Comey's defense team. At the time, he determined there were two sources for the article, including James Baker, the former FBI general counsel.
As part of that investigation, Baker said the FBI's chief of staff instructed him to provide the information and he understood it was being conveyed at Comey's instruction.
Durham ultimately did not recommend Baker or anyone else for prosecution.
Baker could not be immediately reached for comment.

The matter was later investigated a second time — in that case by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia under an investigation code-named Tropic Vortex. That was closed in February 2020, also without charges, according to court papers.
Comey and Trump

The Justice Department filed the criminal information in early October, about a month before the midterm elections. It marks the latest overt investigative step taken by the Justice Department in a politically charged case, a maneuver that runs counter to longstanding norms.

Mr. Trump and Comey have had a contentious relationship for nearly a decade, dating back to when the president fired the former FBI chief early in his first term. His firing is what prompted then-Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein to appoint Special Counsel Robert Mueller, whose investigation dogged Mr. Trump for much of his first term.
The two have exchanged barbs since then, with Mr. Trump calling Comey a "dirty cop" and repeatedly arguing he should be prosecuted, while Comey called Mr. Trump "morally unfit" to be president.

In September 2025, the Justice Department obtained an indictment against Comey that charged him with lying to Congress, alleging he falsely told lawmakers in a 2020 hearing that he had never authorized an FBI employee to serve as an anonymous source.

The indictment was personally signed by Lindsey Halligan, a former Trump White House aide who had been sworn in as interim U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia days earlier. Beforehand, staff in that office circulated a memo that argued charges should not be brought against Comey, CBS News has previously reported.
A judge dismissed the charges on the grounds that Halligan was improperly appointed.

Then, in April of this year, Comey was indicted in North Carolina on allegations that he threatened to kill Mr. Trump by posting to Instagram a photo of seashells arranged to form the numbers "86 47." (Mr. Trump is the 47th president.)

Comey has long denied wrongdoing, and his attorneys have argued the charges against him are politically motivated. They are currently seeking to have the North Carolina charges dismissed on several grounds, including that his prosecution is vindictive and selective. That matter is currently pending.

Comey isn't the only Trump foe to face criminal scrutiny. New York Attorney General Letitia James was also charged by Halligan's office with bank fraud last year. Her indictment was tossed out along with the first Comey indictment. Prosecutors presented her case to grand juries at least twice after that, but the grand jurors declined to re-indict her.

Attorney General Todd Blanche has long denied that the charges against Comey and other Trump adversaries are driven by politics. In an interview with CBS News earlier this year, he said the "86 47" indictment was driven by "local prosecutors" and "local agents."

Asked if Mr. Trump has called him up and ordered him to prosecute certain individuals, Blanche told CBS News he wouldn't discuss his conversations with the president, but "rest assured, he has much better, bigger and important things to do than to worry about me doing my job."

James Comey

title: Judge continues to block Trump from cutting down trees at D.C. golf course
summary: "The Court earlier stated, 'I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees,'" U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote. "The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law."
story: A federal judge on Monday barred the Trump administration from removing trees from East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, D.C., in a colorful ruling that follows a weekslong controversy over President Trump's plans to overhaul the publicly owned course.

"The Court earlier stated, 'I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees,'" U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote. "The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law."

In a 70-page preliminary injunction ruling, Reyes prohibited the government from "removing or damaging" any trees on the golf course while a lawsuit challenging the renovation plan works its way through the court system. The judge also required 10 days' notice before the government makes "any irreparable modification" to the course.
The judge had previously blocked tree removal through Monday.

In a Truth Social post, Mr. Trump called the ruling "unconstitutional" and said his administration would seek appeal. He added that the government would move forward with closing the course on Nov. 15.

"To have to give advanced notices to a judge who has no expertise in Golf, Architecture, Landscaping, Construction, or anything else having to do with building such a World Class Project, is not fair, appropriate, or Constitutional," the president wrote, arguing the project is "totally 'as of right.'"

Mr. Trump has sought to overhaul the golf course — which sits beside the Potomac River — for months, pitching a "World Class Championship Golf Course" fit to host high-profile professional tournaments instead of the current "dysfunctional" course. The D.C. Preservation League sued over the planned changes to the course, arguing the government violated the National Environmental Policy Act by failing to analyze the project's impacts.

Reyes has sparred with the government since it cut down hundreds of trees earlier this month with little notice to the court or plaintiffs. In a hearing two weeks ago, after more than 430 trees were felled, the judge told lawyers for the government that they had "lost credibility," and she was "furious" and "thoroughly unamused."
Mr. Trump said last week the course would close for construction beginning in November, and it would reopen in 15 months. He later said work would begin "IMMEDIATELY."

In her ruling Monday, Reyes argued Mr. Trump's statements about the renovation plans were tough to square with government lawyers' position that it's legally too early to challenge the plans in court because there was no final decision.

"Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting President," she wrote. "This started as a case about golf. That good walk spoiled. But it has become much more. It now forces the Court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys."

Reyes said she was initially reluctant to intervene in the case, writing that she "would much prefer not to have to resolve Lorax v. Once‑ler redux" — a reference to an earlier court hearing in which Reyes invoked the Dr. Seuss character to explain why she wasn't interested in micromanaging the federal government's tree management efforts.
She said she only intervened "because the Government did what it assured all it would not do," by chopping down hundreds of trees on the golf course.
Reyes found that the D.C. Preservation League is likely to succeed in showing the Trump administration's plans for the golf course violate the legal requirement for an environmental review.
She also found that the tree removals were part of Mr. Trump's renovation plan, rejecting the government's argument that they were part of an unrelated maintenance effort.

The judge said she did not find statements by the Department of Interior's deputy chief of staff to be credible, including his description of the agency's tree management plan as "cleaning up" the course.
CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department and the Department of Interior for comment.
Mr. Trump has feuded with Reyes, calling her a "crazed lunatic."

Earlier this month, the Trump administration asked Reyes to recuse herself from the case, arguing that she had shown "open hostility" to the government and that her "histrionics in prior hearings have clearly demonstrated she is no longer impartial."

"To name just a few examples of bias, Judge Reyes has unfairly questioned Trump Administration attorneys' intelligence, allowed her disdain for the Trump Administration to influence how hearings unfold, and systematically disregarded basic separation of powers principles and Article III constraints on judicial authority," government attorneys wrote.
Reyes rejected that request and denied that she is biased, listing out compliments that she has paid government lawyers.

"So what happened? Not sudden onset bias," Reyes wrote in her denial. "Instead, the Government decided to remove over 500 healthy, non-invasive trees from East Potomac Golf Course. It waited until 4:55 p.m. on the Friday of a holiday weekend to give notice that it would begin removing trees within 15 hours. It removed nearly 430 trees in one day and would have destroyed hundreds more but for a rain delay."

title: Venezuelan officials allowed Maria Corina Machado to return, Rubio says
summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio says Venezuela's interim government told the U.S. "weeks and weeks" earlier that opposition leader Maria Corina Machado could return to the country without interference.
story: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that Venezuela's interim government told the U.S. "weeks and weeks" earlier that opposition leader Maria Corina Machado could return to the country without interference, as the Trump administration pushes for a political transition that hinges on the cooperation of senior figures from Nicolás Maduro's former government.

"We spoke to the interim authorities and just said, 'Look, our expectation is that she's a Venezuelan. She belongs in her country. That's the country she's from. She should be allowed to return, and she should be allowed to return unperturbed, having no problems,'" Rubio told reporters. "And they told us that she could fly into the airport if she wanted to. And we communicated that to her team."

The disclosure came a day after Machado returned to Venezuela, and amid U.S.-backed efforts for an overhaul of the country's judicial and electoral institutions that Rubio argued are required before credible presidential elections can be held.

Machado snuck out of Venezuela in late 2025 to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, after spending nearly a year in hiding. Roughly one month after she departed the country, U.S. military forces captured Maduro and left his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, in control. The Trump administration has collaborated with Rodriguez on oil extraction and other issues, though the U.S. has said it expects Venezuela to eventually transition to a democratically elected government. Machado has suggested that she could run for president herself.

No election date has been announced, but Rubio insisted that the interim government was adhering to agreed-upon deadlines for replacing the country's Supreme Court and electoral council, institutions long used by Maduro's government to control political competition.
"We have timelines that are agreed to. And so far, they've met every one of the timelines," Rubio said, dismissing the possibility that Venezuelan authorities could indefinitely delay elections.
"You've got to change the infrastructure of the elections, not in 10 years, not in five years, not in two years," he added. "It needs to happen quickly under the timelines that we've established."

Rubio cited what he described as compliance with U.S. national security demands to diminish Iranian and Cuban influence, pursue criminal organizations and extradite individuals wanted by American authorities, including former Maduro associate Alex Saab.
He also pointed to the administration's ability to grant or withhold sanctions relief and licenses permitting economic activity as an incentive for the interim government to cooperate.
"The United States has significant influence over the direction that these talks go and the results that we get from them," Rubio said.

Asked by CBS News whether Rodriguez and her brother Jorge, who leads Venezuela's National Assembly, had been offered incentives to facilitate the transition — including immunity from prosecution — Rubio said there was "definitely no talk about prosecutions or anything of this nature." He did not directly address whether immunity had been offered.
Rubio said the only time he personally discouraged Machado from returning was immediately after a devastating earthquake, citing the need to prioritize humanitarian relief operations.

"And the reason why it was very simple, because right at that moment, the only thing we were focusing on from a logistical standpoint was getting as many planes with relief aid as possible into the country," Rubio said.

Machado has criticized aspects of the Trump administration's economic deals with Venezuela's interim government, including a U.S.-backed oil deal announced by President Trump earlier this year. Rubio defended the agreement as a means of attracting private investment, saying her objections were separate from the question of democratic elections.
"She doesn't have to agree with it or like it," he said of the oil deal.

Rubio warned that failure to reach a negotiated transition could result in a return to an authoritarian system – or to armed conflict – but expressed confidence that the interim authorities would continue cooperating.
"If that's the interim authorities that try to do harm to this process or stop complying, then we're gonna have a problem," he said. "But I don't expect that. I really, really don't."

Since Maduro's ouster, the Trump administration has suggested Cuba is also in its sights, urging the island's government to make sweeping political and economic changes. Rubio said hours after the Venezuela operation that "if I lived in Havana and I was in the government, I'd be concerned, at least a little bit," pointing to Cuba's alliance with Venezuela. Mr. Trump has mulled "taking Cuba in some form," and hasn't ruled out military action.
Last week, Rubio and the CIA urged Cubans in social media posts to work with the agency if they want to see "positive change."
Asked why he encouraged Cubans to work with the CIA rather than pursue peaceful political change, Rubio said, "I can't answer that."
He added that Cuba needed "very dramatic change" and was "a totally different case from Venezuela."

title: Court dismisses DOJ's request to force California to set aside ballots
summary: A federal appeals court on Monday dismissed the DOJ's effort to force California election officials to set aside thousands of ballots that the Trump administration claims may have been cast by alleged noncitizens.
story: Washington — A federal appeals court on Monday dismissed the Justice Department's effort to force California election officials to set aside thousands of ballots that the Trump administration claims may have been cast by alleged noncitizens.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit said in a 2-1 decision that it lacked jurisdiction over the appeal and granted a motion by the top elections official from Los Angeles County to dismiss the effort.

The federal government, Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez said, failed to allow a federal district court "adequate opportunity" to consider its request for temporary relief. Judge Patrick Bumatay dissented.

The two judges faulted the Justice Department for waiting until less than three weeks before the midterm elections on Nov. 3 to file its lawsuit and only seeking a temporary restraining order from the district court last week. They also pointed out that the department had sought a temporary restraining order as California was already processing ballots.

"The United States's claimed emergency, at least in part, is a self-constructed one," the 9th Circuit said in an unsigned opinion. "At least part of the delay here is attributable to the United States's own delay in filing suit, in realizing that existing California state law governs the issuance and processing of ballots, in recognizing that California has millions of registered voters and processes ballots on a schedule aligned with that scale, and in communicating to the court its desired relief."

Both Bennett, appointed by President Trump, and Sanchez, tapped by former President Joe Biden, authored concurring opinions. Bennett said that even if the court had reached the legal merits of the Justice Department's effort, he would have rejected its bid to force California to set aside the ballots that may be cast by ineligible voters.
Bumatay, who dissented, said the federal government has an interest in protecting the integrity of federal elections.

"The question — does the federal government have the power to stop this potential attack on the integrity of our elections? Under both federal law and the Constitution, the answer must be 'yes,'" the judge, a Trump appointee, wrote. "Simply, the federal government has a sovereign interest in safeguarding federal elections and ensuring that the votes of noncitizens do not undermine our electoral results."
California Gov. Gavin Newsom said the 9th Circuit's decision is a "positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump's disgusting attacks on the Constitution and our country's democracy."

"Trump is illegally trying to seize powers in the Constitution entrusted to others so he can stay in power. This lawsuit is just the latest step," he said in a statement. "Make no mistake: Trump's assault on democracy won't slow down."
Dispute over list of voters

The fast-moving dispute over California's mail ballots was filed earlier this month after Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent letters to California's secretary of state and the top election official in Los Angeles County, Dean Logan, which gave them 48 hours to review a list of more than 20,000 registered voters who the Trump administration believes are "likely" noncitizens and were sent mail ballots.

Los Angeles County told McCotter in a letter dated Oct. 15 that the list of suspected noncitizens contained addresses of registered voters throughout the state, and said his letter did not include information about how the list had been compiled. The county also told McCotter the letter did not provide any information as to how the county was to confirm citizenship status.
A lawyer for Los Angeles County said the Justice Department was asking Logan, the registrar-recorder and county clerk, "to engage in an unlawful course of conduct."

On the same day that the county sent McCotter its response, the Justice Department sued California, Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Logan, and claimed that state officials had failed to work collaboratively with the federal government to identify any noncitizens registered to vote in the state and protect the integrity of elections.

The Justice Department asked a federal judge to order California to put aside mail ballots of people it has identified as suspected noncitizens and to independently verify their citizenship status before counting their ballots.

The judge overseeing the case, David O. Carter, scheduled a hearing for Tuesday afternoon on the Trump administration's request for a temporary restraining order. But the following day, the Justice Department took the extraordinary step of filing an appeal with the 9th Circuit.

Government lawyers argued that because Carter had not yet ruled on their request for emergency relief, his "silence" amounted to a "constructive denial" of their effort to require California to set aside the mail ballots returned by the voters on the Trump administration's list.

The three-judge 9th Circuit panel then held a rare Sunday oral argument session, during which at least two of the judges appeared skeptical of the Justice Department's request for the court to step in.

The 11th-hour lawsuit against California officials was filed less than three weeks before the November midterm elections, when voters across the country will decide which party controls the House and Senate. In California, elections officials began mailing ballots in early October. Los Angeles County has already processed an estimated 550,000 mail ballots, according to court filings.

In the months leading up to the midterms, Mr. Trump has attempted to exert more federal control over elections and pushed Congress to enact a package of voting regulations, including requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote.

The president has repeatedly claimed that hundreds of thousands of noncitizens are registered to vote in federal elections, including more than 190,000 in California. Both federal and California law prohibit noncitizens from voting.
But the Department of Homeland Security has declined to provide California election officials with an explanation of how it identified those alleged ineligible voters.

Instead, in its lawsuit, the Justice Department said the DHS compares information about voter rolls with internal data to identify potential matches between registered voters and possible noncitizens, and then uses "third-party software" to identify matches between voter information and data about that person compiled by the software program. The Trump administration also said it uses internal records and data from the Social Security Administration.

But California officials have argued that the Justice Department's lawsuit does not contain any allegations that those suspected noncitizens will even vote unlawfully in the general election. Lawyers for Logan, the Los Angeles County registrar-recorder and county clerk, also said that the relief sought by the Trump administration exceeds the executive branch's constitutional authority.
The Constitution's Elections Clause gives states the power to set the "times, places and manners" of congressional elections unless Congress steps in.

Amid the ongoing litigation, lawyers for Logan and Los Angeles County said they attempted to analyze the data from the Trump administration's list of alleged noncitizens. The list includes 7,035 records with county addresses, they said. County officials reviewed a sample of 200 of those records and found 112 of them correspond to voter registrations that were canceled or inactive, so no ballot was mailed to that person.
Most of the people in the sample had never voted, and more than one-quarter of them listed a birthplace in the U.S., according to a Los Angeles County election official.

Federal prosecutors sent more letters to at least 18 other California county registrars on Friday with lists of alleged noncitizens registered to vote. The Justice Department demanded the elections officials set aside ballots cast by those it believes are ineligible to vote.
The Justice Department could ask the full 9th Circuit to reconsider its appeal, and the panel gave the government until 7 p.m. local time to make such a request.

title: Bishops lament White House meeting that produced photo with Trump
summary: Two Catholic bishops have expressed regret about agreeing to a White House meeting that produced a publicly distributed photo of them praying with President Trump.
story: Two Catholic bishops have expressed regret about agreeing to a White House meeting that produced a publicly distributed photo of them praying with President Trump.

Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, in a statement titled "A Public Apology," said Sunday that he had received many questions and comments — some of them distraught — about the meeting on Thursday that he and 11 other bishops attended.
He said the meeting was speedily publicized by the White House with photos and a video without consent of the participants, less than two weeks away from the midterm elections.

"I feel a heavy sadness, not only over the pain I caused, but also for the fact that something so sacred to a group of religious leaders, prayer to our Heavenly Father, would be manipulated in that way," Grob said.
The bishop of Des Moines, Iowa, William Joensen, also issued a statement making clear he felt the White House had taken advantage of the bishops.

"I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purpose," he wrote. "I pray I am more prudent and wise going forward, even as I remain resolute in my openness to engaging and praying for political leaders at all levels."

Asked whether the White House had received the bishops' consent for releasing the photos and video, the press office declined to answer. Instead, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers replied, "There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it."

The White House invitation to the bishops, extended in September, offered discussion about such issues as immigration enforcement, religious worker visas, abortion and the use of federal tax credits to support private education, according to Joensen and Grob.

"The meeting was in no way an endorsement of the president, his policies, or his party," wrote Grob. "We were told the meeting was to be a private discussion, that several Catholic members of the Cabinet might make an appearance, and that there could be an opportunity to pray privately with the president."
"It did not take long thereafter for the White House to post a video and photos of the prayer," Grob said.

"I soon began receiving messages of serious concern over the possibility that I had inadvertently participated in a political event less than two weeks before a national election," he added. "I also heard from some who felt wounded because of the ways they or their family had been harmed by the president's policies.

" ... We came in good faith to try to work for the betterment of our fellow human beings, to ease their suffering, to build up the common good, and to pray with a president, not to pose for a political photo opportunity to benefit the few. We should never have been put in that position by the White House.

"I did not go without reservations. I wish I had heeded them," Grob concluded. "Please know that I have heard these concerns, understand how I caused them, and I apologize for any damage my actions have done."

Collectively, members of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops have diverse views on Mr. Trump and his administration's policies. Minnesota-based Bishop Robert Barron, for example, agreed to serve on his Religious Liberty Commission, which was filled almost entirely with conservative Christians. Some other bishops vehemently denounced aspects of Mr. Trump's tough stance on immigration enforcement, saying it runs counter to Catholic teaching.

title: Maurene Comey, James Comey's daughter, was unlawfully fired, judge rules
summary: Maurene Comey was abruptly fired in July 2025 from her job as a federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York. She sued the DOJ over her firing, claiming it was unlawful.
story: Washington — A federal judge on Monday found that the Justice Department unlawfully fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, from her post as a federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York.

U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman said in a 55-page decision that Comey's removal violated the constitutional separation of powers and federal law. The judge retroactively reinstated Comey to her role as a federal prosecutor and ordered the Trump administration to provide her back pay from the date of her firing in July 2025 through Dec. 20, when she accepted a different job.
Comey's lawsuit was one of several filed by former government employees who were fired without cause that tested the limits of the president's power to fire federal officials.
The Trump administration had argued that Article II of the Constitution gives the president unrestricted removal power, and said Congress could not limit the removal of federal prosecutors.

But in his decision, Furman ruled that Comey's firing violated the Civil Service Reform Act, a landmark law enacted in 1978 that provides protections for federal workers. The Trump administration, he wrote, is attempting to "upend" long-settled case law allowing Congress to regulate the removal of so-called inferior officers.
"Indeed, to accept Defendants' argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system," Furman wrote.
Comey's legal team cheered the decision as a "hard-earned victory" for her and all civil servants.

"As the Court correctly held, to accept the government's argument about unlimited executive power 'would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system.' This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law," lawyers Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan said in a statement.
A Justice Department spokesperson said it "disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course."

Comey had served as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan since 2015, handling high-profile criminal cases against figures including Sean "Diddy" Combs, Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell and former Democratic Sen. Robert Menendez.

In a letter to her former colleagues at the time of her dismissal, Comey said she was "summarily fired via memo" by the Justice Department's headquarters in Washington, and was not given a reason for her termination.

The letter she received stated, "Pursuant to Article II of the United States Constitution and the laws of the United States, your employment with the Department of Justice is hereby terminated, and you are removed from federal service effective immediately."

It was initially unclear who made the decision to oust Comey, but in May, the Trump administration said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi "directed" her removal, and her successor, Todd Blanche, "ratified" her termination.

Comey sued the Justice Department over her firing last year, alleging she had probably been fired because President Trump dislikes her father, who has been indicted twice during the second Trump administration. One of the criminal cases was tossed out, and James Comey has denied wrongdoing in the second.
"Ms. Comey's termination — without cause, without advance notice, and without any opportunity to contest it — was unlawful and unconstitutional," Comey's attorneys wrote in their complaint.

The Trump administration attempted to dismiss the lawsuit on the grounds that Comey was required to bring her claims before the Merit Systems Protection Board, the agency tasked with adjudicating appeals from federal employees regarding adverse actions taken against them, but Furman denied the government's motion and allowed the case to continue.
Furman found that because Comey's firing rested on Article II of the Constitution — not a federal law governing the civil service — the federal court had jurisdiction to hear the case.

In court filings, the Justice Department admitted that Comey had received a rating of "outstanding" on her performance reviews from 2019 through 2024, but said that her firing had been carried out under legal authority Congress granted to the attorney general to fire assistant U.S. attorneys.

In defending Comey's firing, the Trump administration relied, in part, on the Supreme Court's June decision allowing the president to fire members of certain independent agencies without cause. In that case, the high court overturned a more than 90-year-old decision that allowed Congress to restrict the president's ability to fire officials from multimember agencies at will.
But Furman said the Justice Department's argument amounted to a "sweeping and unprecedented theory of executive authority."
