title: On dating apps, men use AI to put their best face forward
summary: How much AI is too much when it comes to finding love on the apps? "It's very subtle," one dating app user said of his AI-enhanced photos.
story: Marissa, a 31-year-old Boston resident, downloaded dating apps because she is looking for love. But more and more, she finds herself looking for something else: AI-free photos.

The marketing professional said she routinely comes across dating app profiles that appear to be digitally altered. Usually, the changes are minor and can be easily made using tools like Photoshop, such as editing someone out of a photo. Sometimes, however, the photo appears to be completely AI-generated, she told CBS News, citing a photo she came across on Bumble of a man dressed in a suit tiling a bathroom wall.
"AI aside, I'm not sure what the appeal is there," she said (Marissa asked to withhold her surname for privacy reasons).

Numerous women on TikTok also report spotting photos of men on dating apps that appear to be AI-generated. Their accounts demonstrate how AI is blurring the line between what's real and what's fake in the already fraught arena of online dating. They also raise ethical questions about how far is too far when it comes to manipulating your online persona.

"People want authentic connections and conversations," Kathryn Coduto, an assistant professor at Boston University who studies dating apps, told CBS News in an email. "I think AI has made people more wary and skeptical of others, especially people they don't know."

Of course, dating app users have long relied on filters and other editing tools to polish their photos. But AI tools are upping the ante, allowing people to create high-quality images within seconds, and in some cases, fabricate fake scenes.

"A dater has to think about how they're going to capture someone's attention in a few seconds or less," Coduto told CBS News. "This might mean making your photo look a little better than it might have before."
To be sure, this practice isn't exclusive to men. However, they appear more likely to use AI to spruce up their dating profiles than women, Coduto added.
"So far, men are more interested in AI in the dating space, which isn't surprising," Coduto said. "Women tend to receive more matches and messages, so men have a harder time standing out."
The "digital stylist" who helps men AI their photos

AI can create obvious distortions when it generates photos, such as omitting a finger from someone's hand. For Marissa, a telltale sign is the person's face, which sometimes looks "waxy" in AI-generated photos, she said.
Still, as technology improves, it's becoming harder to distinguish a real photo from one created by AI models.

Lana Li, a Brooklyn, New York, dating consultant who runs the Substack "Love Me Like a Robot," calls herself a "digital stylist." She uses AI to help men level up their dating app photos, and defends using the technology as long as the photos still genuinely represent who they are.

"I can take a picture of somebody and then put them in a different outfit or change their hairstyle a little bit, or put different shoes on them," she told CBS News. "Or if I think their body language doesn't look confident in the picture, I will have [ChatGPT] change that."
The 37-year-old also uses FaceApp to change men's facial expressions. She said the edits are subtle, such as slightly lifting the corner of someone's mouth to make them look "friendlier."

Despite her liberal approach to using AI, there are lines Li is unwilling to cross. For example, one client asked her to digitally alter a photo so that his head was on a marathon runner's body — a request she declined.
"I told him, 'I can't work with you if you want to not represent yourself accurately,'" she said.

Two men who spoke to CBS News on the condition of anonymity to maintain their privacy told CBS News they've used AI in their online dating photos, but in ways they feel stop short of being misleading and remain true to who they are.
A ban on Hinge
One man, a 30-year-old tech employee and client of Li's, said she used ChatGPT to digitally clothe him in more professional garb and to tame his frizzy hair.

"It's very subtle," the New York City resident said, saying he still looked like himself, even with the edits. He emphasized that he doesn't want to "catfish" anyone — a concern for singles even in the absence of AI.

Another man is pulling back after one of his AI photos backfired. The 50-something-year-old New York City resident said he fed photos of himself into Aragon.ai, an AI headshot generator, which produced a picture of him standing on a Manhattan roof with a sunset in the background. It immediately drew hits on his Hinge profile.

"This picture generally got the most likes," he told CBS News. "Now that could just be because it was the first thing they saw. But regardless, it was proving to be effective, and women seemed to like it."
That was, until Hinge banned him. He managed to get his account back but ultimately decided to delete the sunset photo, suspecting it was the reason for his removal from the app.
"How much AI am I OK with?"

Most popular dating apps have policies that limit the use of AI-generated images in people's profiles. Hinge emphasizes the importance of authenticity on its website, noting that people should be able to discern "fact from fiction."
"If you decide to include generative AI images, audio, or video in your profile, it should not be used to misrepresent yourself or your intentions," the company says on its AI policy page.

Hinge also uses automated tools and human reviewers to detect and remove "prohibited material," according to the company's terms of service. If users see suspicious AI material, they can confidentially report it through the app or online.

A spokesperson for Match Group, which owns Hinge, Tinder and a handful of other dating apps, told CBS that as generative AI evolves, the company is "watching closely and listening to daters, who tell us they want more transparency, more authenticity, and more confidence that a real person is on the other end."

Bumble also uses tools to detect and weed out AI-generated content, and lets users report profiles that feature such images. A spokesperson said the company prohibits inauthentic profiles, and Bumble's community guidelines bar the use of "artificially generated photos or enhanced photos to deceive others."

"We enforce this through a combination of AI-powered tools, human moderation, verification features and member reporting, and we take action based on the severity of a violation, up to and including permanently banning accounts," the spokesperson said.
Marissa, the 31-year-old who lives in Boston, said that when she sees a person's profile whose photos bear the hallmarks of AI, she chooses to move along.
"The dating pool is already challenging, and this is just another thing we have to grapple with," she said. "How much AI am I OK with?"

title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion to New Mexico in data privacy ruling
summary: A jury found that the social media company had deceived consumers for years about its data privacy policies.
story: Meta has been ordered by a judge in New Mexico to pay $25 billion to the state after a jury found that the social media company deceived consumers for years about its data privacy policies.

Judge Francis Mathew handed down the amount, which New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez described as "one of the largest, if not the single largest state verdict against a company in American history."
"This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley," Torrez said in a news conference.

In September, jury members found that Facebook had made false or misleading statements by telling consumers that they controlled how their information was shared. The social media giant also misled consumers by claiming it didn't sell or share personal information with advertisers, the jury concluded.

The jury found that the company's "most senior leadership," including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and former chief operating officer Sheryl Sandberg, made misrepresentations about the service's data privacy policies, the judge ruled.
"These communications were part of a coherent strategy designed to mislead the public," Mathew wrote.

The case stemmed from allegations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, to generate targeted ads.
In a statement on Wednesday, Torrez said that the case "has always been about more than one company or one scandal."
He added, "It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences."
C.J. Mahoney, Meta's Chief Legal Officer, said in a statement that the company is confident it will "prevail on appeal."

"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."
Where the $25 billion could go
Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violations of consumer protection laws are funneled toward state education spending.
"We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," Torrez said, while noting that the money would be tied up if Meta appeals the decision, as expected.
Forty-eight other states settled with Facebook in a nationwide case, but New Mexico chose to take the social media company to court on its own.
Attorneys for New Mexico had sought $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing that the company would only change its ways with a sum large enough to affect its stock price.
Lawyers for Meta said the company should pay no more than $3.4 billion, arguing that a much larger award would violate due process, be unconstitutional and not hold up on appeal.
In 2019, the Federal Trade Commission hit Facebook, then called Meta, with a $5 billion fine over its role in allowing Cambridge Analytica to collect users' data without their consent.
Meta argued that New Mexico failed to prove that the tech giant's executives made misleading statements about privacy and that its content moderation practices harmed state residents.
Shares of Meta rose $13.56, or 2%, to $707.81 in Wednesday afternoon trading.

title: Musk says SpaceX-Tesla merger has "a lot of merit." Here's why.
summary: Combining SpaceX and Tesla, whose stocks jumped after Musk said the companies are exploring a deal, would be the biggest corporate merger of all time.
story: Elon Musk on Tuesday said SpaceX and Tesla are exploring a merger — a business combination that one Wall Street analyst said could be worth nearly $5 trillion, which would make it the largest deal in corporate history.

"Both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss this idea at the request of shareholders, and these special committees consist of independent directors," Musk said during SpaceX's earnings call with investors, adding that he sees "a lot of merit to combining the companies."
Tesla's stock price rose $14.01, or 3.8%, to $387.72, while SpaceX shares jumped $14.62, or 9.9%, to $162.41 in morning trading. Here's what to know about a possible merger between the companies.
How big would a SpaceX-Tesla merger be?
The merger would likely be valued at close to $5 trillion, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at investment firm Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News.

SpaceX is currently valued at $1.98 trillion, while Tesla's market capitalization stands at about $1.5 trillion. But Tesla shareholders would likely demand a premium for their shares to agree to the merger, Ives noted.
"For the merger to get passed by shareholders, it would have to be a higher price for Tesla — likely in the $500/$550 per share range in our view," he said.

That would make the combined company one of the most valuable in the world, rivaling that of the most highly valued businesses like chipmaker Nvidia, worth $5.2 trillion, or Apple, valued at $4.95 trillion.
What is the strategic rationale for merging the companies?

The main reason for combining SpaceX, a space exploration and AI company, with an electric vehicle manufacturer is to position them for a future in which artificial intelligence, or what Musk terms "super intelligence," becomes increasingly essential to everyday life.

"There's a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing super intelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass to orbit with the Starmind constellation," Musk said in Tuesday's earnings call.

While Tesla's primary business remains manufacturing EVs, Musk has signaled that the company is shifting away from traditional motor vehicles. In January, the Tesla CEO said the company would phase out production of its Model S and Model X vehicles.

Instead, the company is changing course to focus on developing autonomous products, such as self-driving taxis and humanoid robots. Musk said Tesla will eventually produce 1 million humanoid robots a year as the company transitions to an "autonomous future." The humanoid robot, called Optimus, could hit the market in 2027, Musk said in January.
AI is essential to Optimus, allowing it to follow orders and take on various tasks, as well as to Tesla's push into self-driving robotaxis.

Meanwhile, SpaceX owns xAI, Musk's AI unit that created Grok, the chatbot that is used in the social media app X and other Musk-owned products. Musk's planned Terafab chip factory will tie all the businesses together by manufacturing semiconductors for both SpaceX and Tesla.
Combining the businesses makes sense for a "number of strategic AI and data-driven reasons, and this is the right move for Musk," Ives said in a research note.
What are the hurdles to a merger?
On Tuesday's conference call, Musk underlined that a merger of SpaceX and Tesla is far from assured, noting that a majority of Tesla shareholders would need to vote in favor of the combination.
"I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it," he said.

Musk added, "At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this, and particularly on the Tesla side, we will need a 50% vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders. And that's quite a high hurdle to try to achieve."
Even so, Ives assigns an 80% to 90% chance that the merger will happen by the end of 2027.

title: Should you trust personal AI agents? What security experts say.
summary: The more access you give personal AI agents, the more capable they can be. But should you trust them?
story: Cybersecurity expert Hed Kovetz would love to have a personal AI agent handle some of his administrative tasks and lighten his workload. But he doesn't trust any of the commercially available agents, like Meta's Muse or OpenAI's Dots, with access to his email accounts, banking details, health records and other sensitive information.

"It's tempting to use a personal AI assistant. They access your email, order stuff and pay your bills. I would love to get that kind of help," he told CBS News. "But they could be taken advantage of or decide to go beyond the scope of what they are told to do."

While Kovetz sees tremendous commercial value in such products, he believes leading technology firms rushed them to market without sufficient security measures. For that reason, he advises consumers to be discreet about what they share with personal AI agents. Yet other AI security experts advise that consumers can use the tools as long as they rely on safeguards and are aware of the risks of providing personal data to an AI agent.

"I would be careful about giving full access to some of these commercial AI agents," Kovetz said. "I am aware of the fact that their security and privacy are far from being ready. Some consumers say, 'I don't care, I don't have anything to hide.' But that's not true; they still have medical records, bank accounts."

Such agents are already tremendously popular among consumers. When Meta's Muse first became available last month, it quickly became the most downloaded product in Apple's App Store. But while AI agents promise to save consumers time and even money by reading private correspondence and spending money on a user's behalf, they could also take actions that a user never explicitly authorized, leaving the user with limited recourse.

For example, it may be hard to know whether your AI agent is working for you or a retailer, Lindsay Owens, a consumer protection expert, told CBS News. She noted that Walmart's shopping agent, named Sparky, boosted average consumer basket sizes by almost 40% compared to shoppers who browse normally. Such data suggests that some AI agents could be trying to upcharge their users, she said.
Here's what security experts say they would and wouldn't let an AI agent do for them.
Should you let an AI agent shop for you?

Lynette Owens, a consumer education expert at TrendLife, an organization formed to protect households in the age of artificial intelligence by informing them about its capabilities and risks, also warned consumers against entrusting personal AI agents with too much access and information about them.
When it comes to online shopping, she believes AI agents can be extremely useful for researching products and comparing deals, but she cautions against letting them spend money.

"If you want to offload something like comparing deals, that's OK, but I'm not ready to hand off agency around a purchase, especially a high-ticket one. I wouldn't let it use my credentials like a credit card," she said.

One reason why she doesn't trust any commercially available AI agent to roam the internet with her credit card in hand is that criminals could trick it. Using what's called a "prompt injection," cybercriminals can trick an AI agent into ignoring its original instructions, such as "Don't spend more than $25."

Unlike traditional cyberattacks, prompt injection doesn't necessarily require hackers to break into an account or install malicious software. Instead, an attacker can plant instructions in a webpage, email or document that an AI agent encounters while carrying out a legitimate task.
If the agent mistakes those instructions for commands it should follow, it could be manipulated into revealing private information or taking actions its user never intended.

"We've seen an increase in incidents of prompt injections, and criminals are getting more clever about how they're hiding malicious code on websites," Owens said. "We're so excited about these new capabilities, but with any new technology, the security piece always lags."
Media and technology attorney Douglas J. Wood said consumers are liable if they authorize an AI bot to shop on their behalf, and it misinterprets instructions or overspends.

"If you give an AI agent, e.g., Muse, credit card information, you are making the bot an authorized user with the power to act on it," he told CBS News. "If it exceeds your instructions and spends your money, the card issuer will argue you authorized the purchasing tool."
Under federal law, such an individual would not be entitled to loss protection, Wood explained.
"Since you can't pursue the AI bot for improper use (it is not an entity that can be sued), your only remedy is to cut it off," he said, adding that by then the harm will have already been done.
His advice to consumers is: "Don't be lazy."
"Shop the old-fashioned way with the card in your hands. Authorizing an AI agent to use your card is like giving a bank robber the vault combination and telling him to steal only $100," he said.
How much data are you sharing?

New York-based entrepreneur Chris Franco, founder of marketing firm Woodridge Growth, has taken the opposite tack. He said tech companies have been collecting consumers' personal data for decades for various uses, such as selling it to advertisers, who use it to better market their goods and services.

"We've been giving out personal data to ad platforms for the last 20 years, and all we got back was better ad targeting," he told CBS News. "With these agents, you're sharing information, but the benefits are greater. It's a trade-off, but it's a much better deal."

To be sure, he wouldn't feel comfortable giving a Muse, Dots or Instinct AI agent full rein over his life, and believes it necessary to give it strict instructions while also monitoring its behavior and activity.

He likened giving an AI agent his credit card details to a parent handing off an exclusive credit card for high-net-worth individuals to a teenager without parameters. Both would be unwise, according to Franco.

Franco also allows his personal AI agents, including Muse and Grok Bot, to comb through his Gmail inbox. He's tasked them with organizing his receipts into a spreadsheet so that he can manage — and cancel — subscriptions.
It's a task he'd estimate would take him hours to do manually, if he ever got around to it at all.
"In 10 minutes, it had found a few I wasn't using. I would have canceled them anyway, but this did it way sooner," Franco said.

He acknowledges that it has insight into his personal life, including sensitive family matters, but at the end of the day, believes that the benefits of giving AI agents great access to his life outweigh the risks.

"The upside and pros of giving it context, in my view, are so much greater than whatever sci-fi-like scenarios there are of it going rogue," he said. "I am comfortable with it having that knowledge about me, because it can help me meet my goals faster."
Ask how it works

Matt Fredrikson, a computer engineering expert at Carnegie Mellon and founder of Gray Swan AI, an AI security company, said he gives his AI agents a fair bit of autonomy but also closely monitors their activity, using tools his company builds.
"The consumer-facing agents meant for normal people aren't immediately transparent about what they're doing with your data," he said. "But you can ask for that info if you probe them."
Simply ask your agent for a plain-language summary of how it went about completing the tasks it handled for you.
He also likened outsourcing administrative tasks to an AI agent to hiring a human personal assistant, which comes with a similar set of risks.

"If you have a human assistant, you've built a relationship with them, and there's a reason why you hired them in the first place. You trust them with a certain level of authority and autonomy," he said.

Simultaneously, when working with a human personal assistant, you're engaging in conversation with them and asking them to explain their thought processes. "You have to do that with these agents as well," he said.
Columbia Business School psychology and computer science expert Sandra Matz also drew parallels between working with a human assistant and an AI agent.
"If you wouldn't trust another person to deal with your personal information and process it safely, I wouldn't trust an agent," she said.
She highlighted one distinct difference between AI and humans, though.

"What prevents humans from sharing things they know about you is that they might feel guilty or ashamed, or have a negative emotional response to breaking the trust you've built with them," she said. "You can train an agent not to violate your trust, but they may violate it because they don't have guilt."

title: New charges tossed against ex-FBI officials in Hunter Biden probe
summary: The unsigned and unsworn superseding complaint comes just hours before the defendants were due to appear in federal court in Washington, D.C. for a preliminary hearing.
story: Washington —  A federal magistrate judge on Tuesday rejected the Justice Department's 11th-hour attempt to file new criminal charges against two former FBI counterintelligence officials, saying prosecutors could not take that step without judicial review first.

In a tense exchange, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia expressed shock and anger at the Justice Department for filing an unsworn and unsigned superseding complaint against the two FBI officials after midnight on Tuesday on the public court docket, noting it was never reviewed by him to establish whether there was probable cause a crime was committed.

Filing an unsworn complaint on the public docket and bypassing judicial review, he said, is unheard of and raises questions about the DOJ's motivations. He said he would be ordering that the new version of the charging documents be "struck from the record," though the Justice Department could try to add new charges the proper way.
The docket was later updated to say that the Justice Department's filings were entered "in error."
"We have never had complaints filed that are unsigned," Faruqui said. "It is inappropriate. It harms the defendants."
"I am unaware of that ever happening before in this court," he added. "I am frustrated that I got it in the middle of the night. But I am much more concerned that it is filed on the public record."

John Borchert, a prosecutor from the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C., conceded that the effort by the government to add fresh charges without judicial review in a criminal complaint was a first for him as well.

He asked if Faruqui would agree to let the FBI agent who filed the affidavit in support of the new complaint swear and attest to his filing and then proceed with a hearing to determine if probable cause was met.
Defense attorneys for the two ex-officials balked, with one calling such a move "Kafkaesque" and Faruqui analogizing such an action to simply serving as a notary.

Faruqui accused the government of repeatedly making bizarre moves in the case that only raise concerns, saying it was like throwing gasoline on a fire, citing how the case was charged and the decision to use a special assistant U.S. attorney from out of town to help prosecute the case.

"Everything you're doing is making me more and more concerned," he said.  "Why today on this one case have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases? It makes it look like the United States is afraid of me trying to find probable cause."
"Let me address that squarely. We are not afraid of a probable cause finding," Borchert said.

Faruqui said that while he was dismissing the superseding complaint with the new charge of obstructing a congressional proceeding, the court would still proceed with a preliminary hearing to determine whether the original criminal complaint charging them with lying to Congress, which was reviewed by a magistrate judge, meets the probable cause standard.

Mary Dohrmann, one of Floris' attorneys, told the court that the changes between the original complaint and the new one the government tried to file were substantial and raised concerns about accuracy.
"The evidence is mounting that this prosecution is about some political football, and not the law or the facts in this case," she said.

Criminal complaints in felony cases are typically reserved for more exigent circumstances, such as ongoing threats to public safety or national security. And Justice Department guidelines and norms have typically urged prosecutors to avoid taking overt investigative steps on politically sensitive cases so close to a national election.
Prosecutors filing an unsworn and unsigned superseding complaint overnight is likely to raise further questions about whether the case is politically motivated.

"What is going on at the D.C. U.S. Attorney's Office? In the middle of the night, the government filed an unsigned and unsworn complaint attempting to fix the issues with their original charge against Ms. Floris and adding a new charge just as meritless as the first one," said Floris' legal team in a statement provided to CBS News.

"In our combined decades of DOJ service, we have never seen or even heard of something like this being filed," the lawyers said. "That's because the public lodging of criminal charges must be authorized by the grand jury, a judge, or the defendant herself. Here, the government has taken that power for itself in a desperate attempt to delay our client's right to challenge the charges in court and litigate this case in the media, rather than the courtroom. We have asked to address this outrageous government conduct against a decorated public servant at today's court hearing."
The allegations against Floris and Benavides
The charges center on testimony that Floris and Benavides gave a congressional committee on July 19, 2023 and September 28, 2023, respectively.

The superseding complaint alleges the defendants "knowingly and willfully provided materially false statements to the Committee about their respective awareness of and involvement in the FBI's investigations into Hunter Biden, and thereby corruptly obstructed, and impeded and endeavored to influence, obstruct, and impede the due proper administration of the law."

The complaint is focused on statements they made in testimony concerning their roles on the Foreign Influence Task Force, and one of its counterintelligence operations known as "Round River," which was focused on collecting derogatory informant reporting on, among other things, Hunter Biden, to flag the reporting as Russian disinformation ahead of the 2020 election.
Floris served as the deputy assistant director of the FITF from mid-2019 through mid-2022, while Benavides served as its section chief from mid-2019 through the 2020 election

The complaint alleges that the defendants made false statements in their testimony "for the purpose of minimizing or concealing FITF's engagement with, and communications about, the Hunter Biden investigations and to impede the Congressional investigation."

During the hearing, Ron Safer, an attorney for Benavides, cross-examined FBI special agent Bryan Witt over his communications with the House Judiciary Committee. Safer asked how he determined whether Benavides' alleged false statements were material to the committee's investigation and could have affected its decision-making.

Witt acknowledged that the FBI was not permitted to directly question committee members or their staff, and that agents instead were required to submit written questions for the record — a method he said he had not experienced before in his career.
He added that he had only interviewed Steve Castor, the general counsel for House Judiciary Committee Republicans, a day before Tuesday's hearing.
"Nobody would know from reading that affidavit that you were limited in any way in your ability to question the staffers about materiality," Safer said.

Prosecutors later told the judge that the FBI was limited in its interactions with the committee because of the Constitution's Speech and Debate clause, which insulates the legislative branch's deliberative process from the executive branch.

When Safer pressed Witt further about the conversation with Castor and the written responses from the staffers, Witt admitted that Castor was not present for Benavides' testimony, nor had he reviewed the transcript. Witt also acknowledged that the staffers who reviewed the questions from the FBI were no longer with the committee, and he did not know if they had reviewed the transcript either.
The hearing is expected to continue on Wednesday.

title: Anthropic's IPO lists 93 pages of risks. What could go wrong?
summary: Anthropic's planned IPO requires investors to reckon with the threat posed by AI. "This is not an ordinary technology risk," one expert said.
story: When Anthropic registered for its widely anticipated initial public offering on Monday, the artificial intelligence developer framed its technology as potentially game-changing for all of humanity. A dangerous game.

Nearly a third of the 335-page securities filing is devoted to outlining not only the routine risks any company might face as it seeks to grow its business, but also the extraordinary risks that Anthropic's frontier models could pose.

To be sure, companies planning to go public commonly disclose a sprawling set of risks in their IPO filings, noted Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business.

Yet the extensive risk section in Anthropic's S-1 filing also highlights a financial and operational tension at the heart of AI companies as they pitch themselves to investors. The value of artificial intelligence businesses, which in Anthropic's case is expected to top $1 trillion, depends on the continued spread of a technology that even its developers acknowledge could cause worldwide harm.
Read on for a snapshot of the risks Anthropic outlines in its IPO.
"Existential risks"

Anthropic, which deveoped the Claude chatbot, notes in the IPO filing that its technology could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," a stark contrast to the company's founding mission to build AI for the "benefit of humanity."

"The company is asking investors to fund a race to more autonomous AI while acknowledging that capability could outpace safety," David Hsu, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School who specializes in technology and entrepreneurship, said in an email. "This is not an ordinary technology risk. It is a governance issue with potentially societal consequences."

Anthropic admits that maintaining guardrails around its technology could be difficult, noting that AI models could "resist shutdown" and even engage in "blackmail" to persuade humans to "preserve the model's continued operation or access."

Models could also take actions that run counter to a user's original intent, like gaining access to third-party systems, Anthropic said. And as AI models gain greater autonomy, Anthropic said the potential consequences of such "misaligned behavior" could grow more severe.

Even if humans remain in control of AI, the technology could still be abused. In its IPO document, Anthropic said bad actors could use its models to develop weapons, conduct cyberattacks and engage in other illegal activity.
Self-replicating tech

Anthropic's reliance on its own technology to produce future AI models — a concept known as "recursive self-improvement," or RSI — represents another potential vulnerability. Although AI doesn't yet have that capability, it could come sooner than people are ready for, the company warned earlier this year.

Through RSI, models could replicate flaws or errors in future models, something that would be "difficult to detect or remediate," Anthropic said in the IPO filing. Indeed, new models could develop so quickly that it may not leave enough time for Anthropic to evaluate and safeguard them, the company acknowledged.
Cyberattacks

Anthropic warned that hackers could gain unauthorized access to the company's proprietary data, including information about its finances, models and other intellectual property, as well as users' personal data.

Such threats could come from external sources, such as nation-states or state-sponsored actors, or even company insiders with access to its systems, Anthropic said. For example, bad actors could try to gain employment at Anthropic under a false identity to access proprietary information. Employees could also be pressured to share sensitive data with external actors, Anthropic said.
Legal exposure

Anthropic said it could be sued over harm caused by its AI models. At the same time, Anthropic concedes it may not be able to adequately insure itself against such liabilities, given that the insurance industry has never had to write policies covering AI-related risks.

"With the scale of harm that could result from a catastrophic AI-related incident, no single insurer, and potentially the insurance industry in the aggregate, may have sufficient capacity or expertise to underwrite insurance commensurate with such exposure," Anthropic said in its IPO filing.

title: Convicted murderer escapes prison through fence, steals truck
summary: Authorities say a man serving a life sentence for murder escaped from a prison in northwest Tennessee, stole a truck and remained at large early Tuesday.
story: A man serving a life sentence for killing his co-worker four years ago has escaped from a prison in northwest Tennessee by slipping through a fence, authorities said. Investigators have since released surveillance footage that showed him stealing a truck in the early hours of Tuesday morning.
Officials realized Jacob Morley, 28, was unaccounted for around 11:30 p.m. Sunday at the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, the Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement.
Investigators looked at security cameras and saw Morley escape while wearing his prison uniform, officials said. They did not release any other details, including how Morley got through the fence.

Later, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation released surveillance tape showing Morley stealing a white 2008 Ford F-350, with Tennessee plates and a Lindamood Planting Company logo on the door, at around 1 a.m. local time on Tuesday. The vehicle was stolen from Lake County, which includes Tiptonville, investigators said.
The truck was found Tuesday afternoon in Marion, Illinois, but Morley's location remained unknown, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said.

The bureau said Morley remained on its "most wanted" list as of Monday, and officials have offered a reward of up to $2,500 for information leading to his arrest. In a statement, it urged residents of the area from which the car was stolen "to check home security systems, including doorbell cameras and trail cameras, for any sightings of Morley or the stolen truck."

Prison officials said law enforcement throughout the area has searched buildings and other structures near the prison about 90 miles north of Memphis in an isolated, rural area of flat land tucked near a bend in the Mississippi River near Missouri.
Morley is 5-foot-11 and 240 pounds. He has brown hair and green eyes.
Morley was sentenced to life for killing co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield's body was found in a box under Morley's Carter County home after he had been missing for a few weeks.

Along with first-degree murder, Morley was also convicted of aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest. When Morley saw deputies at his home in 2022, he led police on a chase that ended in North Carolina, authorities said.

Several violent attacks between inmates and by employees have been reported in recent years at Northwest Correctional Complex. A grand jury in July returned dozens of indictments for five inmate murders, assaults against staff and inmates and other violence.

Northwest Correctional Complex can house 1,776 men and can house minors who have been convicted as adults, according to the Department of Correction. In 2023, an audit of Tennessee prisons found the department was struggling to fill open positions at the prison and had a 61% vacancy rate for correctional officers in that fiscal year.

title: Dollar General overcharged people at checkout for years, FTC says
summary: The discount retailer routinely charges customers more at checkout than the prices it displays on shelves, price tags and ads, according to federal and state authorities.
story: The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states on Monday sued Dollar General, accusing the budget retailer of charging customers more for products than it advertised.
The chain, which operates 21,000 stores nationwide, allegedly mislabeled prices for years, "extracting millions of dollars in unlawful overcharges," the FTC alleged.

"Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last," Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement.

The FTC added that American consumers depend on Dollar General's advertised low prices to make ends meet on tight budgets, while prices that don't reflect advertised deals make it impossible for them to manage household finances.
The agency filed its complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee, Dollar General's home state.

"Our goal is 100% accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store," Dollar General said in a statement. "As with other retailers and despite our policies and procedures, occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered, and expected to make things right for the customer. In recent years, we have enhanced our price-accuracy processes and remain committed to continuous improvement."
Dollar General said it was made aware of the FTC's investigation in early February.
"Inaccurate pricing"
According to the suit, thousands of Dollar General stores unlawfully overcharged shoppers.

Dollar General "has for years engaged in deceptive conduct that harms the very consumers it claims to serve," the FTC and states allege in the suit. "Although Dollar General promises convenience, low prices, and value, the company has routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on shelves, price tags, and advertisements. This pattern of inaccurate pricing has persisted for years and affects millions of purchases across the country."
The company also faced thousands of consumer complaints claiming it failed to honor advertised prices at checkout, a sign Dollar General knowingly harmed customers, according to the FTC.
The suit seeks a permanent injunction, along with monetary and other relief.

In its statement, Dollar General said, "FTC staff also demanded a monetary amount that was untethered to — and orders of magnitude larger than — any realistic assessment of amounts attributable to pricing discrepancies."

The company said it "worked tirelessly and in good faith to resolve this matter without litigation," including an "alternative, and in our view, more reasonable, manner of calculating potential settlement ranges."

"Although we respect the FTC's role in protecting American consumers and the State representatives' role in protecting the citizens of their respective states, we will defend this litigation vigorously," it said.

The FTC leveled the unfair pricing allegations against Dollar General as other retailers face scrutiny over how they charge shoppers. Consumer advocates say retailers are developing new artificial intelligence-enabled technology that could be used to charge consumers different prices.

Groundwork Collaborative, a nonprofit think tank focused on economic policy, led an investigation into grocery-shopping platform Instacart and found that in a trial, it had used AI to simultaneously show customers different prices for the same goods from the same store.

title: DOJ asks Washington to set aside ballots from 400 alleged noncitizens
summary: Federal prosecutors said they sent a letter to the Washington secretary of state with a list of 400 people they claimed are not U.S. citizens.
story: Washington — Federal prosecutors in Washington state asked its top election official Monday to set aside ballots from more than 400 people who they believe are not U.S. citizens, expanding the Justice Department's efforts to call into question the accuracy of states' voter rolls just days before the midterm elections.

Neil Floyd, the acting U.S. attorney in Seattle, and Pete Serrano, the top federal prosecutor in eastern Washington, said they believe that many of the more than 400 registered voters are green-card holders, who have legal immigration status but are not U.S. citizens and cannot vote in federal elections.
Still, the prosecutors said that the suspected noncitizens have voted in multiple elections, and Floyd estimated that more than 1,500 ballots have been illegally cast.
"This is not the full number of noncitizens who have been voting in Washington," Floyd said. "This is only the tip of the iceberg."

Floyd and Serrano said they provided Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs with a list of the 405 people who the Justice Department claims are illegally registered to vote and asked for ballots they may cast to be segregated until their citizenship status is confirmed.

In a letter to Hobbs dated Monday, they said some of the people identified by the Department of Homeland Security as noncitizens voted in elections as recently as the August primaries. Some of the people have voted in Washington for more than a decade and have voted more than two dozen times, Floyd and Serrano said.
DHS is expected to send a second list of people who it believes are not U.S. citizens "imminently," which will then be shared with Washington elections officials, the prosecutors said.

Floyd and Serrano gave the secretary of state 48 hours, until Wednesday, to review the list of 400 registered voters to determine whether they are U.S. citizens and direct election officials to not tabulate any ballots received from them until citizenship can be determined.
"If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," they wrote.

Hobbs confirmed his office received the letter from the Justice Department but raised concerns with the accuracy of its list, which shows the last time each person voted. The department included multiple records for people who appear to have last voted in the 1990s, including a record for one individual who last voted in 1994, according to the secretary of state's office. More than 113 million primary and general election ballots have been cast since then.

"We take our responsibility to protect voter information seriously and will only respond to requests that follow due process. We saw what happened in California and don't want Washingtonians to be harassed," Hobbs said in a statement.
He said the timing of the Justice Department's request, made one week before the Nov. 3 election, "is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results."

The Justice Department sought Washington state's unredacted voter registration list last year. After Hobbs refused to turn over the information, the Trump administration sued the state in an effort to obtain the material, which includes voters' names, addresses, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers.

A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuit last month. The Trump administration has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to get their complete voter rolls, and 27 of those lawsuits have been tossed out by federal judges. Three cases remain pending. One, against Oklahoma, was voluntarily dismissed.

Floyd said during a press conference that because Washington refused to provide its unredacted voter rolls, the Department of Homeland Security used a publicly available list of registered voters in the state and compared it with government information to identify those who are allegedly not U.S. citizens. The Trump administration then conducted further investigation to see if those people cast ballots in Washington, he said.
But the secretary of state's office warned that the system used by the Justice Department mistakenly flags legitimate U.S. citizens as noncitizens, which puts their right to vote at risk.
Under federal law, it is a crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and instances of noncitizen voting are rare.

"At a time when thousands of Washington voters already face ballot rejections due to delayed postmarks, our focus should be on ensuring every eligible voter can exercise their right to vote, not creating additional uncertainty about their eligibility," Hobbs said.

The effort to set aside hundreds of ballots in Washington comes after the Justice Department sent letters to election officials in California earlier this month asking them to separate mail ballots cast by registered voters who the government claims are noncitizens.
Trump administration lawyers gave California election officials 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizens and verify their citizenship status.

The Justice Department went on to file a lawsuit against California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan. It asked a federal court to block the state from tabulating mail ballots received from 20,000 people who it believes are likely noncitizens until their citizenship status can be verified.

A hearing is set for Tuesday on the Justice Department's bid to force California to set aside the mail ballots from registered voters on its list. A longshot effort by the Trump administration to obtain an order from a federal appeals court was dismissed Monday night.

So far, the Justice Department has only sent a letter to Washington and has not yet filed a lawsuit seeking to force its election officials to separate mail ballots returned from the 400 alleged noncitizens.

title: High airfares are weighing on Thanksgiving travel plans this year
summary: Average fares for the Thanksgiving holiday were up 31% in August from a year ago, according to aviation pricing data.
story: Some Americans are choosing to stay put instead of traveling for Thanksgiving, typically the busiest time of year for airlines, due to the high cost of airline tickets.

Average fares for the Thanksgiving holiday were up 31% in August, compared to the same period last year, according to an analysis of the latest available data from Cirium. The spike in flight costs has driven down bookings for the period by 1.6%, according to the aviation analytics firm.
Bookings to the following locales have dropped even more substantially, Cirium found:
Newark (-24.6%)Seattle (-15.3%)Miami (-13.2%)Dallas (-12.6%)Denver (-11.6%)San Francisco (-11.7%)
Newark (-24.6%)
Seattle (-15.3%)
Dallas (-12.6%)
Denver (-11.6%)
San Francisco (-11.7%)
Rising jet fuel costs stemming from the war in Iran have increased airlines' operating costs. To offset those expenses, airlines have hiked fares, tacked on passenger surcharges and cut routes.

Airlines have said they expect fares to remain elevated for some time even if the Middle East conflict subsides, noting that their fuel costs are substantially higher than they were this time last year.

"It's expensive to fly airplanes," Scott Kirby, CEO of United Airlines, told Wall Street analysts in a conference call last week. "I think the tide has to rise for everyone or those airlines simply won't exist."
Jet fuel represents airlines' second-largest expense after payroll costs, which have also risen under recently renegotiated labor contracts with pilots and flight attendants.

title: John Thune's balancing act: Inside his push to save the GOP majority
summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune has tried to balance passing the president's agenda and preserving the independence of the Senate. The midterms are his biggest test yet.
story: Sioux City, Iowa — Less than 24 hours after President Trump held a raucous rally inside an airplane hangar in this western Iowa town, Senate Majority Leader John Thune stood alongside Rep. Ashley Hinson in a strip-mall bar and grill a few miles away.

Looking out over a giant water tank that punctuated the flat plains stretching out to the horizon, Thune and Hinson were hosting a roundtable with six local business owners last Friday, a decidedly less boisterous crowd than the one that had greeted the president. The event last Friday was part of Thune's final campaign sprint before the midterms, one of several stops he's made to support his GOP candidates for Senate.

Hinson fielded a reporter's question that has trailed Republican candidates all fall: How is she threading the needle between the president's demands for loyalty and his increasingly unpopular policies? She offered a version of what has become her standard answer: that she would back the president when she agreed with him, and be a "thorn in his side" when she did not.

Thune barely flinched. The exchange was representative of the balancing act he is all too familiar with — a line he's been walking for nearly two years. The South Dakota Republican has led his colleagues through unforgiving terrain, trying to do two things at once: advance the president's agenda and preserve the Senate's independence.

Now, with one week to go before the midterms, the election stands as the clearest test yet of whether that balancing act has paid off. A map that once favored Senate Republicans has turned perilous amid an unpopular war with Iran and stubbornly high gas prices, and their low-key leader faces questions voters are about to answer: Has Thune's approach worked — for Republicans, and for him? And has it been enough to keep the majority?
"Nothing's a guarantee"

One day in early fall, as the Senate prepared to leave Washington for the campaign trail, Thune was in his leadership office near the Senate chamber, where staffers were celebrating the first fireplace lighting of the season.
"Nothing's a guarantee. There are no layups," he told CBS News.

It had been almost two years since his conference chose him as leader, kickstarting a tenure that has largely been spent guiding Republicans through Democratic opposition and navigating the whims of the White House. With the midterms approaching and gas prices glowing on street corners like daily reminders, Thune made the case for staying the course.

"Right now, short-term, you have the gas price issue," Thune said. "But I think we have done the kinds of things that have set the economy up, and job creators up, for success … I think the conditions for growth are there."

Just steps away, behind the closed doors of the Old Senate Chamber, Senate Republicans had elected Thune leader on the heels of the 2024 election. There, beside Ionic columns and crimson drapes, the conference chose a man who was a far cry from the thundering, partisan politics of the moment — one whom colleagues describe with phrases like "team player" and adjectives like "kind."
It was an unorthodox match for the incoming Trump White House, and for a House speaker across the Capitol who had tied himself closely to the president, raising questions about the dynamic to come.

Thune, 65, is a conservative. He's moved much of Mr. Trump's agenda through the Senate. And in more than two decades in Congress, he's built a reputation for working behind the scenes to get results. But he is decidedly not, to the great frustration of online rabble-rousers, the frontman of the MAGA faithful. And his conference might just prefer it that way.

"He's steady, conservative, doesn't lose his temper very easily at all," said Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota. Bernie Moreno of Ohio called him a "super nice guy, incredibly well respected" and "just a very kind human being." Lisa Murkowski of Alaska said he is "a really decent man."

Even among Democrats, it is hard to locate someone who will find fault with him personally. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has called his counterpart a "good and decent American" and "someone who loves his country — as we all do."

With Thune at the helm, the Senate has approved the president's massive tax, border security and defense agenda, grinding through half a dozen marathon overnight vote sessions. There were bipartisan wins, too: a landmark housing measure, stablecoin legislation, a bill to combat revenge porn and one aimed at stopping the flow of fentanyl.
But heading into the midterms, that track record is at risk of being overshadowed by the war's toll on the economy — and by questions about what the Republican majority did, or didn't do, about it.

Though Republicans have increasingly expressed concern over the war and its impact on energy prices, only a handful have been willing to break with the president since the conflict began in February. Across more than a dozen votes forced by Democrats to rein in the president's war powers, the vast majority of the GOP conference has remained united in opposition, granting the president wide deference in steering the conflict. Now, that record is following them on the campaign trail.

Looking out on the Washington Monument from his office, Thune said voters are choosing a path for the future. If Republicans can sell the long-term dividends of their agenda and draw a contrast with Democrats, he argued, "we have a really good chance at keeping the majority."
It would come down to the "home stretch," Thune said, his foot swiveling back and forth on its heel: the messaging, the ground game, the "blocking and tackling of elections."
It's not the picture some had anticipated, Thune conceded. He framed the moment as a test of endurance, echoing a mindset he traces to his Scandinavian ancestors.
"Life is supposed to be hard," Thune said. "I'm willing to do things the hard way."
From South Dakota to the Senate

Thune's grandfather left Norway for the northern plains, laying railroads that would stretch west across South Dakota. Born in 1961, John Thune grew up in Murdo, a town with no stoplights and a population today of around 500.

His father — a World War II veteran, teacher, coach, athletic director and school bus driver — is at the center of almost every origin story Thune tells. His name, Harold Thune, now adorns the high school auditorium.
"He was our hero," Thune said of how he and his four siblings saw him.

Basketball features prominently in the stories Thune and those around him tell about his upbringing. At 6 feet 4 inches tall, Thune was a standout in high school, making first-team all-state his senior year.

After one game in which Thune scored 36 points, he remembers his father pointing out that a teammate had been wide open on a play. "He hated ball hogs," Thune said in his first floor speech of the new Congress in 2025, calling it an attitude he has carried throughout his life.

Another game became the basis for what he calls his "political heritage." After Thune sank five out of six free throws, Jim Abdnor, then a congressman, approached him and joked, "I noticed you missed one." It was the start of a decadeslong mentorship. Thune went on to play basketball at Biola University in California and later worked in Abdnor's Senate office in the 1980s. He served in the Small Business Administration under Ronald Reagan, then returned home to be executive director of the state Republican Party, serve as railroad director and head the state's municipal league. In 1996, he was elected to the first of three terms as South Dakota's at-large representative in the House.

His first Senate bid, in 2002, fell short by fewer than 600 votes. Two years later, he took on Senate Democratic leader Tom Daschle for the seat that Abdnor once occupied, orchestrating a shakeup that would be felt at the Senate's highest levels.

"That was a war," Thune said. He recalled the campaign's first debate at Dakotafest, an agriculture trade show outside Mitchell, where Daschle's wife, mother and daughters were seated directly in front of him. His campaign manager, Dick Wadhams, said the debate was when Washington began to take the race — and Thune — seriously.
"You had several hundred people at this debate in this open field outside of Mitchell, South Dakota," Wadhams said. "I mean, without sounding too much like a homer on this thing, Thune won."

Thune would pull off the upset that November, winning by more than 4,000 votes. Recruited by President George W. Bush, he became the first challenger in half a century to oust a Senate party leader. His stock skyrocketed, and he became a celebrity — at least by Washington standards — overnight. When he arrived in the Senate that winter, days before his 44th birthday, his reputation preceded him.
"He was like the dragon-slayer," said Alaska's Murkowski, who has served alongside him since 2005.

He won in part by casting Daschle as the "chief obstructionist," faulting him for blocking the president's nominees and stalling his agenda. More than two decades later, echoes of that fight remain. Thune rails, in his own Midwestern way, against what he has dubbed the "party of no," after two record-breaking government shutdowns and a Democratic blockade of the president's nominees.
But he has also faced accusations of obstruction himself — from the leader of his own party.
Thune and Trump
Thune's traditional style clashed early with the man who became the GOP's presidential nominee in 2016, nearly a decade before the two were joined in an unlikely partnership.

After the Access Hollywood tape surfaced in October 2016, Thune became the highest-ranking Senate Republican to call for Mr. Trump to withdraw from the race, and he broke with the president on a handful of policies during his first term. When Mr. Trump sought to overturn the 2020 election, Thune said the effort would "go down like a shot dog" in the Senate. After the Jan. 6 attack, he called the president's actions "inexcusable," though he voted to acquit him in the impeachment trial that followed. In the 2024 presidential race, Thune initially backed Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina. But when the party coalesced behind Mr. Trump, so did Thune.

The two worked to mend their differences before taking power in 2025. When Senate Republicans chose Thune as leader to replace Sen. Mitch McConnell, the president-elect said he would "do an outstanding job." Thune, in his first remarks after his election, vowed to work with Mr. Trump on his agenda while preserving the Senate's role as an independent body.

It wouldn't be easy. There were messy confirmation fights over controversial Cabinet picks, the era of DOGE and back-and-forths over trade policy. There was talk of a military invasion of Greenland, the uproar over Jeffrey Epstein, strikes on alleged drug boats, the surprise capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and, finally, the war with Iran.

Every day the Senate is in session, reporters in the halls outside his office pepper Thune with questions about the latest from the White House. But he seldom draws sharp lines between himself and the president, instead signaling disagreement through facial expressions and carefully hedged phrasing. Even as a series of poorly timed administration announcements derailed Senate GOP plans this summer, he spoke out only sparingly.

One day in late June, the tension spilled into public view. The president was set to attend the Senate GOP lunch — not at Thune's invitation — as he pushed a controversial elections bill known as the SAVE America Act, which Thune had repeatedly said lacked the votes. But first, Mr. Trump was due to attend a bill signing in the Capitol Rotunda, where lawmakers from both parties planned to celebrate the landmark housing legislation they had ushered through both chambers. At the 11th hour, the president canceled the signing, demanding that the elections bill pass first.

Thune was on the Senate floor when the president made the announcement. He walked out moments later to a growing crowd of reporters, saying he had just heard the news. Heading back to the floor later that morning, he said the cancellation was the president's call, but he hoped Mr. Trump would find a way to sign the bill. The president was still coming to lunch, and the day was just beginning.

Leaning against a desk, Thune fidgeted constantly as the chamber voted and the president's arrival neared. A stream of senators approached with back slaps and pitying looks. One GOP senator joked about being dressed for a "serious meeting." "Saddle up," said another, to laughter.

It had become a pattern: a White House move that upended Senate GOP plans with no warning to the leader, followed by Thune working the floor, polling his members on what came next, picking up the pieces.

The lunch meeting was explosive and in many ways emblematic of the president's approach to the Senate. Mr. Trump railed against the handful of GOP members who had supported a measure to rein him in on Iran the day before, and got into a shouting match with Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana. Thune said afterward that there hadn't been "much of a back-and-forth."

The pressure around the SAVE Act has been the most unrelenting, underscoring a broader tension between the filibuster's fiercest defender and a president who wants to kill it. Thune forecast the fight in his first floor speech as leader, arguing that the filibuster, and the voice it gives the minority, is essential to keeping the Senate a distinct body.

"Unfortunately, today there are a lot of people out there who would like to see the Senate turn into a copy of the House of Representatives," Thune said. "One of my priorities as leader will be to ensure that the Senate stays the Senate. That means preserving the legislative filibuster, the Senate rule that today has perhaps the greatest impact on preserving the founders' vision of the United States Senate."

The stance has earned him plenty of scorn from the right, amplified on social media, and simmering impatience from the president, who has repeatedly warned that Democrats will scrap the filibuster as soon as they get the chance. But Thune hasn't budged. Democrats may at some point "try and steal the car," he said, "but we're not going to hand them the keys."

Days after the president's lunch visit, the backlash hit home. The South Dakota Republican Party took up a resolution to censure Thune for his "failure" on the elections bill, claiming he had "wantonly and repeatedly acted as a roadblock" to the president's agenda. Delegates swiftly rejected it, but the effort showed the fury Thune faced on the right.

Others back home fault him for the opposite. Mike Levsen, a Democrat and former nonpartisan mayor of Aberdeen, South Dakota, has long viewed Thune as a patriot trying to do the right thing. But he now criticizes him in local news columns for not standing up to the president enough.

"I would say, 'John, what do you think when you get up in the morning, or when you go to bed at night, about what you're doing?'" Levsen said. He called Thune's posture "revolutionary" compared with House Speaker Mike Johnson's. "But boy, we needed some people with some guts. And we just haven't had them."

Since becoming leader, Thune has never publicly sparred with the president. The furthest he has gone came in July, when then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the president's patience with him was "running out" over the SAVE Act.
"Well, maybe she or somebody else ought to get on the phone and get the votes, right?" Thune said. "It's 50 around here."
At the campaign stop in Iowa last week, Thune stuck to his guns and defended how he has led.

"We do things differently, which frustrates people, the president, for example, who wants to get his agenda done quickly. That's not the nature of the beast in the Senate," he told CBS News. "So what we try to do is figure out ways to be able to work constructively with [the president] and his team to get things done."
Would he do things differently, with the benefit of hindsight?
"Not really," he said. "Not stuff that we can control."

Thune has also acknowledged the cost of his pushback. In August, when Mr. Trump declined to endorse him for another term as leader, Thune told reporters, "That's probably expected." But the next month, when Thune's name drew boos from a MAGA-aligned crowd at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, the president came to his defense. Mr. Trump's chief of staff met with Thune before the Senate left for the campaign trail, and Thune visited the White House with his family early this month. The relationship appears to have improved — for now.
With the majority on the line, that goodwill could evaporate quickly.
The fight for the Senate

One week from Election Day, Senate Republicans are looking anxiously at a map that is nearly unrecognizable from the one they saw after the 2024 elections. Then, Democrats, battered by their losses and contending with retirements of their own, appeared boxed out in all but a few states. Now, facing headwinds that the Senate GOP sees as largely beyond its control, Republicans are locked in a fight for their majority's survival.

Long before the war became a driving force in races from Ohio to Texas, Thune was working behind the scenes. He built a slate of candidates with an early focus on heading off primary clashes, along with a formidable fundraising operation that would allow Republicans to flood the airwaves down the stretch.

In Michigan and Iowa, where retirements opened up key seats, Thune moved quickly to back Mike Rogers and Ashley Hinson. He secured the president's endorsement for both despite some reluctance, according to a source familiar with the recruitment effort. (Rogers had been a CNN commentator, and Hinson didn't endorse Mr. Trump's 2024 bid until after the Iowa caucuses.) In New Hampshire, while Republicans courted Gov. Chris Sununu, Thune was quietly talking to his brother, former Sen. John Sununu, with whom he had served.

Elsewhere, it wasn't as straightforward. The push to recruit Gov. Brian Kemp in Georgia fell short, leaving a messy primary to play out. In Texas, where Senate Republicans had backed Sen. John Cornyn for reelection, the president endorsed his opponent, Ken Paxton, a dramatic and costly blow. And in North Carolina, the main super PAC supporting Senate Republicans — the Senate Leadership Fund — scaled back its spending for Michael Whatley earlier this month, a sign of the dimming prospects for holding the seat.

Alex Latcham, the executive director of the Senate Leadership Fund, said Republicans entered the final stretch with an "unprecedented financial advantage and tremendous candidates," crediting Thune's "tireless work."
Whether it's enough to keep the majority remains to be seen.

Kyle Kondik, the managing editor of the nonpartisan Sabato's Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia's Center for Politics, said if Republicans lose the Senate, it won't be because they didn't have enough money, citing SLF's financial advantage. And he said if Thune had had his way on candidates across the board, Republicans could be in better shape, pointing to Cornyn's viability against Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.

"I think Republicans are 50-50 at best to hold the Senate," Kondik said. "The Democrats might actually be a little bit ahead here in the final week. I think it's really close, but they're running a serious risk of losing the majority."
If that happens, Kondik said, he would place the blame for the loss "more at the feet of the president."

"The decision to attack Iran and the consequences of that really opened the door for the Democrats in the Senate in a way that might not be the case had that not happened, because Trump's approval is significantly worse now than it was before the attack, and it's also led to this gas price problem that I think is politically pretty damaging," he added.
Thune has campaigned with GOP Senate candidates in Kentucky, Mississippi, Georgia, Minnesota, South Carolina, Florida, Nebraska and Iowa, along with several fundraising swings.
"I said, 'I'll do whatever I can to help the team,'" Thune told CBS News. "And if that's just staying out of the way, I'm fine with that."
As the war and gas prices have darkened the picture, Thune has urged candidates to "run their own campaigns."
"The president's going to be a factor in every election," he told reporters before the recess. "But I think they need to be their own person, and I think that's the best way to win."

That is where Thune's approach meets the ballot. After two years of approving much of the president's agenda and rarely speaking out against the White House, Senate Republicans may find that distinction hard to draw. It's the same bet Thune has made as leader: that Republicans can stand with the president on policy while keeping some distance from his most unpopular pursuits. Next week, voters will weigh in.
"The job sucks"

Outside Thune's office, where a massive wall-mounted bison head named Murdo for his hometown stands guard, Thune projected tepid optimism as the Senate prepared to leave Washington. Asked whether Republicans had done enough in two years to keep the majority, he said emphatically, "Of course we have."

"We've just got to start talking about it," he said. "If we can stay focused, talk about the future and the two paths over the course of the next several weeks, based on our record of accomplishment, things we got done, things we still need to do, we've got a great argument."
Some of his own members saw it differently, and the frustration was palpable.

"We're going home, preparing for the midterms, and we've not addressed what all of you care about so deeply. That's affordability," GOP Sen. John Curtis of Utah said in a video to his constituents, pointing to high gas and diesel prices. "We just have not done a good job, and I think the voters are going to be loud and clear about how they feel about that."

GOP Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana, who has criticized Thune in recent months as "too cautious" with the Senate agenda, told reporters that Republicans should have turned to affordability immediately after passing Mr. Trump's signature tax bill in summer 2025. Another party-line bill could still come after the midterms, he said, but "you don't know what people's mood is going to be."
If Republicans fail to hold the Senate, the blame game and finger-pointing will be intense. But Thune objected to the idea that he hasn't been aggressive enough with the agenda.
"I don't know how you could be more aggressive," he said in Iowa. "I look back at the last couple of years, and I think we had wins pretty much at every turn."

Some frustration is par for the course in a 53-seat majority, where Thune can lose only three Republicans. He has often described the majority as closer to 46 in practice, with several members emboldened to chart their own path after losing primaries or deciding not to seek reelection. Corralling them, his GOP colleagues understand, isn't for the faint of heart.
"The job sucks," said Ohio's Moreno. "He's got an extraordinarily unwieldy conference, where you have 53 Republicans with 175 ideas, and everybody demands that their idea be the most important one."

There's been no sign that Thune would lose his conference's support in the leadership elections after the midterms. The bigger questions are what Thune himself wants, and whether the president might intervene, especially if Republicans see brutal losses across the board.

In September, reporters had been pressing Thune on whether he planned to run again as leader, and he suggested the midterm results would factor into his decision. In his office, he said he doesn't "like to get the cart ahead of the horse." But asked directly, he told CBS News, "Obviously I'm very interested in seeing how things turn out in the election, but my expectation is, yes."

Murkowski said it's easy to say "woulda, shoulda, coulda" about how aggressively he has steered the conference. But she said she can "only pretend to imagine the different pressures that he is under, the different levers that others are trying to pull."
"More often than not, it's just kind of like, 'Just hang in there, John,'" she said.

Former Sen. Joe Manchin, the Democrat-turned-independent who once offered to caucus with Republicans to help Thune win the top job, lamented his position under a president "who's demanding total loyalty above everything else." Manchin said his hope for Thune going forward is that he "gets his support."
"Who do you think would be able to do a better job than John, trying to hold it all together?" Manchin said.
Thune said the decision on his leadership is "going to be up to our colleagues."
Does he expect support from the president, who could push to replace him if the midterms go badly for Republicans? Thune laughed.
"Hard to say. I don't know. I mean, I don't bank on it," he said. "But yeah, if he found his way to do that, that'd be great."
