title: New details revealed in "People's Court" cold case murder arrest
summary: Michelle Parker went missing on the same day that an episode of "The People's Court" about a dispute between herself and Dale Smith Jr. aired.
story: Court documents are revealing new details about Dale Smith Jr., the man recently arrested in connection with the disappearance of his ex-fiancée Michelle Parker in 2011, including newly recovered text messages and a history of domestic violence and injuries that police never asked about during their initial investigation.

Smith was taken into custody on a charge of second-degree murder earlier this month. Police said that new evidence in the case, as well as advancements in forensic technology, led to the arrest, though some of the exact details were not provided.

Parker, then 33, disappeared on Nov. 17, 2011, the same day that an episode of "The People's Court" about a dispute between herself and Smith aired. Her car was found the next day, but she was never located. Parker and Smith share two children. Parker was reported missing by her sister, who told police that Parker had stopped by her workplace before going to drop off the children at Smith's house. Smith told Parker's mother that Parker dropped the children off and left.

Smith told police that he and Parker "do not talk anymore" and that she had only come by to drop off the children, according to the affidavit. He allowed officers to search his apartment, and nothing suspicious was found, according to the documents.
A history of domestic violence

The investigation found that Smith had a history of domestic violence against multiple women, including Parker. In 2001, while serving in the military, he was found guilty of domestic violence against his wife, Shannon Smith. He was also court martialed for distributing ecstasy at this time, and sentenced to three years in prison.

Military records also described Smith as having a "severe mood swings when subjected to minimal stress." He was prescribed anti-depressants, the military said, but had an "inability to effectively handle any level of stress" and so was removed from primary duties.

Before beginning a relationship with Parker, he was engaged to another woman, Jill Van Mechelen. The pair began dating in 2003, were engaged in 2005 and broke up in 2006. Van Mechelen told police that Smith had choked her on multiple occasions, and threatened to kill both her and her father and "make them disappear," according to the affidavit. Van Mechelen eventually obtained an injunction against Smith.

Parker's sister told police that Parker had also described multiple incidents of domestic violence.Those included an episode where Parker caught Smith at his home with another woman, and he grabbed her by the neck and pinned her against the wall before throwing her out of his house by the neck, according to the affidavit.

Angela Nunez, a friend of Parker's, told police in a 2026 interview that she remembered seeing Parker with bruises on her arms, neck and cheek. Parker also told Nunez that Smith would throw and break things when he lost his temper, according to the affidavit. Nunez also told police she was aware of Smith sending Parker belittling text messages.
Unexplained injuries

The affidavit also includes photos of Smith taken when he was interviewed by detectives. The photos show "recent scratches and abrasions" that detectives say they now believe were "defensive wounds from the victim." Scratches were found on Smith's face and left arm. He also had abrasions on the backs of his elbows.
There is no record of police asking how Smith obtained these injuries, according to the affidavit.
Cell phone records contradict Smith's statements

Earlier this year, police were able to examine additional cell phone data that had been collected, but not analyzed, in 2011.  That included more precise location and user data, as well as messages, from both phones. The examination showed that Parker and Smith had exchanged dozens of texts, which include obscenities and insults, in the days before Parker's disappearance.

Cell phone records showed that Parker's cell phone entered the cell service area nearest Smith's home at around 3:15, 45 minutes before Smith told police she dropped off their children. The phone then stayed in the area for about an hour, contradicting Smith's testimony to police. Video evidence obtained from neighbors also showed that Parker's vehicle was at Smith's home for at least an hour and 10 minutes after he said she left the property, according to the affidavit.

The phone left the area around 4:18 p.m. and then traveled seven miles west, where it was stationary from 5:08 p.m. until 8:46 p.m. before turning off, the affidavit says. The phone was later found in an area lake, even though Parker's purse and other personal effects were left in her car.

At 4:26, Parker's phone was used to respond to"Waterford," which Parker's brother and detectives believed meant she was near the Waterford Lakes shopping center. But at the time the message was sent, the phone was utilizing a cell tower about 11 miles west of the center. The cell phone never traveled near the shopping center, the affidavit said.

Records show that Smith's phone was not used from 4:45 to 9:45 p.m. on the night Parker disappeared. Data showed Smith's phone traveled west to the same area where Parker's phone was last seen. He then continued driving, eventually arriving at his parents' house. He returned back to his residence shortly after 10 p.m.
Records also showed that between Oct. 1 and Nov. 17, 2011, Smith and Parker exchanged 1,013 text messages. Smith never contacted Parker's phone again after Nov. 17.
This story published first on CBS News at 10:45 a.m. on Oct. 27, 2026.

title: House hunter discovers body in vacant home
summary: In an exclusive interview, a homebuyer shares vivid details of finding a dead man during a house tour.
story: Florida resident David Hammersley and his family were fleeing from the hurricanes that plagued Florida and decided to tour homes in Kentucky. While house hunting on Sept. 26, 2022, their realtor showed them a rural 2-acre lot with a main house, a detached garage, and a cottage in Burkesville, Kentucky — a town known as the fishing capital of Kentucky.

"The house was immaculate. No furnishings in it. You can eat off the floor," Hammersley told correspondent Peter Van Sant in "The Mansion Above Dale Hollow Lake," an all-new "48 Hours"now streaming on Paramount+.
Hammersley was impressed with the property, including the sight of a Dodge truck found inside the detached garage.
"And I started to salivate over the possibility of that being part of the deal," he said.
As Hammersley and his family approached the cottage at the far end of the property, they were overpowered by a stench radiating from the cottage.
"It had to be something like a dead raccoon, in my opinion," Hammersley said.
Hammersley and his father-in-law proceeded to investigate, and within moments they stumbled across a horrific scene.
"I saw a man on the floor, his arm outstretched, obviously dead, from gunshot wounds," Hammersley told Van Sant.

They immediately contacted the authorities, who identified that man as Michael "Mike" Harding, a California transplant who resided across the Kentucky border in Tennessee. He had been missing for over a week.

An autopsy revealed that Harding had been shot four times — twice in the head and twice in the torso. Authorities found his phone at the crime scene and lead investigator BJ Burton from the Kentucky State Police examined it to see if it could answer their questions.
"Once you start looking through the text messages and phone calls, it becomes very obvious early on that he was lured to the house," Burton told Van Sant.

Investigators learned Harding had been contacted by a realtor named James Fraser requesting a repair service because Harding worked as an HVAC technician. However, they discovered the number used to contact Harding came from a prepaid cellphone.
"It was pretty evident early on that this is a burner phone," Burton said.

Burton also discovered Harding was going through a contentious divorce with his wife Julie Harding, a captain with the California Highway Patrol. The two were living in separate places — he was in Tennessee and she was in California.

"I feel like he was blinded by love. He truly loved her ... So, I thought he found his dream girl. But to me personally, I just, I didn't like her," Mike Harding's daughter, Heather Cavalieri, told "48 Hours."

Friends and family of Mike Harding told authorities he feared Julie Harding. They got access to her call log and learned that in the months leading up to his murder, Julie Harding had around 194 calls with a man from Houston. His name was Thomas O'Donnell and he was a former car salesman now living in Napa, California.
They also determined that the prepaid phone and O'Donnell's phone were located together a few weeks before Mike Harding's death.

"And the first thing you notice is ... the phone is first turned on when it's in the Houston, Texas, area," Burton said. "I don't think Mr. O'Donnell got out here by accident. The only connection that he had to Michael Harding was through Julie Harding."

On Dec. 8, 2022, just two months after Mike Harding was found dead, authorities arrested O'Donnell for his murder. For Julie Harding, two days after O'Donnell's arrest, she was found dead at the Tennessee home where Mike Harding had been living. An investigator determined she had died by suicide.

Burton believes Julie Harding may have feared she would lose hundreds of thousands of dollars in their divorce, so she conspired with O'Donnell to kill her estranged husband. O'Donnell pleaded not guilty to the murder charge and would face trial three years after his arrest. A Kentucky jury found him guilty, and he was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 20 years.

title: Photos show Ukraine's Starlink was down during fatal strike
summary: Photos obtained by CBS News show Ukraine's vital connection to Starlink was throttled on Oct. 19, inhibiting its interception capacity when a deadly Russian strike hit a park.
story: Kharkiv, Ukraine – Yulia Spichak, a 34 year-old makeup artist in Ukraine's eastern Kharkiv region, dropped her son off at an English-language lesson on Oct. 19 and sat down in a nearby park to send a selfie to her sister, Alina. Seconds later, a Russian drone slammed into the park, killing Spichak and four others, including a 1-year-old girl.

The attack came six days after Elon Musk's SpaceX throttled Ukraine's access to Starlink, which Ukraine has been using to coordinate its defenses against Russian attacks and for some of its offensive operations. In a post on X, Musk accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by also using it for attacks on Russia.

Ukrainian officials told CBS News that the restrictions imposed without advance notice affected ground-based air defense radars and drone interceptors, hindering the military's ability to stop incoming Russian strikes.

"It's an essential part of the air defense infrastructure," Vadym Ivchenko, a Ukrainian member of parliament on the National Security, Defense and Intelligence Committee, told CBS News Monday. "I couldn't say that all other air defenses stopped working, no. But this part is quite essential for the defense of civilians in Ukraine."

CBS News obtained photographs that show Ukraine's ground-based air defense radars' Starlink connectivity dropping to .1 megabytes per second on Oct. 19, the day of the Kharkiv drone attack. That would not be enough to load a webpage, let alone power air defense radars, according to a source familiar with the technology who requested anonymity because he was not permitted to comment on the matter.
On Saturday, Ukrainian officials confirmed that Starlink's access had been restored across the country, with Musk admitting that SpaceX had throttled connectivity.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

Ukrainian officials have also complained of connectivity problems with Starshield, SpaceX's military-grade network, which runs on the same constellation of satellites as Starlink and serves as the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations. But Musk said the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment, and the White House referred CBS News to President Trump's comments last week, during which he told reporters that he did not order the Starlink restrictions in Ukraine.

Alina Spichak, the sister of Yulia, the make-up artist who died in the strike in Kharkiv, revisited the park where she died with CBS News on Sunday. She said the Geran-4 Russian jet-powered drone that killed her sister arrived so quickly the victims didn't hear it coming.

"I understand that everyone has their own lives and nobody wants to look at these horrors. But I believe that the whole world has to know what is happening in Ukraine, that there is a war here and we are being attacked," Alina Spichak said. "I really hope that it will end soon."
This story published first on CBS News at 9:54 a.m. on Oct. 27, 2026.

title: Judge continues to block Trump from cutting down trees at D.C. golf course
summary: "The Court earlier stated, 'I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees,'" U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote. "The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law."
story: A federal judge on Monday barred the Trump administration from removing trees from East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, D.C., in a colorful ruling that follows a weekslong controversy over President Trump's plans to overhaul the publicly owned course.

"The Court earlier stated, 'I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees,'" U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote. "The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law."

In a 70-page preliminary injunction ruling, Reyes prohibited the government from "removing or damaging" any trees on the golf course while a lawsuit challenging the renovation plan works its way through the court system. The judge also required 10 days' notice before the government makes "any irreparable modification" to the course.
The judge had previously blocked tree removal through Monday.

In a Truth Social post, Mr. Trump called the ruling "unconstitutional" and said his administration would seek appeal. He added that the government would move forward with closing the course on Nov. 15.

"To have to give advanced notices to a judge who has no expertise in Golf, Architecture, Landscaping, Construction, or anything else having to do with building such a World Class Project, is not fair, appropriate, or Constitutional," the president wrote, arguing the project is "totally 'as of right.'"

Mr. Trump has sought to overhaul the golf course — which sits beside the Potomac River — for months, pitching a "World Class Championship Golf Course" fit to host high-profile professional tournaments instead of the current "dysfunctional" course. The D.C. Preservation League sued over the planned changes to the course, arguing the government violated the National Environmental Policy Act by failing to analyze the project's impacts.

Reyes has sparred with the government since it cut down hundreds of trees earlier this month with little notice to the court or plaintiffs. In a hearing two weeks ago, after more than 430 trees were felled, the judge told lawyers for the government that they had "lost credibility," and she was "furious" and "thoroughly unamused."
Mr. Trump said last week the course would close for construction beginning in November, and it would reopen in 15 months. He later said work would begin "IMMEDIATELY."

In her ruling Monday, Reyes argued Mr. Trump's statements about the renovation plans were tough to square with government lawyers' position that it's legally too early to challenge the plans in court because there was no final decision.

"Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting President," she wrote. "This started as a case about golf. That good walk spoiled. But it has become much more. It now forces the Court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys."

Reyes said she was initially reluctant to intervene in the case, writing that she "would much prefer not to have to resolve Lorax v. Once‑ler redux" — a reference to an earlier court hearing in which Reyes invoked the Dr. Seuss character to explain why she wasn't interested in micromanaging the federal government's tree management efforts.
She said she only intervened "because the Government did what it assured all it would not do," by chopping down hundreds of trees on the golf course.
Reyes found that the D.C. Preservation League is likely to succeed in showing the Trump administration's plans for the golf course violate the legal requirement for an environmental review.
She also found that the tree removals were part of Mr. Trump's renovation plan, rejecting the government's argument that they were part of an unrelated maintenance effort.

The judge said she did not find statements by the Department of Interior's deputy chief of staff to be credible, including his description of the agency's tree management plan as "cleaning up" the course.
CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department and the Department of Interior for comment.
Mr. Trump has feuded with Reyes, calling her a "crazed lunatic."

Earlier this month, the Trump administration asked Reyes to recuse herself from the case, arguing that she had shown "open hostility" to the government and that her "histrionics in prior hearings have clearly demonstrated she is no longer impartial."

"To name just a few examples of bias, Judge Reyes has unfairly questioned Trump Administration attorneys' intelligence, allowed her disdain for the Trump Administration to influence how hearings unfold, and systematically disregarded basic separation of powers principles and Article III constraints on judicial authority," government attorneys wrote.
Reyes rejected that request and denied that she is biased, listing out compliments that she has paid government lawyers.

"So what happened? Not sudden onset bias," Reyes wrote in her denial. "Instead, the Government decided to remove over 500 healthy, non-invasive trees from East Potomac Golf Course. It waited until 4:55 p.m. on the Friday of a holiday weekend to give notice that it would begin removing trees within 15 hours. It removed nearly 430 trees in one day and would have destroyed hundreds more but for a rain delay."

title: Jay-Z to headline 2027 Super Bowl halftime show
summary: The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Monday night that Jay-Z will be the featured performer for the halftime festivities on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
story: The man who has helped produce the Super Bowl halftime show is stepping into the spotlight: Jay-Z will headline the show himself.
The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Monday night that Jay-Z will be the featured performer for the halftime festivities on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
The announcement included a short video of Jay-Z sitting in SoFi Stadium surrounded by goats with the caption "GOAT's out of the bag."

After days of speculation, Jay-Z is set to return to the stadium where he closed his "Jay-Z 30" concerts over the weekend. The run began with three shows at Yankee Stadium in New York, continued in London and ended in Southern California.

Jay-Z's Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to advise on and help produce the league's entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl halftime show. At the time, Jay-Z said he had told NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, "If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now."
Seven years later, Jay-Z is ready to perform after all.
Since then, the headlining halftime show performers have included Shakira and Jennifer Lopez, Rihanna, Kendrick Lamar and The Weeknd, among others.

Jay-Z, born Shawn Carter, has won 25 Grammy Awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife, Beyoncé — who has performed at two Super Bowls. His catalog includes the albums "Reasonable Doubt," "The Blueprint" and "The Black Album," and hit songs such as "Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem)," "99 Problems" and "Empire State of Mind," his collaboration with Alicia Keys.
His 1996 debut, "Reasonable Doubt," was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame last year.

Jay-Z's career has extended into music publishing, artist management and sports. He co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes.
Jay-Z became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.
Bad Bunny performed at last season's Super Bowl in February. His songs had sharp gains across streaming charts, playlists and music discovery platforms in the hours following the show.

The next morning, the Puerto Rican superstar held the top six spots on Spotify's Top 50 U.S. chart, with another song coming in at No. 8. Eleven other Bad Bunny songs were ranking in Spotify's Top 50 U.S. chart at the time.

title: Video of police being called to youth soccer game draws outrage
summary: One of the league's directors said the parents were being disruptive, but 3-year-old Nevada's mother said, "They're literally kicking him out of this place because he's good at soccer."
story: Viral video of police being called to a youth soccer game near Orlando, Florida, is drawing outrage, with some claiming the cops showed up because a 3-year-old child was too good, while the league's director says the call was made because the parents were being disruptive.

No one disputes that 3-year-old Nevada, who can be seen in several videos dominating on the pitch against kids one and two years older than him, is a soccer phenom. Even Thomas Hayes, one of the directors of the youth league Nevada was playing in, told the cops when they arrived, "The kid is very good ... He's great. Really good."

"He's really advanced compared to the other ones.  He's scoring a lot of goals, but he's pushing the kids and scoring," Hayes was seen saying on police body camera video. Hayes said he's told the kids not to push while they're playing, and that there was another incident with Nevada's parents a few weeks earlier when he swapped some of the players out, including Nevada.
"They don't like that," he said.
He told police Nevada's parents took issue with him telling the refs not to let their son push the other kids, claiming they created "a big scene, arguing with other parents."
Nevada's mom told a different story.
She is seen in the body camera video saying they always stand on the opposite side of the field as the other parents to avoid causing any disruption.
"They're literally kicking him out of this place because he's good at soccer," she told the police.
In one video of the incident taken by the family, Nevada's father is heard saying, "They called the police on a 3-year-old because he's too good."

Nevada's mother told CBS News the coach told Nevada he could stay in his most recent game if he passed the ball, but about halfway through, the cops got involved. She said in the bodycam video that she saw the other parents huddle in a circle talking about him during the game.
In an interview with media personality Lauren Lorosa, Nevada's mom said, "My son is already dressed. I cannot explain to my 3-year-old son that he cannot play today because he is so good."
Hayes said he wanted the family to leave, and he was willing to offer them a refund.

Online, there's been an avalanche of support for Nevada and his family, including from YouTube star Rachel Accurso, better known as Ms. Rachel, who commented on a post about the incident, saying she'd love to have Nevada on her show.
Not everybody has been supportive, with one coach writing, "These parents should be ashamed of themselves."
The league, i9 Sports, wrote on Facebook that it was "aware of concerns being shared regarding an incident at a local i9 Sports program, and we take them very seriously."

"The respectful treatment and well-being of every child and family matter deeply to us," it wrote. "We are working to understand the circumstances and will not speculate or share unverified information."

title: Is the Federal Reserve likely to raise interest rates this week?
summary: Fed officials will unveil their latest interest rate move this week, following the September rate hike, the first in three years.
story: The Federal Reserve is scheduled to meet this week, when U.S. central bankers will decide whether to raise interest rates for the second time this year in a bid to subdue inflation.
Most economists and Wall Street analysts expect the Fed to leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4% when officials release the latest policy statement on Wednesday.

Consumer prices have surged this year, with headline inflation across the U.S. rising at a 3.7% annual rate in September as energy costs jumped. Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and gas categories, rose 2.6% from a year ago amid signs inflation could be seeping into the broader economy. The Fed targets annual inflation of 2%.
Gasoline prices, which have hovered above $4 a gallon for the last three months, accounted for more than half the September increase in consumer prices, according to the Labor Department.

"Although the latest hot inflation readings and rise in inflation expectations will concern Fed officials, they still appear broadly intent on tightening policy at a measured pace," Thomas Ryan, senior North America economist at investor advisory firm Capital Economics, said in a recent research note.

In September, the Fed raised the federal funds rate — what banks charge each other for overnight loans — by a quarter of a percentage point — its first hike in three years, thereby raising borrowing costs across the U.S. economy. The Fed is scheduled to announce its latest interest rate decision at 2 p.m. ET on Wednesday.

The meeting comes at a crucial time, as Americans head to the polls to cast their ballots in the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Many Americans have expressed frustration with the state of the economy as they contend with rising costs of gas, food, utilities and other expenses.
Most economists and investors expect the Fed to raise rates one more time before year-end, likely at its last meeting of the year on Dec. 8-9.

According to CME Group's Fed Watch tool, which uses 30-day Fed funds futures prices to predict rate decisions, traders see an 88% probability that the Fed will hold rates steady in October and a 71% probability the Fed will raise rates in December (no meeting scheduled for November).

In quarterly projections last month, the Fed signaled that its rate-setting committee expected to raise rates later this year. At the same time, some Fed policymakers have signaled that the central bank is in no rush to lift borrowing costs.

"With the policy action we took at our September meeting, there is no need for urgency, and we have time to gather more information," New York Fed President John Williams said in a speech at the University at Buffalo following the Fed's rate hike in September.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will give a press conference after this week's rate decision. Until then, investors are unlikely to get any clues from Warsh, who has argued against sharing forward guidance on rate decisions.

title: Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 workers as it invests more in AI
summary: Roughly a quarter of Microsoft's workforce will be eligible for a "voluntary exit offer" as the company tries to shed workers.
story: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, or roughly one-quarter of its global workforce, as the technology giant invests more in artificial intelligence.

So-called voluntary exit offers are available to eligible employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the U.S., Microsoft said in announcing the buyout program on Monday. Employees must be at the vice president level or below to qualify for a buyout.

"This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's chief people officer, said in a memo to employees.

Microsoft expects to spend $175 billion on AI infrastructure, including through investments in data centers, in 2026 alone, Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said in a July earnings call with Wall Street analysts.

The exit program is the second voluntary buyout offer Microsoft has offered workers this year. In May, Microsoft planned to offer buyouts to about 8,750 people, or 7% of its U.S. workforce, the Associated Press reported, citing two people familiar with the plan who were not authorized to speak about it publicly.
In July, the company said it was cutting 4,800 jobs, about 2% of its global workforce, including many workers in its Xbox video game business.

Microsoft had 223,000 employees globally at the end of June, down from 228,000 at the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings. Around 27% of Microsoft's workforce is eligible for the new buyout offer, according to Agence France-Presse.

The offer is available to mid-level workers for what Microsoft said was a limited period of time. It's designed to let them leave the company with financial padding and career-planning resources, while allowing the company to save on labor costs.
Eligible employees will be made aware of the offer by email on Monday, Coleman said.

Workers in some business units are ineligible for the buyout, the company said. They include employees focused on data centers and those who work in sales and marketing, Bloomberg reported, citing a company spokesperson.

title: Consumers face scarier Halloween costs this year. Here's why.
summary: Americans are forecast to spend a record $13.5 billion on Halloween this year, with the average consumer shelling out hundreds of dollars.
story: Americans are on track to spend a record $13.5 billion on Halloween this year amid rising costs associated with the national scarefest, according to the National Retail Federation.
Consumers are forecast to shell out $4.1 billion on candy alone. Cocoa costs remain elevated despite surging over the last two years, with shipping and other expenses also pushing up treat costs.

Despite higher prices, the NRF expects consumers to spend $400 million more on Halloween this year than in 2025, and $1.9 billion more than in 2024. A poll from consulting firm PwC found that the average person expects to spend about $263; parents often spend the most because they're shopping for multiple Halloween events.
Two-thirds of Americans think Halloween has gotten too expensive, according to a recent survey from personal finance site WalletHub.
Why costumes cost more this year
The general manager of Chicago Costume, Cortland Hickey, told CBS News higher transportation and fulfillment costs are driving up Halloween-related prices this year.

"The tariff costs are pretty much baked into the products as opposed to being a surprise like they were last year," Hickey said. "But now it's the fuel surcharges and the cost of diesel and those kinds of things when you're receiving products on pallets and truckloads. "

For shoppers ordering online, waiting until the last minute can mean paying more for rush shipping or risking a costume that arrives after Halloween. Online shopping is less popular for Halloween purchases this year, with 27% of consumers planning to shop online, slightly down from 31% in 2025, according to the National Retail Federation.
Why candy is expensive

Chocolate prices are expected to be 8% higher than last Halloween, according to the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute. FinanceBuzz found that a 100-piece bag of assorted Halloween candy costs an average of $16.96 in 2026, up 3.5% from last year and 71% higher than in 2021.

Mondelez, the maker of Sour Patch Kids and Swedish Fish, raised prices on gummy candy packs 39%, while Ferrero, whose candy brands include Butterfinger, Crunch and Baby Ruth, raised chocolate pack prices nearly 19%.

The higher prices are a lagging effect of the cocoa market. Cocoa prices have fallen from record highs in 2024 and 2025, but shoppers have yet to see the full benefit because candy makers are still using cocoa purchased during the 2025 price spikes, according to economists.

Most of the world's cocoa supply comes from Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire in West Africa. In 2025, heat waves and heavy rains linked to climate change affected cocoa crops, contributing to shortages and price spikes. Higher U.S. tariffs on cocoa-producing countries also affected prices, although levies on cocoa and other commodities that can't be grown in the U.S. were removed last November.

Some candy makers have cut production costs by replacing traditional ingredients in milk chocolate with cheaper alternatives such as vegetable oil. Products that no longer meet the official criteria for milk chocolate can instead be labeled "chocolate candy," "chocolatey" or "chocolate coating."

According to federal rules, milk chocolate must contain at least 10% cocoa mass and solids, so candy products like Butterfinger, Rolo and Almond Joy that contain 2% or less of cocoa are labeled "Chocolate Candy."

Earlier this year, Hershey's faced criticism for changing Reese's classic recipe in certain products, such as limited-edition or seasonal candies, to use less chocolate. Following the backlash, the company said it will revert to its original recipes in 2027.
How to save

Phil Lempert, editor of the Lempert Report and an analyst focused on consumer behavior, said shoppers should look online for better deals on candy, telling CBS News that ordering on Amazon "is going to be a lot less expensive."

Comparing prices can also make a difference. Checking the price per piece or per pound on variety candy packs can reveal significant differences, with some chocolate assortments costing nearly twice as much as bags of gummy candy.

For costumes, Hickey recommends ditching prepackaged costumes and instead prioritizing items shoppers are less likely to already own or make themselves, such as specific wigs, face paints, special makeup products and props.

The higher costs are also changing when and how consumers shop. About half of shoppers said they started shopping in September or earlier, allowing them to spread out costs and search for deals, according to the NRF.
Lempert also expects Halloween-related costs to continue rising in the years ahead, citing the impact of climate change on global cocoa prices and higher fuel prices, among other factors.
"We're going to see these prices go up through 2027 and probably 2028," he said.

title: Trump's oil and gas stocks gained millions during Iran war
summary: A report from congressional Democrats found the president purchased millions in oil and gas stocks during the war.
story: Washington —  As President Trump boasts about how much money the U.S. oil and gas industry is making from the war with Iran, the president's personal holdings in oil and gas are now worth between $22.5 million and $81.6 million, compared with $12.6 million to $46 million at the end of 2025, according to a new report by Democrats on the Congressional Joint Economic Committee.

The stocks the president holds have increased in value by an average of 43% since the end of 2025, the Democratic minority said, based on data from LSEG Data Analytics. The report also found the president purchased between $4.7 million and $17.5 million in oil and gas stocks between March, after the war began, and the end of August, which is the most recently available data. He also sold between $2 million and $5.4 million in oil and gas stocks in the same timeframe, the minority found.

The report was obtained exclusively by CBS News and is based on the president's financial filings with the Office of Government Ethics. Filers are only required to report transaction ranges, not specific amounts.

But as Americans are paying significantly higher gas prices due to downstream effects from the war, Mr. Trump on Saturday night in Georgia bragged that U.S. oil and gas companies are "making hundreds of billions of dollars."

"And while oil prices are temporarily high and will be falling dramatically in a short period of time, as soon as that war's over, because there's so much oil," he told the crowd. "All in the Hormuz Strait, there are ships waiting to come, we're getting them out so fast. The United States oil and gas business is making hundreds of billions of dollars. … Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what's happened in the Middle East."
The president added that his advisers told him not to mention how much money the oil and gas industry is making from the chaos in the Middle East.

The wealthiest person to serve as president, Mr. Trump has a vast stock portfolio with holdings in all sectors of the economy. He has executed thousands of stock and securities trades this year, worth hundreds of millions of dollars, CBS News has previously reported. The White House says Mr. Trump doesn't make trading decisions himself, and his money managers try to replicate major stock indices.

"President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public – which is why they overwhelmingly reelected him to this office, despite years of lies and false accusations against him and his businesses," said White House spokesman Davis Ingle.

Ingle said Mr. Trump's stock and bond portfolio is "independently managed by third-party financial institutions" and all his holdings are "maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes."

"Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold," Ingle added. "All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers. There are no conflicts of interest."
In a July 2026 interview with CNBC, Mr. Trump said his son, Eric Trump, also handles his finances.

Energy stocks have surged as the Iran war pushed oil and gasoline prices to their highest levels in years, driving profits for oil companies. The share prices of energy companies that are listed on the S&P 500 jumped more than 50% since the start of the year, easily outpacing the broader S&P 500's roughly 11% jump.

In early February, before the Iran war began at the end of February, nationwide, the average cost of a gallon of regular gas was $2.87, and a gallon of diesel cost $3.68. Now, eight months later, it's $4.29, with diesel at $6.28 per gallon. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, is also hovering above $115 a barrel, compared to less than $75 the day before the war began.

"Trump's Iran War has forced Americans to pay much more at the pump while Big Oil rakes in profits and the president's own stock wealth in the oil and gas industry continues to balloon," said Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee. "As Trump — the country's highest ranking public employee — continues to own and trade stocks in companies that stand to benefit from his decisions, his actions raise major concerns about conflicts of interest."
Presidents, vice presidents and members of Congress are allowed to own, buy and sell stocks while in office, although insider trading laws still apply.
The minority said the president's stock purchases or total value may be even higher, since he has not yet reported transactions for September or October.

Among the nine stocks that make up the largest oil and gas holdings in Mr. Trump's portfolio, Chevron and ExxonMobil represent the most significant portion. He owns up to $23.1 million in Chevron stock and up to $18.4 million in ExxonMobil, which saw their stock prices grow nearly 25% and nearly 22% in value, respectively, since Feb. 20.
Democrats on the committee estimated American families have spent an average of $856 more on gas since the war began.
There are occasional reminders that pronouncements the president makes affect policies. In August, Mr. Trump called out ExxonMobil and Chevron by name for making "too much money" on fuel profits.

"They're making too much money, okay?" he said in the Oval Office. "Based on a shortage, they're making too much money. I don't like it. And I should be the last one to say because I'm a big free enterprise guy, nobody bigger."
Energy stock purchases and sales make up a small portion of the president's overall net worth, which Forbes estimated to be roughly $7 billion as of September.

In August, CBS News reviewed the president's oil and gas trades. One notable large transaction was on April 7, the day the president declared a ceasefire in the war. His investment accounts sold between $500,000 and $1 million of ExxonMobil stock, according to a financial disclosure report Mr. Trump filed in late June. The company's share price closed at $163.91 on April 7, before Mr. Trump announced the ceasefire that evening, and it opened down over 6% at $153.52 on April 8.
The cost of living continues to be a top issue for voters.
Last week, Mr. Trump accused Iran of trying to drive up oil prices ahead of next week's U.S. elections.

"Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election," he wrote on Truth Social. "They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."

Since Mr. Trump launched the war with Iran on Feb. 28, the conflict has stymied oil exports in the region, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz. Oil shipments from the Middle East have climbed since then as exporters look for alternate routes and some traffic in the strait is restored. But the disruptions, constricted supply and uncertainty have pushed up prices, even in the U.S., which is the world's largest exporter of total oil products.

The president has made some efforts to bring down fuel prices, including by making a deal with Russia to purchase Russian diesel fuel and waiving sanctions he had just signed into law. But that fuel from Russia, a controversial move, is a drop in the bucket of the United States' massive demand, and does little to lower diesel prices.
On Thursday, the president announced he would invoke the Defense Production Act to spend $150 million to boost gasoline and diesel production.
Mr. Trump has said gas prices will "drop through the floor" once the war is over, but even if that's the case, it's not clear when the war will end.

The president has not ruled out restarting strikes on Iran after the midterms. U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told the Financial Times the war could last another year, although he said he hopes the Iranian leaders "come to the table" before that.
This story published first on CBS News at 9:30 a.m. on Oct. 26, 2026.

title: Dictionary.com announces its 2026 Word of the Year
summary: The viral social media trend "maxxing" has earned its stripes as Dictionary.com's 2026 Word of the Year.
story: From AI chatbots to lifestyle trends, the concept of optimizing one's life came sharply into focus in 2026. That's why Dictionary.com picked "maxxing," a reflection of our increasingly online society, as its latest Word of the Year.

"Maxxing (sometimes -maxxing) is short for 'maximizing,'" says Dictionary.com. "This trendy term can be used on its own or added to the end of any word to convey you're doing something to the fullest or optimizing it as much as possible."

The word was chosen following an analysis of search data, social media trends and news stories "to capture a society that's deeply online and focused on optimization in all forms," Dictionary.com says.

"Maxxing" rose through the cultural lexicons of Gen Z and Gen Alpha quickly, and now works as a noun, verb, adjective and adverb all at once. Leveling up your workout routine? "Gymmaxxing." Your personal care practices? "Healthmaxxing," an umbrella term that covers numerous subgenres, including "proteinmaxxing" and "fibermaxxing."

"Maxxing really stood out this year because not only was it everywhere, in all types of articles, but it crossed a lot of different domains," said Steve Johnson, the director of lexicography for Dictionary Media Group, which runs Dictionary.com.

At work, people talked about "tokenmaxxing," meaning leaning ever harder on AI. In wellness circles, there was "sleepmaxxing." Even leisure received the "maxxing" treatment, with "cozymaxxing," as did politics, when the federal government used "homelandmaxxing" in some of its messaging.
"That's not something that we often get with a lot of slang terms," Johnson told CBS News.
How Dictionary.com picks a Word of the Year

Johnson keeps a running list of words to watch throughout the year, some of which have been rolled over from years prior and tracked for growing usage. To choose an annual winner, Dictionary's lexicographers look at how often a word appears in news articles, on social media and in online searches. They also weigh a word's cultural significance during selection.
"We not only look at the data behind the word usage, but we also are really looking to see what's capturing something distinctive that describes the year," Johnson said.
The latest word choice marks a turn from last year's winner, "67," a term that, despite its virality, left many bewildered over its meaning. "Maxxing" has had the opposite effect, Johnson said.
"'Maxxing' is so accessible," he said. "People do understand it because it's tied to something that people instrinsically get."
What is "maxxing"?

The word itself isn't new. "Maxing out" a credit card, or 100 miles an hour on the highway, are well-established uses that go back decades. But the newer, optimization-focused definition comes from game theory, Johnson said. In the 1940s, academics used "mini-max" to describe a strategy for minimizing their maximum possible losses, an idea that later moved into contemporary games like Dungeons & Dragons. In that context, "min-maxing" referred to building up a character's strengths in one particular area, to the point that its weaknesses no longer mattered.

According to Johnson, words like "looksmaxxing" gave the term its extra "x" and, ultimately, turned it into the trend it has become today. He said "maxxing" started standing out on its own, too, this year, in phrases like, "What are you maxxing?" or "Everyone's maxxing something."

"Looksmaxxing" remains the most popular version of the word by far. Johnson said its use rose more than 1,000% since the start of the year in the media that Dictionary.com analyzed, while "tokenmaxxing" also grew with the proliferation of AI tools.
What "maxxing" says about us
Johnson said the word captures a pressure many people feel, especially online, to constantly do, or be, more.

"Whether it's at work and your career, whether it's in school, in so many aspects of your life, just kind of being more is something that is a pressure that I think a lot of people can feel," he said.
The pressure has also produced its own pushback, as playful versions of the word like "normalmaxxing" reject the drive to optimize everything while still using the same language.
"One of my favorite 'maxxings' is 'nothingmaxxing,' which is just completely paradoxical, right?" Johnson said. "It's going all in an optimizing doing nothing, which also requires a lot of effort."
The flexibility helps explain why the word spread so widely, he said, adding: "It resonates with people."
2026 Word of the Year finalists
Dictionary.com pulled from different corners of internet culture, politics, technology and media to compile a list of finalists. Here are the others that were considered:

Affordability: the quality of being inexpensive, which is an issue at the center of American life and, now, the upcoming midterm elections, as people face increasing costs of housing, groceries, childcare and more.Data center: a building or facility used for processing, storing or transmitting large amounts of computer data, which are cropping up more often around the U.S. with the rise of artificial intelligence.Unc: short for "uncle," Gen Z and Gen Alpha popularized this humorous and lightly pejorative slang term for an older person who's uncool, trying too hard, or just doesn't get it. Odyssey: a long and eventful journey, such as that of Homer's protagonist in his epic poem of the same name, which this summer was adapted into an ensemble blockbuster by director Christopher Nolan.

title: Zookeeper dies after being attacked by leopard, safari park says
summary: The woman was attacked while caring for two Persian leopards in an indoor facility at the Beekse Bergen park in the south of the Netherlands.
story: A keeper at a Dutch zoo has died days after being mauled in a leopard enclosure, the safari park announced on Tuesday.
The woman was attacked while caring for two Persian leopards in an indoor facility at the Beekse Bergen park in the south of the Netherlands.
It is not clear exactly what happened in the enclosure as there are no cameras. The animals were inside due to bad weather and staff are usually kept away from the leopards.
She sustained serious injuries to her head and neck, according to local media. She underwent emergency surgery but died on Tuesday, the zoo said in a statement.

"The keeper started at the Beekse Bergen Safari Park at the age of 17 and worked here, with only a few short interruptions, for nearly 40 years," the park said in a statement on social media. "Her passing also deeply affects us all, and we are intensely grieving with her family, friends, and loved ones. We ask for peace and privacy for her loved ones and our staff, so that they can process this profound loss."
An independent investigation will be launched to establish the circumstances of the incident, the zoo added.
The leopards were behaving naturally, a park spokesperson told Omroep Brabant, a local media outlet.
"They are, and remain, predators," Brabant said.
According to the zoo, the leopard is "a solitary predatory cat found in Africa and Asia" and primarily hunts animals such as deer, monkeys and antelope at night.
Big cats have killed caretakers at other parks around the world in recent years.
Last year, a zookeeper was killed in a lion attack after he stepped out his vehicle at a safari park in Thailand.
In October 2024, a group of lions mauled a zookeeper to death in Crimea after a door inside their enclosure was left unlocked.
In 2020, a 55-year-old keeper at Zurich's zoo was killed by one of the park's Siberian tigers.
In 2018, a lion escaped its enclosure and killed a recent college graduate at a North Carolina conservatory during a routine cleaning.
A Malayan tiger killed a zookeeper at Florida's Palm Beach Zoo in April 2016 after a door that was supposed to be locked was left open and she was attacked.

title: Israelis living abroad spend thousands to fly in to vote in crucial election
summary: Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad have flown in just to cast their ballots in an election many voters see as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu.
story: With a consequential election in Israel Tuesday, tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad have flown in just to cast their ballots.
Ronnie Teram Gil-Ad left Israel for the U.S. with her family a year ago. She shelled out about $3,000 to come back to vote.
"It is my country. The fact that I'm living abroad doesn't mean that this is not my home here. We wanna make a difference," she said.
Gil-Ad, who will fly back to Boston Tuesday night, will have been in Israel for just 36 hours.
"This is my civic duty," she said. And she's not alone.

Another voter, Yael Natra, told The Associated Press she spent thousands of dollars to travel from Toronto to Tel Aviv to be in the country to cast a ballot. It's the first time in the two decades since she left Israel for Canada that she felt she needed to vote in her home country's elections.

"The Israel that I grew up in is disappearing," she said in an interview from Toronto, citing an eroding democracy and deeply divided society. "If something won't change this time, I don't know what's going to be."

AID Coalition, a U.S.-based nonprofit whose stated mission is strengthening Israel's democracy, estimates that as many as 67,000 Israeli citizens have arrived from abroad to vote, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data gathered for its "Fly&Vote" initiative. It says about half have been flying in from the United States, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

Offir Gutelzon helped organize the flights that brought many Israelis to vote with the organization he co-founded, UnXeptable. They say their goal is to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has dominated Israeli politics for 30 years.
Many voters said they see the election — the first national election since the deadly Hamas attack and start of the war in Gaza three years ago — as a referendum on Netanyahu.

Israel has parliamentary elections. The opposition bloc, which polls show will likely have a plurality of votes, is led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who left Netanyahu's government in 2024 accusing him of unnecessarily prolonging the war in Gaza and delaying a hostage deal with Hamas.

The mobilization of expats this year is notable, compared with past Israeli elections, Dahlia Scheindlin, an American-Israeli political analyst, told the AP. While many campaigns have focused on anti-Netanyahu sentiment, she said it's unclear overall how those flying in will vote.
"There are also expats coming in to vote for the pro-Netanyahu side," Scheindlin said.
Turnout is expected to be significant with predictions that up to 70% of Israel's roughly 7.3 million registered voters will cast ballots.
But the hard part begins after the polls close: forming a governing coalition that is stable.

title: Israeli police arrest man with knife near left-wing leader
summary: A man with a knife was arrested at an Israeli election event for left-wing leader Yair Golan as Israelis vote in a crucial election.
story: Israeli police arrested a man with a knife at an event for left-wing leader Yair Golan after what his party described as a "suspected stabbing attempt" Thursday, as Israelis went to the polls in a crucial election.
As Golan mobilized voters Tuesday in Tel Aviv, "an unidentified man wearing a jacket approached him in a threatening manner," his party, The Democrats, said.
"Golan's security guards blocked the man, and as they moved toward him, a large knife slipped from beneath his clothing and fell to the ground."
The guards "immediately subdued him before he could do anything. Police were called to the scene and arrested the suspect."
In a statement, Israeli police confirmed they "arrested a suspect in possession of a knife," but added that "contrary to reports, no attempted stabbing took place."
Golan, an ex-military officer, is the leader of Israel's main left-wing party, The Democrats, which is made up of elements of Israel's once-popular Labour Party.
He is in an electoral alliance led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, but sits further to the left.
Golan is the only candidate for a major party in Israel still supporting a two-state solution with the Palestinians.

Israeli police said that while they were escorting Golan, "officers on-site noticed a suspicious object protruding from beneath the coat of an individual standing near the public figure. The officers detained the individual for a search and discovered a knife in his possession."
The suspect, who police say is a resident of Jerusalem in his 20s, was arrested and taken for questioning.
"Incitement and violence will not deter us," Golan said after the incident, blaming the incident on the "poison machine" run by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"I call on everyone who cares about security and democracy to go out and vote now," he added.
Tuesday's incident follows a spat between Golan and the Israeli state. Golan said the security he was offered was insufficient.

"Only after a prolonged legal battle did the Shin Bet assume responsibility for his security, effective yesterday," his party said Tuesday, referring to Israel's counterintelligence and internal security agency.

"We don't want to imagine how this incident could have ended had it not been for the campaign the party waged that resulted in Shin Bet taking responsibility for Golan's security," they added in a later statement.

title: Photos show Ukraine's Starlink was down during fatal strike
summary: Photos obtained by CBS News show Ukraine's vital connection to Starlink was throttled on Oct. 19, inhibiting its interception capacity when a deadly Russian strike hit a park.
story: Kharkiv, Ukraine – Yulia Spichak, a 34 year-old makeup artist in Ukraine's eastern Kharkiv region, dropped her son off at an English-language lesson on Oct. 19 and sat down in a nearby park to send a selfie to her sister, Alina. Seconds later, a Russian drone slammed into the park, killing Spichak and four others, including a 1-year-old girl.

The attack came six days after Elon Musk's SpaceX throttled Ukraine's access to Starlink, which Ukraine has been using to coordinate its defenses against Russian attacks and for some of its offensive operations. In a post on X, Musk accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by also using it for attacks on Russia.

Ukrainian officials told CBS News that the restrictions imposed without advance notice affected ground-based air defense radars and drone interceptors, hindering the military's ability to stop incoming Russian strikes.

"It's an essential part of the air defense infrastructure," Vadym Ivchenko, a Ukrainian member of parliament on the National Security, Defense and Intelligence Committee, told CBS News Monday. "I couldn't say that all other air defenses stopped working, no. But this part is quite essential for the defense of civilians in Ukraine."

CBS News obtained photographs that show Ukraine's ground-based air defense radars' Starlink connectivity dropping to .1 megabytes per second on Oct. 19, the day of the Kharkiv drone attack. That would not be enough to load a webpage, let alone power air defense radars, according to a source familiar with the technology who requested anonymity because he was not permitted to comment on the matter.
On Saturday, Ukrainian officials confirmed that Starlink's access had been restored across the country, with Musk admitting that SpaceX had throttled connectivity.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

Ukrainian officials have also complained of connectivity problems with Starshield, SpaceX's military-grade network, which runs on the same constellation of satellites as Starlink and serves as the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations. But Musk said the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment, and the White House referred CBS News to President Trump's comments last week, during which he told reporters that he did not order the Starlink restrictions in Ukraine.

Alina Spichak, the sister of Yulia, the make-up artist who died in the strike in Kharkiv, revisited the park where she died with CBS News on Sunday. She said the Geran-4 Russian jet-powered drone that killed her sister arrived so quickly the victims didn't hear it coming.

"I understand that everyone has their own lives and nobody wants to look at these horrors. But I believe that the whole world has to know what is happening in Ukraine, that there is a war here and we are being attacked," Alina Spichak said. "I really hope that it will end soon."

title: Greenhouse gas levels set records again in 2025, U.N. says
summary: Greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere rose to record highs in 2025, locking in climate​ impacts that will persist for centuries, the U.N. says.
story: Geneva — Greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere rose to record highs in 2025, locking in climate impacts that will persist for centuries, the United Nations said on Tuesday.
Levels of the three main greenhouse gases -- the climate-warming carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide -- all rose to unprecedented figures in 2025, the U.N.'s weather and climate agency said.
The World Meteorological Organization said the rise would lead to more long-term temperature increases for the planet.
The WMO's 22nd annual Greenhouse Gas Bulletin comes ahead of the COP31 U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, from Nov. 9 to Nov. 20.
"Another year, another new record," said WMO Deputy Secretary-General Ko Barrett.
"Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, providing energy for more extreme weather and associated risks to our economies and societies.

"The past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this trend is set to continue. Carbon dioxide (CO2) has a very long life-time and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries."
El Nino's impact
The bulletin looks at greenhouse gas concentrations -- the amount of those gases in the atmosphere -- rather than new annual emissions amounts as the world burns more coal, oil and gas.
In 2025, carbon dioxide concentrations were at 426.8 parts per million (ppm); methane at 1,948 parts per billion, and nitrous oxide at 339.1 parts per billion.
That takes them, respectively, to 153%, 267% and 126% of the pre-industrial levels witnessed before 1750.
Of the three major greenhouse gases, CO2 accounts for about 66% of the warming effect on the climate.
Around half of the total CO2 emitted each year remains in the atmosphere; the rest is absorbed by the land and oceans.
From 2024 to 2025, the global average concentration of CO2 rose by 2.8 ppm -- smaller than the record surge from 2023 to 2024 of 3.6 ppm.

WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova said this reflected the "recovery of the land carbon sinks and reduced fire carbon emissions in 2025 after the strong 2023/2024 El Nino," the naturally occurring, climate-warming weather phenomenon.
"However, a 2.8 ppm annual increase is still a substantial addition of carbon to the atmosphere from fossil fuel burning."
It is also above the average growth rate for the past decade of 2.6 ppm -- a figure that stood at 0.8 ppm in the 1960s.

"We can expect to see a further increase in concentrations in 2026 because of fossil fuel burning and the development of a powerful El Nino which will impact land carbon sinks, as it did in 2023/2024," Tarasova warned.
Methane accounts for about 16% of the warming effect on our climate by long-lived greenhouse gases, though it has a much shorter lifetime than CO2.
Around a third of methane emitted into the atmosphere comes from natural sources like wetlands, with the rest from anthropogenic sources such as cattle, rice farming, landfills and biomass burning.

The bulletin said that as countries shift their energy systems toward decarbonization, more attention should be paid to two potent but less abundant trace gases closely related to electricity production and distribution: molecular hydrogen (H2) and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6).
SF6 has been rising steadily over the past three decades. It is used primarily as a spark suppressant in electricity distribution.
Why hydrogen levels have increased over the past decade is unknown but it has begun to be used as an energy storage medium.

title: U.K. charges 2 men linked to alleged terror plot against air base
summary: Two men arrested in connection with the alleged Iran-linked terror plot targeting RAF Fairford in England have been charged with national security offenses.
story: London — Two men have been charged with serious security offenses in Britain after being arrested in connection with the incident last month near RAF Fairford, the air base in England that had been used by the U.S. military to launch strikes on Iran, the U.K. Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Tuesday.
Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both British nationals and London residents, were charged under the 2023 National Security Act.

Abdulkarim was charged with "assisting a foreign intelligence service" in September and "engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities."

The CPS said Essghir was charged with a national security offense after he "approached or was in the vicinity of a prohibited place and his conduct was for a purpose that he knew, or having regards to other matters known to him ought reasonably to have known, was prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom."
Both men were arrested last week on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service in a suspected plot targeting the Fairford air base in England.

Abdulkarim was arrested by Counter Terror Police under the National Security Act last week, along with another 25-year-old man — a British-Iranian dual national who was released on bail pending further investigation.

Police are still investigating a suspected terror plot against Fairford after five men were initially detained on Sept. 27 near the base in western England. All five of those men were also released on bail, but police said they remained under investigation and would be monitored.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government believes Iran "played a part" in the incident at the base, which prompted the U.S. Air Force to remove all of its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford. The base had been home to U.S. long-range bombers for many years, and it was used during the war with Iran to launch strikes on the Islamic Republic.

Residents of a nearby town were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police and bomb-disposal experts searched the area on Sept. 27. They found gasoline in three vans that had been driven by the five initial suspects, parked close to an entrance to the base, but no explosives.

Iranian officials have said repeatedly that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets. The Iranian Embassy in London, however, said in a previous statement that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.

Police said Tuesday that six men remain free on bail in relation to the incident, four of whom were arrested on Sept. 27 — all U.K. nationals and London residents in their 20s — and two others who were detained subsequently, including the 25-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national who was detained on Oct. 1.

title: Climber dies in 5,000-foot fall after reaching mountain's summit
summary: Wolfgang Waschiczek fell to his death a day after reaching the summit of Ama Dablam mountain, according to a trekking company operator.
story: A German climber fell about 1,500 meters (nearly 5,000 feet) to his death on Monday, a day after reaching the summit of Ama Dablam mountain, according to a trekking company operator.
Wolfgang Waschiczek, 57, was reported missing from Camp 3, which lies at around 6,200 meters. He had been resting after reaching the 6,812-meter summit on Sunday, before his planned descent.
"After a successful summit, he spent a night at Camp 3 on Sunday, and on Monday morning, his guide found him missing," Gokul Thapa, head of the trekking company Real Himalaya, told AFP.

Thapa said Waschiczek's personal trekking guide, Sonam Lama, had left him in the tent for a few minutes to return borrowed equipment, telling him to stay inside. When he returned, Waschiczek was missing.
Waschiczek's body was spotted by another Sherpa at Camp 2 at around 8 am on Monday at an altitude of about 4,600 metres, Thapa said.
The body was retrieved by helicopter during the afternoon and taken to Lukla, a town known as a gateway for mountaineers and trekkers heading to the Everest region.
It was then flown to the capital, Kathmandu, where a postmortem will be performed at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital.
"Once the postmortem is done, the body will be handed over to his family members through the embassy," Thapa told AFP.
He said this was Waschiczek's second visit to Nepal.
"He had come to Nepal in 2024 for a trek, and his passing saddened us," he added.
Two Japanese climbers died last week on another peak in west Nepal, the Reuters news agency reported.
Ama Dablam lies in Nepal's Khumbu region and is considered a technically challenging mountain with steep faces.
This is the first fatality on the mountain this year.
Last October, two climbers, one French, aged 65, and the other South Korean, aged 66, died during expeditions there.
This climbing season, more than 300 climbers are attempting to scale Ama Dablam.
Mountaineers have died on other peaks this year.
In July, famed British Nepali climber Nirmal Purja and nine other climbers were killed after being swept away by an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak.
In May, two Indian climbers died on Mount Everest during a record-breaking period of ascents via Nepal's southern route.

In May, American climber Shelley Johannesen died in an avalanche on Nepal's Mount Makalu. Johannesen, co-founder of U.S.-based outfitter Dash Adventures, had successfully reached the 27,838-foot summit before she was struck by an avalanche at around 23,600 feet while coming down.

title: TikTok parent ByteDance's founder is China's richest person again
summary: The founder of Tiktok parent ByteDance, Zhang Yiming, reclaimed the top spot on a list of China's richest people, driven by his company's push into AI.
story: Beijing — ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming reclaimed the top spot on a list of China's richest people, driven by his company's push into artificial intelligence.

The rankings released by The Hurun Research Institute on Tuesday reflected that the country's high-tech sectors were rising while others, like the consumer sector and real estate, were under pressure.
The institute, which has published the list annually since 1999, found a record 1,529 people with more than 5 billion yuan (about $750 million), up 6.6% from last year.
The number of billionaires based on their net worth in U.S. dollars rose to 1,176, up 155 people - 176 more than in the U.S. That was slightly below the 1,185 people in 2021.

Zhang topped the list with $100 billion, up 43%, "almost all of it on the back of AI," and the amount was a record high for China's richest person, Rupert Hoogewerf, Hurun Report chairman, said in a statement. Hoogewerf noted that ByteDance's Doubao is China's most used AI assistant.
AI is the biggest single wealth engine on the list: 160 people - one in 10 - now make their money from AI, he said.
ByteDance is the parent company of popular short-video platforms TikTok and Douyin.

TikTok's U.S.-based operations were shifted to a new joint venture in January made up mostly of American investors due to years of national security-related concerns that almost got TikTok banned in the U.S. ByteDance still holds a minority stake in TikTok's U.S. arm.
One of the investors in TikTok's U.S. venture is Oracle, a tech company chaired by Larry Ellison. His son David Ellison is co-CEO of Skydance Corp., the parent company of CBS News.

Bottled water magnate Zhong Shanshan fell to second place on the list with $61 billion, down 23%, while Robin Zeng, chairman of CATL, the world's largest maker of batteries for electric vehicles, came in third, Hurun said.
Hurun cross-checked its information with entrepreneurs, regulators, industry experts and others to compile the list, while acknowledging limitations.
Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng, a new face on the list, ranked seventh. AI chipmaker Cambricon chair Chen Tianshi was 10th.
Trends in China's economy are reflected on the list

"This year's gains were polarised - entrepreneurs in AI, semiconductors and robotics surged ahead, whilst those in consumer, real estate and traditional manufacturing saw their wealth shrink - a two-speed economy," Hoogewerf said.

China last week said its economy grew 4.5% in the July-September quarter from a year ago, fueled by robust exports, moving closer to meeting its official annual growth target for 2026. For the entire year, Chinese leaders have set a growth target of 4.5% to 5%, down from last year's 5% expansion.

While some industries were thriving thanks to government support for technologies such as AI and electric vehicles, owners of small businesses reported tough times as their customers cut back on spending.
China's domestic demand has been weighed down by a yearslong downturn in its property market.
The Hurun list reflected that, as well.

Hoogewerf said Lei Jun, chairman of Chinese smart consumer electronics maker Xiaomi, was this year's "biggest faller," with his wealth halved to $25.1 billion. Consumer fortunes also fell across the board, Hoogewerf said.
"Today, for the first time ever, not a single mainland property developer remains in the Top 100 - the only property names left at the top are the Hong Kong landlord families," he said.
