title: 'Vertigo' star Kim Novak plans to become compost after death
summary: Kim Novak, 93, reveals she's arranged to have her body composted after death so loved ones can plant trees, calling it "a beautiful expression."
story: Laurence Leamer has written a new book about the muses of the late director, "Hitchcock's Blondes: The Unforgettable Women Behind the Legendary Director's Dark Obsession."
Kim Novak's final act comes with a twist even Alfred Hitchcock couldn't have scripted.

The "Vertigo" star has arranged to have her body turned into compost after her death so friends and loved ones can use the resulting soil to plant trees. The 93-year-old, who is the subject of "Kim Novak's Vertigo," a documentary about her life and career, first confirmed her plans to People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA).
Novak, who lives on a ranch in Oregon, told Fox News Digital she made the arrangements "a few years ago."
'CRIMINAL MINDS' STAR MANDY PATINKIN SHARES UNCONVENTIONAL PLAN FOR AFTER HIS DEATH

Kim Novak is seen here in this undated photo. The actress confirmed to Fox News Digital she's arranged to have her body turned into compost, so friends can plant trees in her honor. (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)

"The idea is that I get to live after I'm gone through trees," Novak said. "It's an exciting adventure because this is what I want after I pass. I want to keep living. And one thing that I've always been short on is patience. And a tree has to have patience. I will get to continue to express myself and be an observer of life. To me, it's a beautiful thought. It's given me great peace of mind because I'm going to keep growing. So I'm excited about that."
"It sounds funny perhaps, but it isn't really," she said. "I can't imagine being turned into ashes or being put under the ground. Both of those concepts are not too attractive to me."
Kim Novak arrives at Hotel Excelsior during the 82nd Venice International Film Festival on Sept. 1, 2025, in Venice, Italy. (Getty Images)
Novak isn't afraid of death, even if her plans may strike some as unconventional. The lifelong nature lover said her connection to the environment has given her peace about what comes next.
WATCH: ALFRED HITCHCOCKS BLONDES HAD A GREAT DEAL OF SEX, AUTHOR CLAIMS

"Some people may not even be aware that's a choice," Novak said. "And I know some people don't like to talk about death, or think they're going to be turned into ashes or be underground. It sounds awful. But you have a choice. You can decide what comes next."
Frank Sinatra and Kim Novak are seen here in a scene from the film "The Man With The Golden Arm," circa 1955. (United Artists/Getty Images)

"For me, this was a beautiful concept, the idea of becoming one with the soil," Novak continued. "And with compost, of course, everything grows so much better than if you didn't have it. It helps with growth. You become part of the process. It's natural, it's real, it's honest, it's pure. And I even get to choose the kind of flowers that are going to be part of my compost — forget-me-nots."

American actress Kim Novak poses with the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement trophy at a ceremony during the 82nd Venice Film Festival in Venice, Italy, Sept. 1, 2025. ( Li Jing/Xinhua via Getty Images)

Although human composting is legal in Oregon, Novak has arranged for her remains to be transported to an Earth Funeral facility in Washington state to undergo the process, known as natural organic reduction.
"I’m in Oregon, so it's not that big a deal," Novak said.
Kim Novak poses after receiving an Icon Award for her career during the 51st Deauville American Film Festival on Sept. 6, 2025, in Deauville, France. (WireImage)
"However, they’re going to have to pack me in ice in order to make it all the way to this place," she said with a laugh.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Kim Novak bites a pearl necklace in a 1950s publicity portrait. (Getty Images)
Novak acknowledged that additional options may now be available since she made her arrangements years ago.

"I'm having all of my compost, once it's done, delivered to friends and family, a bit of it," she said. "I have instructions for all of them to plant a tree or a shrub, but preferably a tree, because I look forward to keeping growing. That's what it's all about for me. I want to keep growing. This is a beautiful expression of life continuing after death."
American actress Kim Novak with British director and producer Alfred Hitchcock on the set of his movie "Vertigo." (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)
When Novak began planning her final sendoff, she knew she didn't want to be buried or cremated. She began exploring other options.

Kim Novak delivers a speech prior to receiving an Icon Award for her career during the 51st edition of the Deauville American film festival, in Deauville, northwestern France, on Sept. 6, 2025. (Loic Venance/AFP via Getty Images)
"Here in Oregon, there was one place where I could have had a tree planted over me," she said. "However, it was only one tree. I'd like to be many trees."

According to The Associated Press, Novak was the world's top box-office star from 1958 to 1960. The outlet reported that she stepped away from Hollywood in 1966 to pursue a private life devoted to painting.
Kim Novak poses with her painting at a photocall during the Febiofest Prague International Film Festival on March 20, 2015, in Prague, Czech Republic. (Getty Images)

"Leaving Hollywood taught me that how I live my life matters," she said. "When I left, what mattered the most was being out in nature. I’ve always wanted to be close to nature and live a natural life. Painting has allowed me to continue expressing myself while out in nature. And every day of my life, I’m painting. I can’t wait to wake up each day and start working on a new painting. Sometimes, I’ll stick with a painting for months just because I haven’t fully figured out what I want to express. It’s been a wonderful way to live a life of expression."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
James Stewart and Kim Novak on the set of "Vertigo," directed and produced by Alfred Hitchcock. (Corbis via Getty Images)

"Films were wonderful too," she said. "It’s just all the other stuff that went with it that wasn’t very appealing. But playing a character, becoming one with another person, that always gave me joy. When I look back at my life, I remember all the wonderful opportunities I was given to become a different, beautiful character. But even then, I was drawing too. I used to always draw the characters I was playing in my script. Every time I’d find some new feeling about my character, I would draw it and paint it."

Novak's film credits include Otto Preminger's "The Man with the Golden Arm," Joshua Logan's "Picnic," "Pal Joey" and "Bell, Book and Candle." Today, she continues to pursue painting away from Hollywood. But Novak believes her story won't end with her death.
Kim Novak attends the "Hommage A Kim Novak" photocall during the 66th annual Cannes Film Festival on May 25, 2013, in Cannes, France. (Getty Images)

"I made my decision because I want to do something good for the environment, and others can too," she said. "After we're gone, the Earth is still here, and we need to protect it. Life goes on when we're no longer here. And in some ways, this doesn't make you feel like you're dying. You're continuing to live on becoming part of the environment. It's something beautiful to look forward to, not dread."

Kim Novak poses at a photocall during the Febiofest Prague International Film Festival on March 20, 2015, in Prague, Czech Republic. (Getty Images)

"I don't want to be forgotten," she said. "I want to be remembered not just for films, but for what it made me into, what it turned me into. All the ways I transformed in life, I got to express myself in my art. And I'll continue to express myself."

title: ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ star Sarah Drew met husband leading worship at Christian youth camp
summary: Sarah Drew reveals how meeting husband Pete Lanfer at a Christian youth camp nearly 30 years ago gave her a grounding force against Hollywood's chaos.
story: The "Grey's Anatomy" alum is starring in Lifetime's "When I Said I Do," inspired by Clint Black and Lisa Hartman Black's hit duet.
"Grey's Anatomy" star Sarah Drew found lasting love long before she found Hollywood fame.

Drew opened up about meeting her husband while leading worship at a Christian youth camp nearly three decades ago. The actress, who has been married to Peter Lanfer for 24 years, credited their shared faith and strong partnership with helping her navigate the highs and lows of Hollywood. Drew and Lanfer married in 2002 and have two children.
"He's been my steady rock really and safe haven – since way before I had any success in this industry," Drew told Fox News Digital while promoting her upcoming movie, "Jimmy."
‘CHARLIE’S ANGELS’ STAR JACLYN SMITH LIVED APART FROM HER HUSBAND FOR 17 YEARS DURING THEIR 35-YEAR LOVE STORY
Sarah Drew and her husband, Pete Lanfer, have been married for 24 years. The couple met nearly three decades ago while Drew was leading worship at a Christian youth camp. (Paul Archuleta/FilmMagic)

"And we have been real partners in parenting and in being humans in this world together," she added. "And I think anytime one of us is feeling shaky, the other one is always able to provide a safe harbor and some real like rock-solid strength for the other. So, I do think probably he's my greatest grounding force."

Drew described the entertainment industry as an unpredictable business that can celebrate an actor one moment and discard that person the next, explaining why she refuses to let Hollywood determine her self-worth.

"I think that it's very easy for Hollywood to tell you who you are. And what I mean by that is, they love you one second, they've forgotten you the next. You're gorgeous one second. They're tearing you to pieces the next. You're working all the time one second, all of a sudden, you're not working anymore, and you don't know what's going on. You never know when you're gonna work again. There is no stability anywhere."
Drew said the industry's constant uncertainty makes it difficult for actors to find a sense of stability in their careers.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Sarah Drew credited her husband and Christian faith with keeping her grounded in Hollywood. She described Peter Lanfer as her "steady rock" and said her identity as a child of God matters more than her success as an actress. (Tiffany Rose/Getty Images)

"There is no place to be grounded in Hollywood. It just doesn't exist," she explained. "We are players to the whims of whoever is making the thing at the certain time and whoever's decided who's interesting or not, and I can't do anything about that."

"If I were not sure that my identity was firmly rooted first as a child of God, whose total identity is so much bigger than just who I am as an actress, if I wasn't rooted in that truth — and I know that truth to my cellular level and in my bones — I could so easily get caught up in the highs and think I'm God's gift to the Earth and then fall so miserably into I am absolutely worthless based on how Hollywood has decided to value me at any given time," she added.

Drew said her faith has helped her maintain a strong sense of identity beyond her career, reminding her that being a child of God, a wife, a mother and a friend matters more than her success as an actress.
Scene from Frank Capra's 1946 classic, "It's a Wonderful Life," starring Donna Reed and Jimmy Stewart.  (AP)

Drew stars in "Jimmy," a biographical drama scheduled for nationwide theatrical release Nov. 6. The film follows actor James Stewart's military service, his struggles upon returning to Hollywood and his eventual comeback in the 1946 Christmas classic "It's a Wonderful Life," directed by Frank Capra.
Drew stars as Hedda Hopper, one of Hollywood's most influential and feared gossip columnists.

"18 months before we started shooting, Aaron Burns …reached out to me and told me that he'd gotten the rights and had a script for this movie, ‘Jimmy,’ that he was gonna make about this incredibly important time in Jimmy's life. And I've always been a huge fan of Jimmy Stewart," she said.

Drew said Burns told her he wanted her to play Hedda Hopper, but she didn't know much about the gossip columnist. Burns told her about "this formidable and complicated person." Drew said she doesn't "generally get the opportunity to play roles like this, so I said yes before I got off the phone, before I read the script."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Sarah Drew has turned down acting opportunities because of their messages. The "Grey's Anatomy" star said she prioritizes projects that offer hope, redemption or meaningful connections over money, prestige or network affiliation. (Eric McCandless/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

The "Supernatural" star's Christian faith has also influenced her decision to turn down acting opportunities. While Drew isn't opposed to exploring difficult subjects onscreen, she said she has rejected projects that she believed lacked a meaningful message.
"I have turned down jobs because I'm like, I don't know what we're supposed to walk away from this feeling," Drew explained. "I don't see any hope. I only see cynicism. Then I'm not interested."
Drew said she has always been drawn to stories that offer something meaningful rather than leaving audiences feeling hopeless.

"I just don't understand choosing something that is only going to make people feel darker or more devastated or more hopeless, like those kinds of things," she said. "And I think that that does very much stem from my faith and from my sense of the story that sort of bubbles through my life and has all through my upbringing. And through my adult life and as a parent and as a friend and all of these things, is that I want there to be hope associated with everything that I touch or am a part of – something that you can really like look toward as a beacon of goodness in some ways."

That philosophy also plays a central role in how Drew evaluates potential projects, a process she said often involves conversations with her husband. Rather than focusing on the prestige or financial rewards of a project, Drew said the couple first considers whether the story is one she wants to tell.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Sarah Drew stars as influential Hollywood gossip columnist Hedda Hopper in the upcoming biographical drama "Jimmy." The film follows James Stewart's military service, his struggles returning to Hollywood and his comeback in "It's a Wonderful Life." It is scheduled for a nationwide theatrical release Nov. 6. (Gilbert Flores/Variety/Penske Media)

"It almost never is about what I might get paid, how fancy the project is, what network it's going to be on," she explained. "Those things are absolutely secondary to the first question, which is, 'Do you want to tell the story? Is this story that you think is going to resonate with people?'"

"I find that the stories that I'm drawn to are the ones that help people feel less alone and where someone can see themselves in a story," Drew said. "They can pick a redemption arc or a restoration arc and feel a little less alone. And they might laugh and cry and think on their way through the story of it, but at the end of it, they're like, 'Me too. I've also been through something like that. I know what that feeling is, and I feel a little less burdened and a little less alone because I have this opportunity to have this cathartic experience in a way that made me feel seen.'"

title: Sacha Baron Cohen says 'Ali G: Who Iz I?' is his last in this style of comedy, calling them too risky
summary: Sacha Baron Cohen reveals why "Ali G: Who Iz I?" will be his last over-the-top comedy, citing dangerous stunts and severe dehydration on set.
story: Comedian Adam Carolla says he was troubled by what he saw during COVID, when some performers appeared less willing to question authority or push against conventional thinking.
Sacha Baron Cohen is done starring in over-the-top comedies.

In a recent interview with The Hollywood Reporter, the 55-year-old actor confirmed that his new movie, "Ali G: Who Iz I?," will be his last in the risky, character-driven comedic style that made him famous.

"I want to do stuff that challenges me," he told the outlet. "So again, I’m not doing 'Borat 3,' which also would be incredibly challenging. Again, this movie I just did is the most challenging movie I’ve ever done, but I’m not doing more."

The actor has said he was done with this style of comedy in the past, but decided to make this movie because he is "terrified of where our society is headed" and thinks of his comedy as a way to comment on it.
Cohen says he is not going to make any more comedies like "Borat." (Taylor Hill/FilmMagic)
SACHA BARON COHEN’S RIPPED NEW LOOK FOR MARVEL ROLE HAS FANS DOING A TAKE

He explained that through his films, he can "show the extremism on both sides of the political spectrum and the danger of virtuous violence." He added that at the end of the day, he also "wanted to make the funniest film that’s ever been made."

"These really are the hardest movies to make, but I suppose I made it because I’m scared of this world of conspiracies and lies that are spread by social media and now by AI," he said. "If we don’t have these shared facts, then democracies crumble, and we can’t have a tolerant society. And to make people laugh is therapy."
Cohen's early breakthrough came in 2000, with "Da Ali G Show," and he later gained international recognition with the release of "Borat" in 2006.
He followed that up with "Bruno," "The Dictator," "Who is America" and "Borat Subsequent Moviefilm," as well as some dramatic roles in "The Trial of the Chicago 7," "Les Misérables" and "Disclaimer."

Cohen made a name for himself playing characters such as Borat and Bruno. (Steve Granitz/WireImage)

Throughout the interview, Cohen explained that these comedies "are dangerous to make" and are "incredibly demanding" on the body, but that he and his crew "try to limit the risks and keep everybody safe."
He described the final scene of his latest project as "an eight-hour continuous scene that takes place over 12 locations" with a lot of different elements, filmed as "a continual shot."

"There’s gunfire in it. There’s a medical procedure. There are drones, there are explosions, and it’s taking place in the desert," he said. "On the way to shooting it, I bumped into one of the great stuntmen and he said, 'You will go to hospital if you make this movie,' because I explained I’m wearing a prosthetic head in a fat suit. He said, 'You’ll be so dehydrated you’ll be in hospital for two weeks.'"

The "Balls Up" star explained that he hired "an endurance specialist who does the Tour de France" to be next to him throughout filming and that, despite the precautions, "a number of people went to the hospital for dehydration."

Cohen said a number of people went to the hospital for dehydration while filming ""Ali G: Who Iz I?" (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)

"I was about to do a scene [in 'Borat 1'] and we had a cop who had his gun on his thigh and I said, 'Why is your gun on your thigh?' He goes, 'Well, I need to be really fast to draw in this area.' I said, 'Well, how close are you to me?' And he said, 'I’ll be with you within three minutes.' I realized that was not a good thing to do, so I pulled that scene."

title: David Spade and Dana Carvey call out Hollywood for focusing too much on race and gender
summary: David Spade and Dana Carvey urge Hollywood to stop labeling actors and directors by race and gender at award shows on their popular podcast.

David Spade and Dana Carvey call out Hollywood's focus on race and gender.

In a recent episode of their "Fly on the Wall" podcast, the two comedians questioned Hollywood's emphasis on race and gender, with Spade arguing that the industry should "stop separating us like that" by highlighting those distinctions.

"On race, let me just say at any of these award shows, I saw a clip the other day saying, 'And this gentleman won, and he's the first Black director to win for this documentary,' I wish they would quit saying that because I think everyone we can't all be equal to you," Spade said. title: Josh Brolin credits strict morning ritual with helping him stay sober for 12 years
summary: Josh Brolin revealed the moment he woke up on a sidewalk outside his house and questioned the direction of his life, leading to 12 years of sobriety.
story: The trailer for 20th Century Studios' "Whalefall" starring Austin Abrams, Josh Brolin, John Ortiz and Elisabeth Shue. Directed by Brian Duffield.
Josh Brolin starts his mornings with a commitment to sobriety.
The "Dune" star said he joins a recovery meeting on Zoom every morning at 6 a.m. sharp, making the daily commitment a cornerstone of his life after years of struggling with drinking.
"Drinking got boring in the end," Brolin told The Telegraph when asked how long he had been sober.
JOSH BROLIN WATCHED MAN GET BIT BY LION WHILE GROWING UP ON WILDLIFE RANCH
Josh Brolin said he worked as a stock trader full-time in his 30s, when his Hollywood career was floundering. (Getty Images)

"Which way was I going to go for the rest of my life?" he said.
Brolin said he attends the daily meetings as part of his recovery, insisting sobriety has brought him more enjoyment than drinking ever did.

title: Michael Douglas gets explicit about how he filmed sex scenes before intimacy coordinators
summary: Michael Douglas reveals the choreography behind filming sex scenes, stressing trust and communication with co-stars before intimacy coordinators existed.
story: Michael Douglas discusses surviving stage 4 cancer, maintaining a lasting marriage and his close relationship with son Cameron. The Oscar winner has written a new memoir, "One Helluva Ride."
Michael Douglas is opening up about the "art" of filming sex scenes, revealing that the intimate moments require extensive communication and trust between actors.

During a recent appearance on "Happy, Sad, Confused" with Josh Horowitz, the 82-year-old actor reflected on filming sex scenes earlier in his career, before intimacy coordinators became commonplace on movie sets.
"There’s an art to sex scenes in films. It’s not easy to do things like shadowing people when you’re on top and this and that," Douglas said.

"But the big thing with sex scenes is trust," he continued. "And as long as the lady is trusting me — obviously I trust her — it’s like a dance. You’re taking the lead."
Douglas explained that actors carefully discuss each movement before filming begins.
BILLY BALDWIN ADMITS HE REFUSED TO KISS CO-STAR AFTER WEEKS OF TENSION ON SET

"You just talk it out slowly. ‘Kiss, kiss, bite. Looking at you. Is it all right to touch your breasts?’ ‘Yes.’ ’All right, I'm touching your breasts. Kiss. Kiss,'" he said. "You do it, and it’s just like choreographing a fight scene."

title: Jason Alexander admits ‘Seinfeld’ fame sent him to therapy
summary: Jason Alexander revealed on a podcast that he was in therapy while "Seinfeld" was still airing and explained why the fame was so overwhelming.
story: Comedian Tim Young tells Fox News Digital that anti-Israel protesters are interrupting the comedian's stand-up performances in hopes of getting a reaction that will spread across social media.
For Jason Alexander, fame wasn't all it was cracked up to be.

The "Seinfeld" star was a guest on Daniel Lubetzky's "Build or Break" podcast and discussed the iconic sitcom that helped shape his career. Alexander told Lubetzky that therapy was the only way he was able to cope with how much the show changed his life.
"You literally went to therapy?" the host asked.
JOHN GOODMAN ADMITS HE FELT 'FRIGHTENED' AFTER THE SUDDEN FAME HE EXPERIENCED FROM 'ROSEANNE'
Jason Alexander said he needed therapy to deal with the way "Seinfeld" fame affected him. (Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for Netflix)
"You bet," Alexander replied. "I was in therapy while it was happening."
When Alexander was asked why, he explained that the transition from the fame that "Seinfeld" brought him would be hard for anyone.
Michael Richards, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Jerry Seinfeld and Jason Alexander all starred in NBC’s "Seinfeld." (Vinnie Zuffante/Getty Images)

"The transition from successful at your job to international celebrity, let me just tell you, I don't care how well you've been raised or who you are, you're going to need some therapy," Alexander said.

Alexander went on to explain that he had one vision for himself when he was young, one dream to accomplish, and that was to make it to Broadway.
Jason Alexander leaned on therapy after "Seinfeld" ended in 1998. (Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images)
"My fantasy of a successful life for myself as an actor growing up in New Jersey was getting across the river and working on those Broadway stages. That was the pinnacle for me," he began.

He continued, "I didn't think about television. I didn't think about film. I dreamt about a life in the theater. God gave me that starting at age 21. By the time I was 30, I'd won a Tony Award. And now they throw in my path 'Pretty Woman,' some of the other films, 'Seinfeld.' And I now live a life as an actor that I never dreamt of, never. I never thought I would have this kind of money, that I could keep my family the way I keep them, that I would have these opportunities, that I would work with the people I've met."
Comedian Jerry Seinfeld is credited as a star and co-creator of "Seinfeld." (Todd Owyoung/NBC via Getty Images)
Alexander said that when "Seinfeld" ended, his first thought wasn't to try and replace that level of success, rather he was in awe that he was able to get there in the first place.

"So, if you hit that and then that goes away, I would never go, 'Why couldn't I keep that?' I go, 'I can't believe I ever got that.' That's not what I was thinking. So for me, life gave me more than I ever dreamed of," he said. "I didn't expect that to last. I objectively could sit back. And one of the reasons that we were so adamant at the end about making money on 'Seinfeld' is because I grew up at a time when if you had a hit series on television, you never worked again. I mean, that was it."

title: Blood sugar spikes may be tied to everyday habits you can control, expert says
summary: Jim LaValle reveals how post-meal glucose spikes, insulin resistance and sleep apnea are deeply connected, plus the 10-minute walking habit.
story: Metabolic health expert Jim LaValle explains how chronic stress, inadequate sleep and everyday dietary choices can affect blood sugar regulation and contribute to insulin resistance.
Everyday habits — from what you eat for breakfast to how much you sleep — can have a significant impact on blood sugar levels, according to a metabolic health expert.
Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels is essential for energy, organ function and overall metabolic health, while frequent or prolonged spikes and drops can contribute to health complications.

Jim LaValle, a Texas-based clinical pharmacist and metabolic medicine expert, told Fox News Digital that understanding how food, exercise, sleep and stress affect blood sugar is key to keeping levels in check.
POPULAR DIET SLASHES LIVER FAT BY 67% WHILE REVERSING PREDIABETES IN SOME PEOPLE
LaValle recommends monitoring blood sugar after meals, known as postprandial glucose, to better understand how different foods, beverages and eating habits affect blood sugar levels.
"Do I spike more from eating rice, or do I spike from eating quinoa? How much can I eat?" he said. "I think that's a foundational issue."
Stable glucose levels are essential for energy, organ function and overall metabolic balance, while spikes and drops can contribute to long-term health effects. (iStock)
The metabolic health expert noted that insulin resistance occurs when cells become less responsive to insulin, a process that can be influenced by inflammation in the body.
Normally, insulin helps move glucose from the bloodstream into muscle cells, where it can be stored as glycogen for later use.
THINK YOUR CORTISOL IS TOO HIGH? EXPERT REVEALS THE TRUTH BEHIND VIRAL WELLNESS CRAZE

LaValle said he’s a "big believer" in eating a higher-protein breakfast rather than one that’s heavy in carbs, pointing to naturally elevated cortisol levels in the morning and their potential impact on blood sugar.
"You've got to watch how many sugars are in food, how many refined carbohydrates you're [eating]," he added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

One of the simplest lifestyle habits to help lower blood sugar, according to LaValle, is taking a 10-minute walk after eating. Regular exercise is an "obvious" healthy practice, he added, although he acknowledged that it's not easy for everyone.
The expert recommends taking a 10-minute walk after eating to balance blood sugar levels. (iStock)

"It’s easy to say, ‘eat better, exercise, sleep better,’ but then people are working 16-hour days or are single parents, they get home, they open up their pantry and destroy a bag of cookies because that's the first thing they can eat and their blood sugar’s plummeted," he said.
Even a little movement after eating can be beneficial, LaValle said, particularly in a modern world that’s "eliminating the need to move."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
LaValle also emphasized the importance of managing stress, which can contribute to insulin resistance.
Along with healthy eating, exercise and stress management, getting adequate sleep is "huge for glucose regulation," he added.
"You've got to watch how many sugars are in food, how many refined carbohydrates you're [eating]," the expert advised. (iStock)

"When you don't sleep, and you don’t get enough rest to reset your body for the next day ... all those hormones that are supposed to be getting released get skewed," LaValle said, noting that insulin regulation is particularly affected by inadequate sleep.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
LaValle noted that sleep apnea is often associated with conditions such as diabetes, prediabetes, high blood pressure and obesity, emphasizing the importance of healthy sleep habits.
Hyperarousal of the brain can contribute to insomnia, LaValle added.
Sleep hygiene is important for keeping weight and stress in check, the expert said. (iStock)
For someone who’s "jacked up all day long," feeling overcommitted and anxious, that heightened state of stress can disrupt sleep and, in turn, interfere with glucose regulation.
Inadequate sleep can also affect appetite and eating behaviors, potentially making blood sugar management more difficult.

"Then you're going to start to put weight on and then, when you don't get enough sleep, you’ve got to eat more to fuel your brain," LaValle cautioned.
"So you eat more, you're not efficient at packaging that fuel up, you're moving less ... and those are the things that you have control over."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Diagnostic test could flag which men need aggressive prostate cancer treatment and which don't
summary: The Decipher genomic test could help doctors decide which high-risk prostate cancer patients need abiraterone hormone therapy and which can skip it.
story: Musician Wayne Singleton shares how a routine physical led to a rare prostate cancer diagnosis at 33 years old, and encourages others to prioritize regular health checks.
A new diagnostic test could improve the prostate cancer experience for millions of men.

Researchers at University College London (UCL) analyzed a tissue-based molecular test called Decipher to determine which men with high-risk prostate cancer were most likely to benefit from stronger treatment — and which might avoid unnecessary medication and side effects.
The analysis focused on abiraterone, a hormone therapy that was shown in the STAMPEDE clinical trial to cut the risk of death in half among men with high-risk, localized prostate cancer.
The findings were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Congress 2026 in Madrid, held Oct. 23–27.
JOE BIDEN SHARES HEALTH UPDATE AFTER PROSTATE CANCER DIAGNOSIS WHILE ISSUING WARNING TO OTHERS
Not every cancer is alike, and treating someone more aggressively than necessary could have "increased side effects and poorer quality of life," noted a UCL news release.
Because prostate cancers differ at the molecular level, not every patient benefits from adding hormone therapy.
Adding a hormone therapy called abiraterone to standard treatment for men with high-risk, localized prostate cancer could cut the risk of death in half, the trial found.

To determine whether Decipher could help guide that decision, researchers examined test scores from more than 27,000 patients in real-world data and 401 men with non-metastatic prostate cancer who had participated in the STAMPEDE abiraterone trial.
PATIENTS REMAIN CANCER-FREE NEARLY 3 YEARS AFTER RECEIVING EXPERIMENTAL IMMUNOTHERAPY

Higher Decipher scores predicted worse outcomes, meaning the cancer is more likely to spread and additional treatment may be valuable. A low Decipher score suggested more intensive treatment may be unnecessary.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Lead researcher Dr. Sarah Howlett of UCL Cancer Institute commented in a statement that for men with very high-risk prostate cancer, preventing spread of the disease is "critical."
"Understanding who benefits most from additional treatment can make a meaningful difference," she added.
A genomic test could help to personalize treatments for prostate cancer patients, the researchers suggested. (iStock)
The findings suggest that genomic testing could help tailor treatment, according to the researcher.

Men with high-risk prostate cancer and low Decipher scores may face a lower risk of spread and could avoid more intensive therapy, while those with high scores may be the strongest candidates for additional treatment.
Identifying the same pattern in both a large, real-world dataset and a randomized clinical trial strengthens the findings, Howlett noted.
CANCER WARNING SIGNS MAY APPEAR IN DNA YEARS BEFORE BLOOD TESTS DETECT TROUBLE
"But further validation in other datasets is needed before the test is used routinely to make these decisions," she said.

Elai Davicioni, medical director of urology for Decipher test maker Veracyte, also commented, "We believe this growing evidence gives physicians a stronger reason to use Decipher before making decisions that can affect both cancer outcomes and patients’ quality of life."

Men with high-risk prostate cancer and low Decipher scores may face a lower risk of spread and could avoid more intensive therapy, while those with high scores may be the strongest candidates for additional treatment. (iStock)
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel, who was not involved in the study, also commented on the findings.
"Prostate cancer varies from person to person," he said. "Medical science is increasingly aware that it is not one size fits all."
Localized prostate cancer, which has not yet spread, may contain mutations that predict how aggressive the disease will be and indicate whether it could respond to targeted therapies, Siegel noted.
About one in eight American men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in their lifetime, according to the American Cancer Society. (iStock)

Certain targeted therapies are being used more with widespread prostate cancer, according to the doctor, as they include "more powerful anti-androgens, which works not just on the testes, but on the adrenals as well."
Hormone therapies have "significant side effects," including fatigue, and "don’t always help," he added.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Siegel said the study’s strength was its combination of a randomized treatment group with Decipher testing, which helped identify in advance which patients were most likely to respond to intensive hormone therapy.
"This is the personalized, precise approach of the near future," he said.
Many men, but not all with high-risk localized prostate cancer, will have a cancer recurrence after local therapy, according to Dr. Dahut. (Getty Images )
Dr. William Dahut, M.D., chief scientific officer at the American Cancer Society, noted that many men with high-risk localized prostate cancer will have a recurrence after local therapy.

"This study shows that by combining drugs that interfere with the male hormone testosterone with standard therapy, the risk of cancer recurrence decreases," the Maryland-based doctor, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Traditionally, if a more intensive therapy benefits some patients, it is offered to all men — even though only a subset may actually benefit, according to Dahut.

"However, a diagnostic test can greatly improve the treatment experience for a patient by potentially only subjecting patients to more intensive therapies whose genomic test predicts the greatest risk of recurrence," he said.
Dahut encouraged patients to speak with their doctors about intensive therapy to decrease the risk of cancer recurrence, as well as to ask about available genomic testing.

The doctor noted that since the study was conducted with a drug to block testosterone and the oral drug abiraterone, it's "unclear whether the Decipher test would be as accurate with other possible combinations that a patient might receive."

Prostate cancer is the second-leading cause of cancer death behind lung cancer, according to the American Cancer Society. About one in eight American men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in their lifetime.

title: People living past 100 in one tiny village share 3 daily habits
summary: National Geographic's potential blue zone in Sardinia's Bolotana has 10 centenarians among 2,262 residents, and their plant-based diet holds secrets.
story: Blue Zones Founder Dan Buettner explores why women in a small Italian village are reaching age 100 at remarkable rates, highlighting the importance of friendships, shared responsibilities and everyday movement.
National Geographic researchers believe they may have discovered a new "blue zone."

A blue zone is a geographic region where residents show unusually high rates of longevity and survival into old age. The newest blue zone candidate is a small village called Bolotana, located on the Italian island of Sardinia.
In a 2024 snapshot, 10 of the village's 2,262 residents were at least 100 years old, according to National Geographic — roughly 10 times the Sardinian average and 11 times the U.S. average.
PEOPLE WHO LIVE TO 100 HAVE 3 DRINKS IN COMMON, LONGEVITY EXPERT SAYS
A team of researchers, including Dan Buettner — founder of Blue Zones, a company focused on longevity, and a National Geographic Fellow — set out to investigate Bolotana’s exceptional lifespan.
The findings were published in Frontiers in Aging.
Bolotana’s hilly streets encourage residents to walk as part of their daily routines. (Marisa Montibeller)
Buettner highlighted three lifestyle habits that are common among Bolotana’s long-lived residents.
They move throughout the day: Residents walk steep streets to shops, cafés, workplaces and friends’ homes.
They eat a largely plant-based diet: Beans, vegetables, wheat, olives and olive oil are traditional staples.
They stay socially connected: Residents regularly gather with friends, family and neighbors through meals, church and community activities.
"Here, men are participating more, and that could explain why women are doing better."
The study did not establish that these habits directly cause longevity, but researchers are examining how the village’s environment and traditions may contribute to its unusually high survival rates.

"The international team of demographers, their population scientists … were able to examine the birth records, death records and baptismal records and see that this is probably the richest, most complete data on centenarians in the world," Buettner told Fox News Digital.
AMERICA'S LIFESPAN HAS DOUBLED SINCE 1776 — EXPERTS REVEAL WHAT CHANGED
"For those of us who want to make it into our 90s and 100s in full health, this place does it better than anyplace else in the world."
The strongest longevity advantage appeared among Bolotana’s women, who ranked second only to Hong Kong for life expectancy at age 70 and survival from age 70 to 100.
Bolotana, Sardinia, is home to ancient olive groves. (Marisa Montibeller)
What sets Bolotana apart

The original Sardinian blue zone was identified in the late 1990s and formally described in research published around 2000. Located in the mountainous region roughly 68 miles from Bolotana, it is known for unusually strong male longevity, according to Buettner.

Although Bolotana remains partly pastoral, it is also an agricultural community. Buettner suggested that this may mean men spend more time at home helping with household responsibilities, potentially reducing the burden on women.
Dan Buettner, middle, is pictured with two centenarian women of Bolotana. (Marisa Montibeller)

"In the original blue zone in the highlands, the [women] worried about the finances and raising children and the leaky roof," he said. "They're all alone. Here, men are participating more, and that could explain why women are doing better, because they're only bearing half the stress load instead of almost all of it."
Buettner believes the village’s strong social connections may be one factor behind the women’s longevity, although the study did not establish a cause.
GEORGIA WOMAN CELEBRATES 112TH BIRTHDAY, REVEALS HER SECRET TO A LONG LIFE

"We see women gathering in the library, baking bread together, making sweets together and going to church together," he said. "So, you see a much more socially connected society among the women in Bolotana than in the other blue zones."
As in many parts of Italy, Bolotana has a strong Catholic tradition. Buettner said church attendance may provide residents with faith, social connection and a sense of belonging.
Bolotana church culture connects its residents to faith and to each other. (Marisa Montibeller)

"It’s a sense of community, but it's also people proactively understanding that sitting down with a friend and talking about your troubles and your day with somebody who cares about you is a much more powerful drug than a pharmaceutical," Buettner said.
"The human species has shown this over and over, and Bolotana is a perfect example."
The Bolotana diet
Diet varies among blue zones, but Bolotana’s traditional fare is largely plant-based, with a focus on beans, vegetables, wheat, olives and olive oil, along with some cheese and meat.
DOCTOR'S 10 RULES FOR LIVING LONGER, CELEBRATING MORE BIRTHDAYS AND MAKING EXTRA YEARS COUNT
"About 90% of a centenarian's diet has been all plant-based," Buettner said. "Not protein, by the way. These aren't protein loaders. These are complex carbohydrate loaders."
Dan Buettner prepares a traditional minestrone with Anna Maria Filia in Bolotana. (Marisa Montibeller)

A Bolotanese breakfast might consist of a piece of bread or cheese with local olives and a cup of coffee. Lunch, the biggest meal of the day that starts in the early afternoon, is "almost always" a minestrone soup made with locally grown seasonal vegetables and lots of beans.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Beans are the cornerstone of the longevity diet here," Buettner said. "Garbanzo beans, lentil beans, pinto beans, cannellini beans — these are really the all-star of the diet."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Traditionally, residents ate meat about five times per month, usually as a celebratory food.
In the highlands, people traditionally cooked with lard, Buettner said, while Bolotana residents use olive oil from ancient trees.

Giaccomo Nieddu maintains an ancient olive grove in Bolotana. The oil contains unusually high levels of odd-chain fatty acids, which researchers are studying for possible links to longevity. (Marisa Montibeller)
Researchers are studying whether the oil’s unusually high levels of odd-chain fatty acids could be relevant to longevity.
‘Not chasing’ longevity
Bolotana residents are not deliberately pursuing longer lives, the longevity researcher noted. The region has little emphasis on gym culture or biohacking.
"These are real humans with an average set of genes," Buettner said. "These aren’t superhumans with superhuman discipline or better genes."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"They’re not chasing longevity," he added. "It is the product of their environment."
Because Bolotana’s streets are steep and residents rarely drive within town, they typically walk to shops, cafés, workplaces and friends’ homes, Buettner said.
"It’s this sort of unconscious walking that’s far more important for longevity than going to the gym."
Bolotana residents walk steep hills for everyday tasks and socialize regularly. (Marisa Montibeller)
Buettner said Bolotana is an example of how daily routines and surroundings can encourage movement without requiring residents to schedule formal exercise.
Residents of walkable American communities have a three- to five-year life-expectancy advantage over those in less-walkable areas, he said.
Centenarians Salvatore and Nina spend time socializing daily in Bolotana. (Marisa Montibeller)

"If we want a healthier America, we have to start thinking about shaping our neighborhoods and our cities so people can unconsciously move and not rely on heaping another obligation on their busy lives to remember to go to the gym," the expert said.

"Most of the things that lead to Bolotana longevity are also pleasant and make the journey a joy," he added.

title: Sharpen memory and fight brain fog with simple 60-second trick from a neurologist
summary: Dr. Rhonda Voskuhl explains why crosswords and sudoku miss the mark for brain fog and which timed word games actually target verbal memory loss.
story: Estrogen loss during menopause can affect verbal memory, processing speed and focus. A neurologist shares why targeted brain exercises may be more helpful than random cognitive games for addressing specific challenges.
Brain games, crosswords and math puzzles are often promoted as ways to sharpen memory, but neurologists warn that generic exercises may not address the specific cause of mental fog.
Dr. Rhonda Voskuhl, a professor of neurology at UCLA and co-founder of Cleopatra RX in Los Angeles, says brain exercises only work if they target the specific mental function that is slowing down.
"You can’t just do random cognitive exercises," Voskuhl told Fox News Digital at the Livelong Women’s Health Summit in New York City in September. "They’ve got to fit the problem."
DOCTOR REVEALS '10-YEAR RULE' FOR EVALUATING BRAIN FOG AND DEMENTIA SYMPTOMS
The problem, she said, is verbal memory. "Doing math is not going to help … You need an exercise that will help you with words."
Generic brain games like Sudoku or number puzzles often fail to clear up mental fog because they do not target the specific brain functions that are slowing down. (iStock)
Mental fog — especially the kind triggered by midlife hormone changes during perimenopause and menopause — impacts very specific areas of the brain, according to Voskuhl.

When estrogen levels drop, overall intelligence and basic logic remain completely normal. Instead, the brain takes a hit in two main areas: verbal memory (recalling names and words) and processing speed (thinking quickly under pressure), experts say.
FORGETTING NAMES AND LOSING KEYS MAY SIGNAL SOMETHING OTHER THAN DEMENTIA
Games like Sudoku and other number puzzles primarily exercise logic and math skills, so they may not improve word-recall difficulties.

"It’s not a global problem with the brain," Voskuhl said. "It’s not global brain atrophy, but there are some regions on MRIs and research studies that show that the hippocampus, the memory area, will have some atrophies, some functional connection issues."
Effective cognitive training must match the person's specific weakness, a neurologist said. (iStock)
To understand why word-based exercises may help, it is useful to distinguish between the following two stages of memory, experts say.
DAILY EATING HABIT LINKED TO BETTER BRAIN HEALTH IN OLDER ADULTS, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS
Encoding: How the brain takes in and stores new informationRetrieval: How the brain pulls up that stored information when it's needed
Encoding: How the brain takes in and stores new information
Retrieval: How the brain pulls up that stored information when it's needed
Brain fog typically affects retrieval, not encoding. The word or name is still stored safely in the memory, but the brain's search engine is running slowly.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Building a better brain workout
To effectively target brain fog, Voskuhl says exercises need to focus on two things: finding words and working quickly.
"It’s basically processing speed," she said. "So you need an exercise that is going to be something that makes you rush, makes you do it quickly."
Midlife mental fog from estrogen loss affects localized brain areas tied to verbal memory and processing speed while leaving overall IQ, math logic and general reasoning intact. (iStock)
The following types of exercises target processing speed and active word recall.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Timed word games: Set a 60-second timer to list as many words in a single category as possible (like naming animals or foods).Speed reading and quick summaries: Read a short article quickly, then immediately summarize it out loud in two or three sentences.Rapid recall drills: Use flashcards or picture prompts to name objects or people as fast as possible without pausing.
Timed word games: Set a 60-second timer to list as many words in a single category as possible (like naming animals or foods).
Speed reading and quick summaries: Read a short article quickly, then immediately summarize it out loud in two or three sentences.
Rapid recall drills: Use flashcards or picture prompts to name objects or people as fast as possible without pausing.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Experts recommend focused exercises built around speed and active word recall, such as timed category drills, flashcard recall, and rapid reading summaries. (iStock)
Instead of using generic puzzle apps, Voskuhl recommends paying attention to where you stumble in daily life and picking games that match those challenges.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

People "know themselves," she said — "what they are bad at or what they used to be good at and now they’re not as good at ... Once you know those things, you should think about what kind of games [to play]. You can play around with different games. You can see if it pushes you."

title: Selena Gomez's vaping admission highlights hidden health risks doctors say millions face daily
summary: Selena Gomez called vaping "stupid" after it altered her voice, but doctors warn the health risks go beyond vocal cord damage for millions.
story: High-potency nicotine, constant puffing and difficult withdrawal can make vaping hard to quit. Addiction experts explain why some users return to cigarettes—and how treating dependence may help break the cycle.

When Selena Gomez revealed to her millions of followers that heavy nicotine vaping had noticeably altered her voice, calling the habit "stupid," her confession highlighted a larger issue with the practice.

For the singer and actress, the physical toll manifested in her vocal cords. But medical professionals emphasize that her experience is only a visible symptom of a deeper health crisis affecting millions of Americans who use e-cigarettes every day.

While often marketed as a safer alternative to conventional cigarettes, e-cigarettes pose significant health risks. Aside from the immediate vocal strain and airway inflammation noted by otolaryngologists, major health institutions warn that regular vaping exposes the body to a cocktail of toxic chemicals, cardiovascular strain and respiratory risks.
SELENA GOMEZ WARNS FANS AFTER VAPING HABIT LEAVES HER WITH PERMANENT CONSEQUENCE
Specialists emphasize that e-cigarettes deliver more concentrated doses of nicotine than traditional cigarettes, rapidly driving chemical dependency in the brain.

"With e-cigarettes and vaping, you can get a very high dose of nicotine, and that directly correlates to addiction and how difficult it can be to break these patterns," Trent Carter, a nurse practitioner and CEO of Renew Health in New Mexico, previously told Fox News Digital.
Selena Gomez’s public admission about vaping altering her voice underscores that vocal strain is merely one sign of broader health damage. (Getty Images)
Carter notes that high nicotine intake without traditional smoke can carry its own health consequences.

"It can lead to sleep disturbances, increased anxiety, and if you have underlying cardiac problems or high blood pressure, it’s going to raise your heart rate and elevate your blood pressure, leading to all sorts of issues."

According to the American Lung Association, the aerosol produced by e-cigarettes contains fine chemical particles, heavy metals such as nickel and lead, and organic compounds. Over time, inhaling these irritants can trigger chronic airway inflammation, irreversible lung tissue scarring, and obstructive pulmonary conditions.
NEVER SMOKED A CIGARETTE? YOU COULD STILL BE AT HIGHER RISK FOR LUNG CANCER
A major concern among physicians is the chemical composition of e-liquids. Even nicotine-free formulas contain flavorings and solvent agents like propylene glycol and vegetable glycerin.
When heated by the device’s coil, these liquids break down into toxic compounds, including formaldehyde and acrolein, both known to damage cellular structures in the respiratory system.
The continuous, all-day accessibility of vape devices creates a seamless behavioral routine that can lead to hundreds of puffs daily. (iStock)

Doctors stress that because modern e-cigarettes have only been widely used for a little over a decade, long-term health consequences are still unclear. While immediate effects may appear as hoarseness, coughing, or reduced athletic endurance, the larger impact poses risks to long-term vital organ function.
For many attempting to quit vaping, traditional tools like nicotine patches or gum can fall short because they don't address the psychological habit.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"While a patch or gum can help with physical cravings, if you aren't addressing the behavioral aspect, you're missing a huge component," Carter said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Beyond physical cravings, high-dose nicotine consumption elevates heart rate and blood pressure while exacerbating issues like anxiety and sleep disruption. (iStock)
"Vaping can become constant throughout the day. Subconsciously, you might not even realize how frequently you're doing it, or that you're using it to cope with underlying anxiety or lack of sleep."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
For those inspired by Gomez, health professionals urge people to seek comprehensive support rather than simply switch nicotine delivery methods.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The goal shouldn't be to find another way to consume nicotine, it should be to treat the dependence itself," said Carter.

title: Catholic drinking habits are changing as Americans rethink alcohol's risks
summary: Catholic adults now report drinking rates near the levels of Protestants as shifting health views and social habits reshape moderate drinking in America.
story: Josh Gowin explains how research has shifted the understanding of alcohol's health risks, including its association with reduced brain volume, as drinking habits and social norms continue to change.

A historic shift in American drinking habits shows Catholic alcohol consumption reaching record lows, though scientific experts caution against attributing the drop strictly to religious or cultural changes.
The share of Catholic adults in the United States who report drinking alcohol has fallen to 55%, according to a Gallup report authored by analyst Frank Newport.
That marks a decline from the 2002–2004 period, when 79% of Catholics reported consuming alcoholic beverages. Over that same timeframe, self-reported Protestant drinking rates remained flat at 54%.
HEAVY DRINKING SURGES AMONG AMERICANS IN ONE AGE GROUP AS OTHER GENERATIONS CUT BACK
"Drinking has dropped significantly within both the group of those who have no religious identity and, in particular, among Catholics," Newport wrote in the analysis.
However, experts urged caution when drawing sweeping conclusions from subgroup survey data.

Dr. Joshua Gowin, an associate professor in the Department of Radiology at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus who studies alcohol's effects on the brain, noted that self-reported polling figures can fluctuate based on sampling.
Historically, Catholics were far more likely to drink than Protestants, but a sharp drop in Catholic drinking has completely eliminated that long-standing gap. (iStock)
"There's definitely a general pattern of alcohol use decreasing across groups," Gowin told Fox News Digital.
"As far as the subgroups go, it wasn't clear or necessarily compelling to me that one group was showing a broad trend that wasn't reflected in the other groups," he went on.
BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG
"It seemed like really only one data point showed that effect ... which made me a little skeptical that this is a broader phenomenon versus a single survey sample."
Despite methodological limitations in tracking specific religious subgroups, researchers agree that broader social and health trends are driving a shift in overall drinking habits.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Gallup findings indicate that a majority of Americans now view moderate drinking — defined as one or two drinks per day — as bad for their health.
In the latest polling, 52% of Catholics said moderate alcohol consumption is bad for health, alongside 56% of adults with no religious affiliation and 48% of Protestants.
Perceptions surrounding alcohol health risks have changed, with a majority across all religious demographics now viewing moderate drinking (one to two drinks daily) as bad for their health. (iStock)
Gowin noted that this public shift reflects decades of neuroscience and medical research.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Twenty years ago, there was still kind of a push and pull between some benefits of alcohol and then some things that even then we knew were potentially harmful," he said.
"It's not like the serious problems have gone away."
"Over time, we've gotten a lot more clarity on the things that are bad for our health ... the balance has just shifted more in favor of the evidence for negative health effects."
Gowin pointed out that large-scale neuroimaging studies now consistently link higher alcohol consumption to reduced brain volume, reinforcing public health warnings.
The report’s author cautioned that the drop may reflect normal survey variation rather than a long-term cultural shift. (iStock)
Researchers also attribute shifting consumption patterns to broader societal changes, including shifts in social behavior and loneliness.
Much of America's alcohol consumption has historically occurred in group settings, and changes in how people gather socially may be influencing drinking habits, they believe.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
At the same time, experts caution that a drop in general social drinking does not mean severe alcohol problems have dissolved.

"One of the things that is a bit of a contradiction ... is that although the overall prevalence among all adults is down for the number of drinkers, there is actually a larger number of alcohol-related deaths in the past few years," Gowin noted.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"It's not like the serious problems have gone away."
