title: Brazil’s rapid election count puts spotlight on voting security ahead of US midterms
summary: Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro leads Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva heading into Brazil's runoff as the voting system his father attacked may hand him victory.
story: Footage from a polling station in Rio de Janeiro showed electoral officials retrieving the voting results reports and disconnecting the machines after the first round of voting on Oct. 4, 2026. (Reuters)

SAO PAULO, Brazil— About 125 million Brazilians voted Oct. 4 on machines that print no paper ballots. Less than four hours after polls closed, the country knew its presidential election was headed to a runoff between conservative challenger Flavio Bolsonaro and leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

That process has been in place for over three decades, and Brazilians have become accustomed to its speed, simplicity, accuracy and routine. The system is robustly audited, completely disconnected from the Internet, and is the largest digital voting system deployed on the planet.
Eleven days before the U.S. midterms, Brazil’s system, analysts say, could offer Americans a more secure way to vote.

The system has been widely praised and was also mentioned in President Donald Trump’s 2025 executive order on elections, where he cited Brazil’s biometric voter identification as an example. Yet Brazil’s count runs partially on the kind of paperless machines that the president has vowed to scrap.
STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS
Election workers prepare and seal electronic voting machines ahead of the upcoming general elections in Brasilia, Brazil, on Sept. 23, 2026.  (Mateus Bonomi/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Over the years, Brazil merged federal, state and municipal databases into a digital voting record, whereby voter identity, eligibility and single ability to vote can (and usually must) be verified biometrically. Nearly 9 in 10 voters unlock the machines with a fingerprint.

Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, or TSE, which designs the machines and oversees elections, says there has been no proven fraud since their 1996 debut. The 499,248 machines used on Oct. 4 never connected to the internet. Their software was open to inspection by parties, universities and watchdogs for 11 months before being digitally signed and sealed in public. Last December, the Brazilian government invited a record 149 outsiders to try to break the system; evaluators concluded nothing they found could alter results or reveal how anyone voted.
An electronic voting machine at a Regional Electoral Court (TRE) facility in Brasilia, Brazil, on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026.  (Ton Molina/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
On election day, randomly drawn machines are fed paper ballots on camera as federal auditors and foreign observers watch and specifically track results.

Meanwhile, at closing, every machine used at every polling station prints its tally, which is then posted in front of the polling place with a QR code, so anyone can check it against the national count. In an email to Fox News Digital, TSE said each file’s digital signature "confirms that the result was produced by the electronic voting machine registered for that polling station."

Karina Stange Calandrin, a political scientist and professor at Instituto Brasileiro de Mercado de Capitais (IBMEC), says the system combines three traits rarely found together: voting is electronic, votes hashed to voter eligibility are stored locally in the machine and tallying is automated.

"It is an extremely secure and safe system. The machines never connect to the Internet and even the central database system used to transmit tallied votes to TSE must match results issued physically and locally by each individual machine without human interference," she said. Corrupting it, she added, would require breaking the seal of each machine and installing software that wouldn’t match the TSE’s version, automatically disqualifying its tally — a scale of collusion so large that it "simply could not pass undetected."
COLOMBIA'S 'EL TIGRE' SECURES PRESIDENCY AS LEFTIST RIVAL FINALLY CONCEDES DEFEAT

Brazil's right-wing senator and presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL) gestures next to federal deputy and candidate for governor of Rio de Janeiro, Douglas Ruas (L) during a campaign rally on the eve of the general election, in Campo Grande neighborhood, in the western zone of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil on October 3, 2026. Brazilians go to the polls on Oct. 4, 2026. (Douglas SHINEIDR / AFP via Getty Images)

The machines passed their toughest political test in 2022, when former President Jair Bolsonaro, now serving a 27-year sentence for plotting to overturn his 2022 defeat, spent years attacking their credibility without evidence. Bolsonaro is presently serving time under house arrest.

This year, for the first time, a Bolsonaro appointee ran the TSE: Justice Kassio Nunes Marques. Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, finished first with 47% to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s 45%. The machines at the center of the senior Bolsonaro’s controversy may yet hand victory to his son.

Florencia Ferrer, CEO of e-stategiapublica, which has audited elections in 17 countries, has no doubt the Brazilian system is the most modern and secure in the world. "In India votes are electronic, but each voter gets a printed version of their vote to take home, which weakens voter safety and augments coercion rates," she says, adding that Estonia’s internet voting and the Philippines’ electronically tallied paper ballots carry their own risks.

An engineer from the University of São Paulo’s Polytechnic School who audited the machines in 2014, and declined to be named due to the sensitive nature of his work, agreed. "While no system is completely infallible... we have found no traces of tampering, wrong-doing or malicious intent," he told Fox News Digital.

Still, some defend higher scrutiny. Security researchers say a clean record is not proof enough, and the Carter Center said voters should at least see a printed version of their ballot deposited into a separate area of the machine; otherwise, results integrity rests on software alone. Germany’s top court ruled in 2009 that voters must be able to check their ballot without expert help, effectively barring a Brazilian-like system.
Brazil’s machine has traveled mostly on loan to countries in Latin America, Africa and Asia. Paraguay adopted it permanently in 2006, with machines that now print each individual vote.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Brazil's President and presidential candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (C) waves next to Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin (L) and to his candidate for São Paulo's governor, Fernando Haddad during a campaign rally on the eve of the general election, in São Paulo, Brazil on October 3, 2026. Brazilians go to the polls on Oct. 4, 2026,  (Luis Robayo/AFP Via Getty Images)

"It’s obvious Washington and the remainder of the U.S. are way behind both technology as well as security when it comes to polling on voting day," Ferrer said. U.S. elections are run in thousands of local jurisdictions under 50 sets of state rules and about 30% of 2024 ballots came by mail, which is slower to process. Brazil has one national election authority, compulsory voting and no mail-in ballots.
Brazilians will vote this coming Sunday on Oct. 25. The winner is expected to be known and certified in under five hours.

"The question is not whether Brazil has invented a perfect voting machine. No voting system is perfect. It is whether democracies can combine the speed and consistency of digital tabulation with independent verification, public scrutiny and rules that citizens across the political spectrum have reason to trust," Ferrer said.

Solly Boussidan is an international journalist covering Latin America for Fox News Digital. He has previously covered international affairs, war, finance and travel for several U.S. and international outlets. He is currently based in Brazil.

title: CHAOS INC.: Who's who in the global mayhem network? Communists, Antifa, agitators in the red-green alliance.
summary: The Communist Youth of Greece backed French student protests, linking education demands to anti-austerity activism across Europe and beyond.
story: Violent riots spread across France as 'Big Money in the Morning' breaks down the economic damage and massive arrests. Fox News Digital Senior Editor of Investigations Asra Nomani exposes 'Chaos Inc,' a network of 101 global activist groups, communist organizations and labor unions coordinating the unrest. Nomani highlights how these groups use specialized handbooks to train rioters and amplify chaos.
Fox News Digital's "Who's Who in Chaos Inc." is a living database mapping the organizations, local chapters, international networks and funders organizing or amplifying major protest movements.
The directory identifies each group's mission, ideology, organizational role and documented protest activity, distinguishing direct organizers and participants from supporters and amplifiers.

The database will be continuously updated and organized by country as new organizations, chapters, coalitions and connections emerge, providing a running picture of how local protest movements connect to broader national and transnational networks.

Tens of thousands of secondary school students and their supporters march from Republic to Nation square on Oct. 6, 2026, in Paris, France. Nationwide student protests and violent school riots have disrupted over 700 secondary schools and led to roughly 5,000 arrests across France. What began in late September 2026 as peaceful blockades in the low-income Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis has rapidly escalated into a major public order crisis for President Emmanuel Macron's government. title: White House tempers its tough talk on Canada trade as inflation tops voter concerns
summary: Trump’s combative approach to Canada appears to be softening just days before midterm elections where tariff fueled inflation is a primary concern for voters.
story: The Trump administration’s combative approach to Canada appears to be softening slightly, just days before the midterm elections in the U.S., where tariff-fueled inflation is a primary concern for voters.
Trade talks with Washington have seen a “slight intensification” in recent days, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday.
President Donald Trump, likewise, seemed to back off some of his angrier rhetoric over the weekend, when he told reporters a potential trade deal with Canada would be “settled pretty soon.”
“They’re willing to give us anything at this moment,” Trump added.
Carney, however, said the opposite. “To the extent any progress has been made, it’s because the U.S. is coming closer to our position,” he told reporters in Ottawa.
Ever since advanced trade talks collapsed in August, the Trump administration has slapped 50% tariffs on hundreds of categories of Canadian imports. Ottawa has responded in kind.
But the two leaders’ most recent statements came after the United States unilaterally announced that it would lift some tariffs on Canada late last week and replace them with others.
For Subscribers
The move to alter tariffs came at the urging of Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who is facing a tight re-election battle in Maine.
Control of the U.S. Senate will be decided Tuesday by a handful of very close races, several of them in Canadian border states where polls show Trump’s tariffs are broadly unpopular.
In Alaska, candidates across the political spectrum have called out Trump’s trade war with Canada as a drag on consumers.
The same is true in Michigan, where the Republican nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, has called for an end to the trade war with Canada.
For Subscribers
The economies in all three of these states are deeply intertwined with their Canadian neighbors.
In Washington, a White House official who is not typically involved in trade talks suggested over the weekend that a trade agreement was imminent.
The U.S. and Canada are “very close to finally having a deal,” said Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, on Fox News.
But neither the American nor the Canadian statements since then appeared to support such a sunny reading of the situation.
The Commerce Department, which oversees trade, did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday from NBC News.
“Canada remains in constructive dialogue with our U.S. counterparts on a range of priorities,” said a spokesperson for the minister responsible for trade with the United States.
Meanwhile, Carney said he didn’t know whether the motivations of American officials hoping to revive talks were different this time.
“We have very clear bottom lines, red lines, which meant that we were not willing to sign what was offered in August,” he said Monday.

title: University of Utah apologizes to Pat McAfee after students mock the ESPN host
summary: The University of Utah apologized on Monday to ESPN’s Pat McAfee after a handful of students mocked him as “corny” and “creepy,” triggering the college football personality during his assignment last week to Salt Lake City.
story: The University of Utah apologized on Monday to ESPN’s Pat McAfee after a handful of students mocked him as “corny” and “creepy,” triggering the college football personality during his assignment last week to Salt Lake City.
Students had made moderately disparaging remarks about the former Indianapolis Colts punter, which were taped and published on the school’s Instagram, though the footage has since been deleted.
“We sincerely apologize for creating any perception that Pat was unsafe or unwelcome on our campus,” the university said in a statement on social media.

“Nothing could be further from the truth. Pat and the entire GameDay crew are always welcome at the University of Utah and we deeply appreciate the opportunity ESPN provides to showcase our university and community,” the statement said.
McAfee said he wasn’t annoyed by the actual criticism as much as he was by students being allowed to use the university’s platform to make those points.

“One kid goes, ‘Ah, he’s corny.’ Another kid calls me creepy,” the ESPN personality said on  “The Pat McAfee Show” on Monday. “OK if these kids would have done this on their own blogs, all good. I mean, everybody’s taking shots at me anyways for everything; I get it.”

“The university puts that out,” he continued. “Like, as I’m about to go out and do an infomercial for the place, and then I’m walking in front of thousands of these people. This is how the university feels about it. It’s an uncomfortable feeling. I’m like, I’m getting a lot of shrapnel from a lot of places. The university is putting this out? That something I just had never experienced really in my entire life.”
For Subscribers
McAfee appeared to draw a comparison between himself and right wing provocateur Charlie Kirk, who was gunned down on Sept. 10 last year at Utah Valley University in Orem.
For Subscribers

“I thought to myself, did something else happen pretty scary at a college gathering in the state of Utah recently?” McAfee said. “Like, should we be amplifying reasons why people hate my guts? So I don’t know, it was a lot of mixed feelings.”
McAfee is among the most polarizing figures in modern sports media.
Last year he was forced to apologize to a University of Mississippi student after he amplified a false rumor that she was having an affair with her boyfriend’s father.

title: CDC’s deputy director to depart after four months in the role
summary: Dr. Jennifer Shuford, the CDC’s deputy director, is leaving the agency after less than five months. It’s the latest example of the leadership turnover that has roiled the CDC.
story: Less than five months into her tenure as the deputy director and chief medical officer of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Dr. Jennifer Shuford will leave the agency next month, a spokesperson said.
Her exit is the latest example of the leadership churn that has roiled the country’s top health agencies under the Trump administration.
Shuford’s last day will be Nov. 12, the CDC spokesperson said. In a statement provided on Shuford’s behalf, she said she was leaving to spend more time with her family.
“I am so thankful to President Trump and Secretary Kennedy for giving me the opportunity to help lead CDC. It has been an amazing experience and I will be forever grateful for it,” she said.
The spokesperson said Satish Pillai, who leads the agency’s Ebola response, will serve as acting deputy director and chief medical officer while the CDC looks for a permanent successor.

President Donald Trump announced in April that Shuford had been appointed to CDC leadership, and she started her dual roles in June. Previously, she was Texas’ chief state epidemiologist during the Covid pandemic, then was appointed in 2022 to be commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services. In that role, she oversaw the response to the measles outbreak centered in West Texas last year, which led to more than 750 cases and the deaths of two school-age children.

The CDC has lost several top leaders over the last year and a half. The agency went without a permanent director for about a year after Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. fired CDC Director Susan Monarez in August 2025, just 29 days into the role. The Senate confirmed the current director, Dr. Erica Schwartz, in August.

In February, the CDC’s principal deputy director, Dr. Ralph Abraham, stepped down, and Dr. Allison Arwady, director of the CDC’s National Center for Injury Prevention and Control, announced her departure in June.
The agency also saw a wave of departures last year after Monarez’s firing: Four senior officials resigned, three of whom cited concerns about political interference in the CDC’s scientific process.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Schwartz announced Shuford’s departure in an email to staff Tuesday morning, which was viewed by NBC News.

“I am deeply grateful for Dr. Shuford’s outstanding leadership and commitment to CDC and public health, especially as she has navigated an exceptionally demanding, high-profile, and constantly evolving environment over the past several months,” Schwartz wrote.
Other federal health agencies have also undergone major leadership shake-ups this year.
Calley Means, a central advocate for Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” movement, resigned last week from his senior adviser role at the Department of Health and Human Services.

Dr. Marty Makary also resigned in May from his role as commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration after opposing the Trump administration’s moves to expand access to flavored e-cigarettes. The same month, the FDA’s vaccine chief stepped down, and the leader of the FDA division regulating over-the-counter and prescription drugs said she had been fired.

title: Florida mom arrested after leaving 4 kids home alone during dayslong trip to Vegas
summary: A Florida mom was arrested and charged with child neglect after she left her four kids home alone for nearly three days while she was in Las Vegas, the local sheriff reported Monday.
story: A Florida mom was arrested and charged with child neglect after she left her four kids home alone for nearly three days while she was in Las Vegas, the local sheriff reported Monday.

Irene Miller was busted after a dispatcher received a 911 call on Oct. 21 from one of the kids in the Kissimmee home who reported “that her 9-year-old brother had been injured by a dumbbell that fell on his head,” the Osceola County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement.
When the deputies arrived at the residence, they found four children ages 14, 12, 11 and 9 — and no adults watching over them.
While paramedics took the injured boy to a nearby hospital for treatment of what turned out to be an apparently minor injury, the deputies tracked Miller down by telephone.

“She told the deputy that she was working in Las Vegas and would return on October 23, 2026,” the sheriff’s statement said. “Deputies learned that Mrs. Miller had left for Las Vegas on October 18, 2026.”
Miller, according to the statement, told deputies that she had a babysitter coming from Tampa in the mornings to get the children ready for school and to check on them after school.
Kissimmee is located near Orlando and about 70 miles east of Tampa.
For Subscribers
Miller also said she did not insist that the babysitter stay the night at the house with the children, the statement said.
For Subscribers
While the children were taken to their father’s home, sheriff’s detectives were dispatched “to meet Irene Miller as she exited her flight from Las Vegas on Friday morning,” the statement said.

Miller, 50, was charged with four counts of child neglect without great bodily harm and booked into the Orange County jail. As of Monday, a search of jail records showed that she was no longer behind bars.

​“The Osceola County Sheriff’s Office will not tolerate child neglect,” said Sheriff Chris Blackmon. “These cases will be investigated, and charges will be brought against the parents who are not properly supervising or caring for their children.”

title: Alex Pretti’s parents demand DOJ release evidence of fatal ICE shooting
summary: The parents of Alex Pretti, the ICU nurse and U.S. citizen who was killed in Minneapolis said they were “begging” the Justice Department “to do what is right.”
story: The parents of Alex Pretti, a U.S. citizen and ICU nurse who was fatally shot by immigration officers in Minneapolis nine months ago, slammed the federal government and demanded the release of all the evidence related to their son’s death.

Michael and Susan Pretti said at a news conference Tuesday that the federal government has kept them in the dark for 275 days — even after they sent a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche over the summer “begging for basic information the law affords,” including the identities of the officers involved in the shooting.
Alex Pretti's family calls for government accountability
“At every turn, they have ignored us, misled us and shielded Alex’s killers,” Michael Pretti said.
“We want our son’s killers to be brought into justice once and for all,” Susan Pretti said. “We are here begging for the Department of Justice to do what is right.”
Kiersten Pels, a spokesperson for the Department of Justice, told NBC News that communications between federal officials and victims’ families “do not typically occur” during an investigation.

“As is standard practice, communications with family members, if any, come at a later stage of a case, such as indictment, initial appearance, plea, trial, or sentencing,” Pels said in a statement. “The timing is consistent with how these types of investigations proceed.”
The Department of Homeland Security referred all questions to the FBI.

Tuesday’s news conference comes nearly a week after Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said the federal government stopped sharing information with Minnesota authorities who are investigating Pretti’s killing.

Moriarty’s office sued the Trump administration in March to compel federal officials to share key evidence pertaining to Pretti’s death and the shootings of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan man who was wounded by an ICE officer, and Renee Good, who was fatally shot by another ICE officer.

The three Minnesota shootings took place in January, after the Trump administration deployed more than 3,000 immigration officers and agents to the state as part of “Operation Metro Surge,” the DHS’s largest immigration enforcement operation.

In July, Minnesota officials said the federal government was starting to turn over evidence in the cases, including police body camera video and hard drives containing statements. Moriarty said at the time that she expected to receive “all the evidence.”

That changed this month, according to Moriarty. In a statement last week, she accused the federal government of withholding evidence related to the fatal shootings of Good and Pretti and “obstructing our investigations for however long they can.”

“Our lawsuit was filed to gain access to all of the evidence and our efforts to obtain it will continue. We have filed our motion for summary judgment to bring an end to the case and secure the evidence to which we’re entitled,” Moriarty said. “The federal government responded with a motion to dismiss; their aim is clear.”

In the motion filed by DOJ attorneys at the U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., last week, the federal government argued it has the authority to decline sharing information with state authorities if no formal legal proceedings are underway.

The Trump administration has previously suggested that state prosecutors have no jurisdiction to investigate federal officers, while Minnesota officials have said the federal government can’t be trusted to investigate itself.

“This is not normal. This is not justice. It is morally wrong,” Michael Pretti said at the news conference. He decried that the lack of cooperation between federal and local authorities in investigating his son’s killing “is just baffling, disappointing and reprehensible.”
Steven L. Schleicher, a lawyer for the Prettis who was also at the news conference, said his clients are entitled to see any evidence about the shooting under the Crime Victims Rights Act.
“How is it possible that the Department of Justice is not sharing evidence,” Schleicher said. “What are they hiding?”

During his confirmation hearing in July, Blanche was asked about his commitment to sharing information on the ICE-involved shootings in Minnesota with state officials. He said he expected the investigations into those cases to be run as usual, adding that “the definition of full cooperation can be disputed.”

Videos showing Alex Pretti’s killing haunt his family every day, his parents said. At the same time, according to them, those images were crucial in contradicting the Trump administration’s narrative of the shooting.

“The federal government went on TV and lied about Alex. They tried to slander his memory to cover up their crime,” Susan Pretti said. “Not only was it wrong, it was shameful, unfair, unacceptable. We want to clear our son’s name.”

title: White House tempers its tough talk on Canada trade as inflation tops voter concerns
summary: Trump’s combative approach to Canada appears to be softening just days before midterm elections where tariff fueled inflation is a primary concern for voters.
story: The Trump administration’s combative approach to Canada appears to be softening slightly, just days before the midterm elections in the U.S., where tariff-fueled inflation is a primary concern for voters.
Trade talks with Washington have seen a “slight intensification” in recent days, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday.
President Donald Trump, likewise, seemed to back off some of his angrier rhetoric over the weekend, when he told reporters a potential trade deal with Canada would be “settled pretty soon.”
“They’re willing to give us anything at this moment,” Trump added.
Carney, however, said the opposite. “To the extent any progress has been made, it’s because the U.S. is coming closer to our position,” he told reporters in Ottawa.
Ever since advanced trade talks collapsed in August, the Trump administration has slapped 50% tariffs on hundreds of categories of Canadian imports. Ottawa has responded in kind.
But the two leaders’ most recent statements came after the United States unilaterally announced that it would lift some tariffs on Canada late last week and replace them with others.
For Subscribers
The move to alter tariffs came at the urging of Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who is facing a tight re-election battle in Maine.
Control of the U.S. Senate will be decided Tuesday by a handful of very close races, several of them in Canadian border states where polls show Trump’s tariffs are broadly unpopular.
In Alaska, candidates across the political spectrum have called out Trump’s trade war with Canada as a drag on consumers.
The same is true in Michigan, where the Republican nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, has called for an end to the trade war with Canada.
For Subscribers
The economies in all three of these states are deeply intertwined with their Canadian neighbors.
In Washington, a White House official who is not typically involved in trade talks suggested over the weekend that a trade agreement was imminent.
The U.S. and Canada are “very close to finally having a deal,” said Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, on Fox News.
But neither the American nor the Canadian statements since then appeared to support such a sunny reading of the situation.
The Commerce Department, which oversees trade, did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday from NBC News.
“Canada remains in constructive dialogue with our U.S. counterparts on a range of priorities,” said a spokesperson for the minister responsible for trade with the United States.
Meanwhile, Carney said he didn’t know whether the motivations of American officials hoping to revive talks were different this time.
“We have very clear bottom lines, red lines, which meant that we were not willing to sign what was offered in August,” he said Monday.

title: Motorist led astray by GPS in Georgia stumbles upon house fire and saves sleeping family of 14
summary: A large Georgia family survived flames that completely destroyed their house — thanks to a Good Samaritan who stumbled upon the blaze after his GPS took him a different way home.
story: A large Georgia family survived flames that completely destroyed their house — thanks to a Good Samaritan who stumbled upon the blaze after his GPS took him a different way home, officials said Tuesday.

Firefighters in northwest Georgia were called at 11:58 p.m. on Oct. 17 and rushed to 28 Rowlls Road, where they found the structure completely engulfed by flames, Lyerly Fire Chief Tim Deberry told NBC News.
James and Larita Burke, their 11 adopted children and one grandchild made it out safely with a helping hand from 37-year-old motorist Casey Sparks, officials said.

Sparks had been playing softball that day in Dalton, Georgia, and was headed home to Concord, Alabama, when his GPS kept putting him on Georgia State Route 114, a highway he had not used on the way up.
“I redid my GPS like two or three times and it kept telling me to go that way,” Sparks told NBC News. “So it’s like ‘All right, I guess we’re going this way.’”
A short time later, Sparks spotted flames near Lyerly, which is about 60 miles south of Chattanooga, Tennessee.
“It was a glow, like a bonfire,” he said. “I mean you could see the glow from the fire from the hill.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Sparks rolled up to the scene and spotted a teenage boy fighting a losing battle against flames with a garden hose.
“The whole front of the house had caught on fire, so there was no point in even trying to help him put it out,” said Sparks, a welding equipment repairman. “It was too far gone.”
Before rushing into the house, Sparks said he told his 13-year-old son to call 911.
Deberry said Sparks likely saved lives with his fast action.

“He had actually come in, opened the door, started yelling, ‘Get out, the house is on fire!’ and started getting them out of the house,” the fire chief said. “If they would have been in there for probably no more than five more minutes, there would have been fatalities.”
Sparks recalled spotting a little girl in a hospital bed, grabbing her and handing her to a neighbor outside.

“I scooped her up and tried to go out the door that I came in, but it was completely engulfed,” Sparks said. “So I found another door and went outside and handed her over the fence and then went back inside to help get everybody else out. “
Sparks said he was never in fear during those tense moments, but working on adrenaline and trying to stay focused on the task at hand.
“We’re  from the South, man, and we help each other. We help our neighbors,” Sparks said. “I mean, I would hope somebody would do the same for me.”
James Burke, 58, told NBC affiliate in Chattanooga WRCB that he’s grateful for Sparks and the motorist’s seemingly uncooperative GPS.

“He was on the wrong road. His GPS put him on the wrong path,” Burke said. “He’s never been down that path before, and he said he knew that something was bringing him down that road when he saw the fire from the top of the hill; he knew he had to take action. I’m so thankful that he did.”
Burke told the outlet he fell asleep in his recliner that night as the rest of his family were in their beds. He said he woke up to a stranger yelling at him in his living room.
“The next thing I know, some guy was telling me in my living room, ‘Hey, you’ve got to get out of here. Your house is on fire,” he told WRCB.
Sparks said he can laugh now at the frustration he felt in the moment on that late night of Oct. 17.  Now Sparks believes a divine hand was working OT to put him on that road through Lyerly.
“Now I see it, I wasn’t putting two and two together at the time,” he joked. “I was seeing we had three hours to drive and I guess we’re going this way.”

title: Neil Young sues for the second time over Trump’s use of ‘Rockin’ in the Free World’
summary: Rock star Neil Young filed a $10 million lawsuit on Monday over President Donald Trump’s use of his song “Rockin’ in the Free World” at campaign events — the second time the artist has sued over Trump’s use of his music.
story: Rock star Neil Young filed a $10 million lawsuit on Monday over President Donald Trump’s use of his song “Rockin’ in the Free World” at campaign events — the second time the artist has sued over Trump’s use of his music.
In the five-page filing, Young’s lawyers say the artist “has suffered damage to his reputation and brand as a result of the implication that he supports Donald J. Trump in any way.”

The lawsuit was filed in federal court in Virginia against the Trump 47 Committee, a joint fundraising committee, alleging copyright infringement over president’s repeated use of his hit song, specifically mentioning an October rally in Ohio.

“Rockin’ in the Free World is a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten,” the lawsuit says.

Monday’s lawsuit marks the latest instance of musicians condemning Trump’s use of their songs without their permission. Young has previously criticized the playing of his songs during the president’s political events, and he sued over Trump’s use of “Rockin’ in the Free World” and another song, “Devil’s Sidewalk,” in 2020. That lawsuit, filed against Trump presidential campaign, was settled shortly after it was filed, Young’s team said.
“Rockin’ in the Free World” offers a criticism of societal inequities, which Young’s team pointed out in the lawsuit.

“The lyrics paint vivid street-level portraits — a mother discarding her baby, addicts lost in despair, garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity — while the repeated chorus delivers a savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn’t shared by all,” the lawsuit said. “In short, the Song is the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for.”
For Subscribers
Reached for comment, the White House referred NBC News to the Republican National Committee. Neither a spokesperson for the RNC nor “Trump 47” immediately responded to a request for comment.
For Subscribers

Several other artists have previously pushed back on Trump’s or the White House’s use of their music. After the White House used artist Kesha’s music in a military-themed social media post just weeks before the start of the Iran war, she said in a post that she did “NOT approve of my music being used to promote violence of any kind.”
Olivia Rodrigo also hit back at the Trump campaign for using her music in a video, writing in a post, “Ew don’t use my sound ever again ty.”

Last year, Sabrina Carpenter called a White House video on apparent immigration enforcement actions that used her music “evil and disgusting,” telling the White House, “Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda.”

One important part of cleaning your vacuum will include cleaning and/or replacing your vacuum’s filter, as Knoll mentions. Many vacuums come with reusable filters, but if you’re due for a new filter and happen to have the Shark Navigator Lift Away, one of the most popular upright vacuums on the market, you should consider this filter replacement.

The filter is compatible with more than 20 versions of the Shark Navigator Lift Away, so if you have one, chances are it is compatible. It includes two HEPA filters, four foam filters and four felt filters which, combined, help sift out dust, pet dander and more, according to the brand.
Why do you have to clean a vacuum?

It’s important to clean your vacuum regularly because doing so will ultimately help it do  its job effectively and for as long as possible. “A vacuum with things stuck in the hose or a dirty filter can really affect how well it works,” says Knoll, who says he and his team go through tons of vacuums.
Cleaning your vacuum means more than emptying out the dust bin, too — for a thorough clean, you should also remove, if possible, the brush roll, nozzle, hose, filter, and attachments.
How do you clean a vacuum?

The steps for cleaning different types of vacuums may vary slightly depending on whether it is an upright, cordless or robot vacuum, but for the most part, many of them have some of the same parts: brush roll, filter, hose and crevice and/or upholstery attachments. Below are some of the most general steps you should take to clean your vacuum.

For upright vacuums, unplug the appliance. For cordless and robot vacuums, be sure to remove the battery. Identify the main parts of the vacuum, including the brushroll, filter, suction head, hose, dust bin and attachments. These are the main parts to clean. Some of them are easier to clean if you remove them, while others, like the brush roll, aren’t necessarily, so you don’t have to remove it to clean it, according to Knoll.

If possible, find and remove the filter, dust bin and attachments, says Knoll. “Most of these things come apart relatively easily,” he says. “For modern vacuums like Shark, Dyson, and Bissell, you’ll usually have clearly labeled tabs/switches, so you can flip them and remove the dust bin, brush roll, hoses, or filters.”

Start with the dust bin. “It’s a little different for each, but for most dust bins, there are two locking clasps on the right and left sides of the bin that you need to flip to remove it,” says Knoll. Manually remove as much debris, dust and dirt as possible and empty it into the trash. Rinse out the dust bin with a small amount of warm water. Spray the inside with a small amount of Dawn Platinum Powerwash Dish Spray, rinse it out again and then dry with a microfiber cloth.

Move onto the filter of the vacuum. “The filter usually sits above or under the dust bin. If it’s disposable, toss it and get a new one,” says Knoll. “If it’s reusable (most are these days), add a little drop of mild Dawn dish soap and run some water through it.” It’s extremely important to allow the filter to dry completely before reattaching it and using the vacuum, because it can grow mildew and create odors, according to Knoll.

Clean the brush roll, hose and attachments of the vacuum (if applicable). You don’t have to remove the brush roll to make it easier to clean, according to Knoll. “If you turn the vacuum over, you’ll usually see hair wrapped around the brush roll,” says Knoll. “Use scissors to cut between the bristles, then pull the hair out. If you’re having trouble getting the hairs out, cut more, or grab an old hairbrush or a metal tool made for getting hair strands out of bristles, to pull them out.”

To clean the hose and attachments, use an object to push out any lodged debris that may be inside. Knoll says he rolls a ping pong ball through the hose to be sure nothing is lodged. Try using something like a long-handled brush, like the Desin Flexible Drain Brush Set, to push debris out of the other end of the hose. After, follow the steps above and rinse it with warm water and a small amount of mild dish soap, and dry it completely before reattaching.
How long should a vacuum last?

Your vacuum’s longevity heavily depends on how often you use it and how you maintain it. As a professional home cleaner, Knoll says he and his team use vacuums at least three to four times a day, and they last around two years at least, but this is more than the average person. “That said, civilian vacuums used every two to four weeks should easily last three to five years,” he says. “Some traditional upright vacuums can last as long as 10 years. A traditional Sanitaire Tradition upright can last this long.”
How do you know when it’s time to replace your vacuum?

Before you decide to spend money on another vacuum, it’s important to make sure you’ve done your due diligence when it comes to vacuum maintenance to determine if it’s ready to be thrown out, according to Knoll. “If you clean the filters, remove any clogs, check the brush roll, and it barely picks anything up, it’s probably time to start looking into a new vacuum. Overheating is another sign, or if it repeatedly shuts off,” he says. “This is usually a sign of a failing motor, and the motor is one of the few pieces that are really hard to replace.”
How often should you change your vacuum’s filter?

It depends on the type of filter, according to Knoll. “Disposable vacuum filters should be changed every six to 12 months,” he says. “For reusable/washable filters, I’d clean them every two to three vacuuming cycles. For foam filters, I’d check them monthly and replace them when they start to break down or no longer clean properly.”

Frequently asked questions

You can use an artificial tree  for an average of ten years, but most can last up to twenty years if cared for properly, says Jami Warner, executive director of the American Christmas Tree Association.

To store your tree, Warner recommends keeping it in a box or bag to prevent dust and dirt from accumulating, and to protect the branches and foliage. It’s also important to store your tree in a cool, dry place and away from direct sunlight — strong sunlight could lead to discoloration over time. Additionally, Warner says storing your tree with a container of baking soda or unused coffee grounds, which can absorb odors, may keep it smelling fresh.

Any way you look at it, “the impact of a real or artificial tree on the environment is negligible,” says Bert Cregg, a professor at Michigan State University’s Department of Horticulture and a researcher of Christmas tree production, culture and genetics. “Both of these have next to no impact when you look at it compared to what most people do in the rest of their lives.”

But because you can reuse artificial Christmas trees for years, you might think they’re more eco-friendly than live trees that you have to  dispose of after the holiday season. Alternatively, since artificial Christmas trees are largely made from plastic, they can end up in landfills when they’re trashed.Many studies have been conducted around the topic, including some commissioned by the American Christmas Tree Association.

If you’re concerned about sustainability in regards to your Christmas tree selection, Cregg recommends buying a live tree from a locally owned family farm or reusing an artificial tree as many times as you can before purchasing a new one. You can also often buy artificial trees secondhand. If you plan to replace your artificial tree while it’s still in good condition, you should try to donate it rather than throw it away, says Warner.

For those who suffer from certain allergies, bringing a live Christmas tree into the home during the holiday season can cause irritation, says Dr. Nina Shapiro, a pediatric ear, nose and throat specialist at Westside Head and Neck in California. Does this mean that artificial trees are better for those with allergies? Not necessarily: You can have the same reaction to an artificial tree, according to Shapiro.

“Real or artificial, the allergic reaction may be due to contaminants such as mold, ragweed pollen and dust rather than the tree itself,” says Shapiro. And for artificial trees:  “the longer the tree stays in the home, the more likely dust and mold develops, making people more susceptible to allergies,” she says.

To help reduce allergic reactions, Shapiro recommends  wiping down your tree — real or artificial — with a wet cloth or using a towel and a spray bottle filled with water before setting it up. The same goes for ornaments and lights, as well as other decorations you place around your home.

If you can, clean your tree and other decorations outside your home, which helps prevent dust and other allergens from releasing inside. And when it’s time to store your artificial tree, consider investing in a storage bag with a tightly zipped seal to prevent moisture and dust from getting in.

Branches and needles of a live Christmas tree aren’t great for pets. If they eat either of those or drink the water a real tree sits in, pets might experience anything from a mild upset stomach to more severe symptoms like organ failure (which is possible for a pet who ingests plant fertilizer), according to Dr. Zay Satchu, chief veterinary officer and co-founder of Bond Vet. This aligns with guidance we found from the FDA, ASPCA and American Veterinary Medical Association.

Pets sometimes see Christmas trees — real or artificial — as toys. They do the same with ornaments, lights, tinsel and other decorations — all of those items can be dangerous if ingested, according to Satchu. He recommends consulting ASPCA’s Animal Poison Control to learn about the potential dangers of seasonal plants and other items before decorating your home, as well as asking your vet for additional guidance before bringing anything new into your home this holiday season.

Aluminum artificial Christmas trees add a retro look to your home, which explains why they’re making a bit of a comeback, according to Warner. That said, it’s important to decorate aluminum Christmas trees carefully since they are flammable. This means you should avoid using traditional lights to embellish it.  “Aluminum can conduct electricity really well but can be a bit dangerous, as it can cause voltage spikes or even fire hazards because the metal branches could short circuit the lights,” says Warner. “But don’t despair as there are options such as LED lights or, for a funky, retro vibe, a color wheel that shines colors on the tree without any direct contact. And battery-operated lights are another safe bet.”

title: Alexander brothers, ex-luxury real estate brokers, to be sentenced on federal sex trafficking charges
summary: Federal prosecutors are seeking life sentences for Oren, Alon and Tal Alexander.
story: Two former luxury real estate brokers and their brother were each sentenced to 30 years in federal prison, seven months after they were convicted of drugging and raping women in a sex trafficking ring.

Federal prosecutors sought life sentences for Oren and Alon Alexander, a pair of former powerful real estate brokers, and their brother, Tal, in a New York City courtroom Tuesday afternoon. Attorneys for the brothers, who have asserted their innocence, asked the judge to give the men the mandatory minimum instead.

U.S. District Judge Valerie Caproni characterized the brothers as “Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde.” On one side they were described as gentlemen who loved their children, she said, and on the other described as “sadistic, misogynistic, sexual predators.”
“Your conduct was monstrous,” Caproni said in her sentencing.
But Caproni added that she did not believe the Alexander brothers were beyond redemption, declining the request to give them life sentences.

The men were found guilty in March of 10 counts, including conspiracy to commit sex trafficking and sex trafficking by force, after a trial that included testimony from 11 women who described being lured, drugged and sexually assaulted over a period of years.
Six of the women were part of the indictment.

In a sentencing memo, prosecutors in New York’s Southern District said more than 70 women came forward with allegations of abuse and accused the brothers of exploiting their wealth, influence and connections to target victims.

Victim statements from 11 women, some using court-assigned pseudonyms, were read at the hearing prior to the judge’s decision. The women asked the judge to impose a sentence that was appropriate for the profound impact the men had on their lives.
One victim, Maya Miller, described the trauma of her rape by Tal Alexander as having settled into her nervous system.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
“I carry a quiet funeral inside me,” Miller said.

Another victim, Olivia Lane, told the judge that she was “profoundly incapacitated” and after having a fraction of one drink while meeting Oren Alexander. She described being raped at least a dozen times while being terrified and in pain.
She then directly addressed the men.
“You are weak, you are inhumane,” Lane said. “You never had power and look at you now.”

Two women described the men as having almost inhuman eyes during their assaults. Isa Brooks said, “Their eyes went black during the attack like I was being mauled by animals.” Lane said, “I remember looking at him and seeing a monster, black eyes.”

The women also emphasized the Alexander brothers’ lack of remorse or acknowledgment of their victims throughout the trial. Victim Katie Moore noted in her statement that after five weeks of trial and being found guilty, the men “cannot even look us in the eye as we speak today.”
“These men spent years treating women and girls like their humanity meant nothing,” Moore said.
The brothers honed their methods together, attacking women in a way that was designed to humiliate and degrade them, prosecutor Elizabeth Espinosa said at the sentencing.

“When they were done, they bragged to each other and their friends ... the defendants knew exactly what they were doing and they did it anyway and they did it over and over and over again,” Espinosa said.

At trial, prosecutors said the brothers raped the women after having promised them parties and trips. One woman testified that she lost control of her body after she had a drink with Alon Alexander at a New York City club.
When she awoke, she testified, they were naked on a bed. She kept trying to get up, and he kept pushing her back down, she said.
When she told him that she didn’t want to have sex with him, she testified, he responded, “‘You already did.’”

In a sentencing submission, attorneys for the brothers acknowledged that they sometimes behaved insensitively toward women but categorically denied that any of them had raped or sexually assaulted anyone.
At trial, the attorneys described the sex as consensual and said the women were motivated in part by financial gain.
“All the stories were rehearsed,” Tal Alexander’s attorney, Deanna Paul, said in her closing argument. “They’re looking for money.”

Paul urged the judge to consider giving her client the mandatory minimum of 15 years in prison, saying that the jury’s verdict has not changed the attorney’s view of the evidence. The defense lawyer said that 15 years is already an extraordinary punishment, so “what would another 20 or 30 years accomplish?”

Attorneys for the other two brothers similarly asked the judge to give the men 15 years. Marc Agnifilo, who represents Oren Alexander, told the judge that the men all stopped their “sexually aggressive” behavior after meeting their wives.
“All three defendants stopped, and that matters,” Agnifilo said.
Each of the brothers were given an opportunity to address the court directly before he issued his sentence.
Oren Alexander was the first to ask the judge for a lighter sentence. He once again denied the assaults in his comments before telling the judge that he has built a new life and family.
“My son needs me and I need to be there for him and I ask your honor to impose the minimum sentence,” he said.

Tal Alexander was next to speak and expressed regret over his past actions. “The person who stands in court is not the same man as before,” he said, asking the judge to consider the entirety of his life in the decision.

“I wish I showed more maturity,” he said. “I cannot undo moments when I was immature and careless with other people’s feelings. I understand the jury found me guilty and I know words cannot change that.”
The last brother to speak, Alon, insisted that he was innocent and that he had never raped any women. He invoked his two young daughters when asking for the mercy of the court.
“I am afraid of being Daddy in the photograph,” he said.

Caprio appeared unmoved by their statements, emphasizing that the rapes were not a result of “party culture or hookup culture” as they described. The judge noted that it was not enough to rape the women, the brothers sought to humiliate them.

“That marriage would transform them from sexual predators to normal gentlemen, I disagree,” Caprio said. “Rape is about power ... having a girlfriend or a wife doesn’t mean you are not going to rape or humiliate women.”

title: Florida police called to youth soccer game after alleged dispute involving 3-year-old player
summary: It was supposed to be a fun weekend soccer game for children.
story: It was supposed to be a fun weekend soccer game for children. Instead, an alleged dispute involving a 3-year-old player ended with police being called to a Florida park, footage of which has since gone viral online and sparked outrage.
The Winter Park Police Department said in a statement that officers responded to a call from a soccer league official alleging a disturbance involving the child’s parents.

Nevada Pierre’s parents insist the 3-year-old was “scorned” for playing too well at a game Saturday, according to the police report. But the game’s sports league director argued the child was removed “due to behavior” and said his “unruly parents” were “upset with their son’s playing time,” the police report said.
Officers determined the “incident was a civil matter between those parties and not criminal. No one was arrested, trespassed, or forced to leave the park,” police added in a statement.
“The league requested the family leave and offered to refund the league cost to the family,” police said Monday. “The family stated the game was over and they were leaving.”
“The family was cooperative with the officers,” police added.

The dispute, however, has long since left the soccer field, and video footage of young Pierre weaving between players and scoring goals has gone viral online, along with the call to police as the incident has gained steam.
High-profile children’s educator and entertainer Ms. Rachel labeled the incident “sick.”
“The police were called on a 3-year-old Black boy because he’s too good at soccer. He was kicked out of the league. The cops showed up at the game,” Ms. Rachel wrote online. “I’m LIVID!”
She then invited Pierre onto her popular children’s show to “share his amazing skills.”
“I need my sports people to show up!!! This is racist, sick, traumatizing and disgusting,” Ms. Rachel said.
Civil rights attorney Ben Crump also posted on X decrying the incident.
For Subscribers
“A 3-year-old was allegedly removed from a youth soccer league because he was too good,” Crump wrote. “If this child was punished for excelling, what message does that send to every young athlete?!”
For Subscribers

Former professional football quarterback Robert Griffin III also expressed his outrage. “Calling the cops on a 3-year-old is crazy,” he said, labeling Pierre a “soccer phenom.” He added, “Punishing a 3-year-old child for being too good at a sport is ridiculous.”
i9 Sports, the organization behind the youth soccer program, said in a statement to NBC News that it is reviewing the incident.

“We are aware of concerns being shared regarding an incident at a local i9 Sports program, and we take them very seriously,” the group said, adding that it “reached out to the family and have begun a review that includes speaking with those involved.”
“The respectful treatment and well-being of every child and family matter deeply to us,” the program added.

In the 911 dispatch call obtained by NBC News, the local league official is heard saying, “I just have an unruly parent here,” referring to Pierre’s mother as “just really really disruptive.” He then accused her of “following me around and calling me names and in front of this whole bunch of people.”
In an interview with ABC News, Pierre’s mother, Martasia Griffin, said that she merely “spoke up” for her son and that the family was left feeling “embarrassed” after police were called to the game.
In videos shared on Pierre’s official Instagram page, his parents show snippets of him playing and say the toddler scored 10 goals at the weekend game, despite being taken off early.

“The league kicked Nevada out because every week no one could take the ball from him some of the parents for the other team didn’t feel that it was fair, mind you he is a 3 year old playing with 5 years old,” a statement alongside a video on his page said.

title: Alex Pretti’s parents demand DOJ release evidence of fatal ICE shooting
summary: The parents of Alex Pretti, the ICU nurse and U.S. citizen who was killed in Minneapolis said they were “begging” the Justice Department “to do what is right.”
story: The parents of Alex Pretti, a U.S. citizen and ICU nurse who was fatally shot by immigration officers in Minneapolis nine months ago, slammed the federal government and demanded the release of all the evidence related to their son’s death.

Michael and Susan Pretti said at a news conference Tuesday that the federal government has kept them in the dark for 275 days — even after they sent a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche over the summer “begging for basic information the law affords,” including the identities of the officers involved in the shooting.
Alex Pretti's family calls for government accountability
“At every turn, they have ignored us, misled us and shielded Alex’s killers,” Michael Pretti said.
“We want our son’s killers to be brought into justice once and for all,” Susan Pretti said. “We are here begging for the Department of Justice to do what is right.”
Kiersten Pels, a spokesperson for the Department of Justice, told NBC News that communications between federal officials and victims’ families “do not typically occur” during an investigation.

“As is standard practice, communications with family members, if any, come at a later stage of a case, such as indictment, initial appearance, plea, trial, or sentencing,” Pels said in a statement. “The timing is consistent with how these types of investigations proceed.”
The Department of Homeland Security referred all questions to the FBI.

Tuesday’s news conference comes nearly a week after Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said the federal government stopped sharing information with Minnesota authorities who are investigating Pretti’s killing.

Moriarty’s office sued the Trump administration in March to compel federal officials to share key evidence pertaining to Pretti’s death and the shootings of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan man who was wounded by an ICE officer, and Renee Good, who was fatally shot by another ICE officer.

The three Minnesota shootings took place in January, after the Trump administration deployed more than 3,000 immigration officers and agents to the state as part of “Operation Metro Surge,” the DHS’s largest immigration enforcement operation.

In July, Minnesota officials said the federal government was starting to turn over evidence in the cases, including police body camera video and hard drives containing statements. Moriarty said at the time that she expected to receive “all the evidence.”

That changed this month, according to Moriarty. In a statement last week, she accused the federal government of withholding evidence related to the fatal shootings of Good and Pretti and “obstructing our investigations for however long they can.”

“Our lawsuit was filed to gain access to all of the evidence and our efforts to obtain it will continue. We have filed our motion for summary judgment to bring an end to the case and secure the evidence to which we’re entitled,” Moriarty said. “The federal government responded with a motion to dismiss; their aim is clear.”

In the motion filed by DOJ attorneys at the U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., last week, the federal government argued it has the authority to decline sharing information with state authorities if no formal legal proceedings are underway.

The Trump administration has previously suggested that state prosecutors have no jurisdiction to investigate federal officers, while Minnesota officials have said the federal government can’t be trusted to investigate itself.

“This is not normal. This is not justice. It is morally wrong,” Michael Pretti said at the news conference. He decried that the lack of cooperation between federal and local authorities in investigating his son’s killing “is just baffling, disappointing and reprehensible.”
Steven L. Schleicher, a lawyer for the Prettis who was also at the news conference, said his clients are entitled to see any evidence about the shooting under the Crime Victims Rights Act.
“How is it possible that the Department of Justice is not sharing evidence,” Schleicher said. “What are they hiding?”

During his confirmation hearing in July, Blanche was asked about his commitment to sharing information on the ICE-involved shootings in Minnesota with state officials. He said he expected the investigations into those cases to be run as usual, adding that “the definition of full cooperation can be disputed.”

Videos showing Alex Pretti’s killing haunt his family every day, his parents said. At the same time, according to them, those images were crucial in contradicting the Trump administration’s narrative of the shooting.

“The federal government went on TV and lied about Alex. They tried to slander his memory to cover up their crime,” Susan Pretti said. “Not only was it wrong, it was shameful, unfair, unacceptable. We want to clear our son’s name.”

title: Motorist led astray by GPS in Georgia stumbles upon house fire and saves sleeping family of 14
summary: A large Georgia family survived flames that completely destroyed their house — thanks to a Good Samaritan who stumbled upon the blaze after his GPS took him a different way home.
story: A large Georgia family survived flames that completely destroyed their house — thanks to a Good Samaritan who stumbled upon the blaze after his GPS took him a different way home, officials said Tuesday.

Firefighters in northwest Georgia were called at 11:58 p.m. on Oct. 17 and rushed to 28 Rowlls Road, where they found the structure completely engulfed by flames, Lyerly Fire Chief Tim Deberry told NBC News.
James and Larita Burke, their 11 adopted children and one grandchild made it out safely with a helping hand from 37-year-old motorist Casey Sparks, officials said.

Sparks had been playing softball that day in Dalton, Georgia, and was headed home to Concord, Alabama, when his GPS kept putting him on Georgia State Route 114, a highway he had not used on the way up.
“I redid my GPS like two or three times and it kept telling me to go that way,” Sparks told NBC News. “So it’s like ‘All right, I guess we’re going this way.’”
A short time later, Sparks spotted flames near Lyerly, which is about 60 miles south of Chattanooga, Tennessee.
“It was a glow, like a bonfire,” he said. “I mean you could see the glow from the fire from the hill.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Sparks rolled up to the scene and spotted a teenage boy fighting a losing battle against flames with a garden hose.
“The whole front of the house had caught on fire, so there was no point in even trying to help him put it out,” said Sparks, a welding equipment repairman. “It was too far gone.”
Before rushing into the house, Sparks said he told his 13-year-old son to call 911.
Deberry said Sparks likely saved lives with his fast action.

“He had actually come in, opened the door, started yelling, ‘Get out, the house is on fire!’ and started getting them out of the house,” the fire chief said. “If they would have been in there for probably no more than five more minutes, there would have been fatalities.”
Sparks recalled spotting a little girl in a hospital bed, grabbing her and handing her to a neighbor outside.

“I scooped her up and tried to go out the door that I came in, but it was completely engulfed,” Sparks said. “So I found another door and went outside and handed her over the fence and then went back inside to help get everybody else out. “
Sparks said he was never in fear during those tense moments, but working on adrenaline and trying to stay focused on the task at hand.
“We’re  from the South, man, and we help each other. We help our neighbors,” Sparks said. “I mean, I would hope somebody would do the same for me.”
James Burke, 58, told NBC affiliate in Chattanooga WRCB that he’s grateful for Sparks and the motorist’s seemingly uncooperative GPS.

“He was on the wrong road. His GPS put him on the wrong path,” Burke said. “He’s never been down that path before, and he said he knew that something was bringing him down that road when he saw the fire from the top of the hill; he knew he had to take action. I’m so thankful that he did.”
Burke told the outlet he fell asleep in his recliner that night as the rest of his family were in their beds. He said he woke up to a stranger yelling at him in his living room.
“The next thing I know, some guy was telling me in my living room, ‘Hey, you’ve got to get out of here. Your house is on fire,” he told WRCB.
Sparks said he can laugh now at the frustration he felt in the moment on that late night of Oct. 17.  Now Sparks believes a divine hand was working OT to put him on that road through Lyerly.
“Now I see it, I wasn’t putting two and two together at the time,” he joked. “I was seeing we had three hours to drive and I guess we’re going this way.”

title: Authorities launch manhunt for convicted killer who escaped from Tennessee prison
summary: Jacob Allen Morley, 28, is alleged to have stolen a Ford F-350 flatbed truck after breaking out, state prison authorities said.
story: Authorities in Tennessee launched an intense manhunt for a convicted murderer who they said escaped from a state prison, stole a work truck and remains on the loose.

Jacob Allen Morley, 28, escaped from the state’s Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville sometime before he was reported missing at 11:30 p.m. Sunday, prison officials said in a statement Monday.
“Further review of security cameras confirmed Morley breached the perimeter fence and exited the facility in his TDOC uniform,” the Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement.
By 1 a.m. Monday, he is alleged to have stolen a white Ford F-350 flatbed truck in the city of about 3,500, about 100 miles north of Memphis, state law enforcement and corrections officials said.

Tiptonville is near the Mississippi River and the state line with Missouri. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation placed Morley on its most-wanted list and asked residents of the city to check for any video they may have of him.
“Residents are urged to check home security systems, including doorbell cameras and trail cameras, for any sightings of Morley or the stolen truck,” the bureau said in a statement.

Security video shows a man in a beanie walk around the rear of the vehicle to the driver’s side door of the flatbed truck. It then shows the truck’s windshield wipers moving before the truck is driven away.
Morley is 5 feet, 11 inches tall and weighs 240 pounds, the Correction Department said.
It said a reward of up to $2,500 is available to anyone who has information leading to his capture. Anyone who sees him is asked to immediately call 911 or 1-800-TBI-FIND.

Morley fatally shot his co-worker Cody Birchfield, 34, in the back of the head in 2022, according to court documents shared by the Carter County Clerk’s Office. Birchfield’s body was found in a large metal box under Morley’s residence, the documents say.
Morley was convicted in February 2025 and sentenced to life behind bars.
He was also convicted of abuse of a corpse, tampering with evidence and aggravated burglary — the latter for stealing tools from the victim, according to the court documents.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Morley was described at trial as a “loner,” the clerk’s office said. He claimed self-defense and said he had mental health issues, including bipolar disorder.

title: Neil Young sues for the second time over Trump’s use of ‘Rockin’ in the Free World’
summary: Rock star Neil Young filed a $10 million lawsuit on Monday over President Donald Trump’s use of his song “Rockin’ in the Free World” at campaign events — the second time the artist has sued over Trump’s use of his music.
story: Rock star Neil Young filed a $10 million lawsuit on Monday over President Donald Trump’s use of his song “Rockin’ in the Free World” at campaign events — the second time the artist has sued over Trump’s use of his music.
In the five-page filing, Young’s lawyers say the artist “has suffered damage to his reputation and brand as a result of the implication that he supports Donald J. Trump in any way.”

The lawsuit was filed in federal court in Virginia against the Trump 47 Committee, a joint fundraising committee, alleging copyright infringement over president’s repeated use of his hit song, specifically mentioning an October rally in Ohio.

“Rockin’ in the Free World is a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten,” the lawsuit says.

Monday’s lawsuit marks the latest instance of musicians condemning Trump’s use of their songs without their permission. Young has previously criticized the playing of his songs during the president’s political events, and he sued over Trump’s use of “Rockin’ in the Free World” and another song, “Devil’s Sidewalk,” in 2020. That lawsuit, filed against Trump presidential campaign, was settled shortly after it was filed, Young’s team said.
“Rockin’ in the Free World” offers a criticism of societal inequities, which Young’s team pointed out in the lawsuit.

“The lyrics paint vivid street-level portraits — a mother discarding her baby, addicts lost in despair, garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity — while the repeated chorus delivers a savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn’t shared by all,” the lawsuit said. “In short, the Song is the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for.”
For Subscribers
Reached for comment, the White House referred NBC News to the Republican National Committee. Neither a spokesperson for the RNC nor “Trump 47” immediately responded to a request for comment.
For Subscribers

Several other artists have previously pushed back on Trump’s or the White House’s use of their music. After the White House used artist Kesha’s music in a military-themed social media post just weeks before the start of the Iran war, she said in a post that she did “NOT approve of my music being used to promote violence of any kind.”
Olivia Rodrigo also hit back at the Trump campaign for using her music in a video, writing in a post, “Ew don’t use my sound ever again ty.”

Last year, Sabrina Carpenter called a White House video on apparent immigration enforcement actions that used her music “evil and disgusting,” telling the White House, “Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda.”

title: Amid 2028 speculation, Wes Moore urges Marylanders to back him on redistricting
summary: Maryland’s Democratic governor is fighting a tough campaign in his state — and it’s not his re-election effort.
story: BALTIMORE — Maryland Gov. Wes Moore is expected to cruise to re-election on Nov. 3. But he’s sweating the campaign nonetheless.

Moore’s political prowess is being tested at home beyond his own race for a second term, as Maryland voters prepare to take sides on a ballot question that would allow state Democratic leaders to redraw congressional district lines in a way that favors the party even more than the current 7-1 map.

Moore and his allies — including former President Barack Obama — are framing a vote for the ballot question as a vote to fight back against President Donald Trump and Republicans, an argument that might usually be expected to find purchase in a deep-blue state.

But it has become apparent in recent weeks that support for the ballot measure may not be as strong as Moore and other Maryland Democrats had hoped, and a major late effort has ramped up to promote passage of the measure. If it doesn’t pass, it would be a major political setback for Moore amid wide speculation that he’s gearing up for a potential 2028 presidential campaign.

Moore and his allies in Annapolis sought to redraw congressional districts this year, arguing that the Legislature could draw a map with all eight districts favoring Democrats to replace the current map in the wake of GOP redistricting efforts elsewhere.

But the effort was halted by state Senate President Bill Ferguson, a fellow Democrat who claimed that the push didn’t have the support of a majority of lawmakers in his chamber. Ferguson noted that Maryland Democrats tried to draw a more favorable congressional district map in 2021, only for a state judge to toss it out in 2022.

The ballot measure stemmed from that, seeking to address the state constitutional issue that sank the 2021 map first. In August, Ferguson and other Democrats in the Legislature overwhelmingly moved to put a measure before voters to eliminate the requirement that Maryland’s congressional districts obey natural boundaries, like the Chesapeake Bay. The state’s lone GOP U.S. House member, Andy Harris, represents a district concentrated on the state’s Eastern Shore.
After a legal challenge, Maryland’s Supreme Court allowed the question to be put to voters in a form rewritten by state judges.
With Election Day closing in, passage of the ballot question is far from certain.

A poll released this month by the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, found that a majority of likely Maryland voters (53%) planned to vote against the measure. That included 42% of Democrats, 74% of Republicans and 59% of unaffiliated voters who planned to vote no.

“To me, there was a broader underlying, interesting question about democracy. Do people want district lines to favor one party over the other? And most Marylanders don’t like that idea,” Mileah Kromer, the director of the UMBC Institute of Politics, told NBC News.
Kromer’s survey used plain language instead of the legalese that will appear on the ballot defining Question 3 and still found broad opposition from members of both parties and independent voters.

“Certainly there are a lot of Democrats who want to see some fighting back against President Trump but maybe don’t believe that, you know, redrawing congressional district lines just to favor their outcome is the way that they’d like to do it,” Kromer said.

She added that part of the reluctance of Maryland voters in particular is the fact that Democrats would gain only one seat in redistricting efforts. A similar measure that passed in California last year allowed the state to redraw congressional district lines in a way that gained Democrats advantages in five seats, overriding the state’s independent redistricting commission just months after Texas redrew its congressional maps to boost Republicans in an additional five seats.
A national fight over district lines
The two states’ moves last year set off yet more state redistricting efforts this year. A number of red states succeeded in redrawing their maps, while others still face legal challenges.

A longtime Democratic strategist in Maryland also pointed to the fact that Maryland voters are usually especially well-informed about national politics, particularly those who live in counties that border Washington.

“I wonder if there aren’t a lot of people in the state, Democrats in particular, who don’t feel like co-opting the Republican strategy of mid-decade redistricting is the best way to fight back,” said the strategist, who, like others in this article, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “If they heard anything in the news about mid-decade redistricting, it’s about, you know, Republicans or Donald Trump breaking the rules. They may not be that comfortable with that.”
Still, Kromer cautioned that the UMBC survey was conducted before the groups backing and opposing the ballot question began spending heavily on TV, digital and physical advertising.

Maryland’s Democratic voters are “upset about the Trump administration, and the messaging of, like, fighting back against Trump could be a really, really good messaging strategy,” Kromer said. “It might actually knock people more into the attitude of ‘I don’t like it, but it’s necessary.’”
After the poll was released last month, Moore and his allies began spending in earnest to persuade voters to support the ballot measure.

So far this month, Fight Back MD, a group supporting the measure, has spent $550,000 on TV ads urging voters to vote in favor of Question 3, according to AdImpact. Last week, Moore’s campaign decided to switch advertising from promoting his re-election bid to urging voters to support the measure.
But even raising money among Democrats to support the measure has been an uphill battle, with the redistricting divide between Moore and Ferguson still present behind the scenes.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Moore’s campaign released an ad last week featuring some of the state’s Democratic leaders urging voters to support Question 3, which was backed by a $700,000 investment by the campaign. On Monday, the campaign used an additional $500,000 on a TV and digital ad featuring Obama telling voters to support Question 3.

One state leader noticeably absent from the push is Ferguson. While he worked in August to convene a special session to pass a measure to put the redistricting question to voters, he hasn’t publicly or privately committed to pursue redistricting during next year’s legislative session if it passes next month.

Meanwhile, some donors who had expressed interest in the redistricting campaign have shown hesitation to donate this fall because Ferguson refuses to commit to passing new congressional maps, according to an operative familiar with the pro-Question 3 campaign.

Ferguson’s communications director, David Schuhlein, told NBC News that Ferguson “is primarily focused on retaining our Democratic state Senate seats and also trying to build on that and gain one or two more in a couple of districts throughout the state, and that takes an immense effort from him and the rest of our leadership team.”
“That’s where most of his efforts have been focused from the primary till now,” Schuhlein added.
Redistricting on the 2028 campaign trail
Moore in recent years has demurred about his potential presidential aspirations, but his out-of-state travel schedule has fueled speculation.
